articles.title: Cognitive-Affective Factors Associated with Psychological Distress in Young Adults: A Cross-Sectional Structural Equation Modelling Study
articles.authors: Rose Seneviratne; Matt Garner; Emma Claire Palmer-Cooper
articles.abstract:
Objectives: To examine concurrent associations among cognitive-affective factors associated with psychological distress in young adults. 
Methods: Cross-sectional structural equation modelling was conducted in a community sample of 841 young adults aged 18 to 30 years. Psychological distress was specified as a latent factor indicated by depressive symptoms (PHQ-9), anxious symptoms (GAD-7), and perceived stress (PSS-10). Mindfulness facets (FFMQ), metacognition (MSAS-18), resilience (ER89), and creativity (RDCA) were entered into two models with alternative structural orderings. Model fit was evaluated using the CFI, TLI, RMSEA, SRMR, AIC, and BIC.
Results: Model 1 showed acceptable-to-good fit (CFI = .98, TLI = .94, RMSEA = .07, SRMR = .03) and better comparative fit than Model 2 (CFI = .97, TLI = .90, RMSEA = .09, SRMR = .06). Model 1 statistically accounted for 53.9% of the variance in latent psychological distress. Acting with awareness (β = -.29), nonjudging (β = -.39), and nonreactivity (β = -.20) showed unique negative associations with distress, whereas observing showed a small positive association (β = .08). Resilience showed a direct negative association and negative indirect associations in configurations involving acting with awareness, nonjudging, and nonreactivity. Metacognition showed negative indirect associations involving acting with awareness and nonreactivity. Creativity showed a bivalent pattern: a positive indirect association involving observing and a negative indirect association involving nonreactivity.
Conclusions: Acting with awareness, nonjudging, and nonreactivity showed the clearest unique associations with lower psychological distress in young adults. These findings identify candidate self-regulatory capacities for prospective testing in preventive and therapeutic intervention research.

articles.title: “It’s not that I don’t have a life, it’s that I choose to have many”: A Qualitative Exploration of Video Gamers’ Perceived Motivations for Gaming and their Impact on Psychological Health.
articles.authors: George Farmer; Tom Buchanan; Nina Smyth; Tina Cartwright
articles.abstract: While several factors have been highlighted as either facilitators or inhibitors of basic psychological needs in video gaming, there is little evidence to identify the specific mechanisms by which these effects operate. Using qualitative semi-structured online interviews with 15 video game players (MAge = 38.28, SD = 12.65) and analysed using Reflexive Thematic Analysis, this study explored experiences in video games and gaming culture that provided either a source of need satisfaction or need frustration. Participants discussed experiences that provided a sense of competence, mood management, social connection, and positive disengagement, as well as experiences that could be unfair, unpleasant, toxic, or generally stress-inducing. This study highlights specific factors that promote positive well-being and contribute to negative well-being in players and illustrates less-explored experiential factors that are vital to video gaming as a psychologically restorative activity.

articles.title: The Association Between Family-Related Variables and Cross-Cultural Adaptation: A Meta-Analytical Review and Migrant Family Adaptation Framework
articles.authors: Kinga Bierwiaczonek; Aisha Vogel; Dinh-Hung Vu; Colleen Ward; Rongtian Tong; Mike W.-L. Cheung; Nora C. G. Benningstad; Evita Willemiek van Duin; Karine Lindholm; Jonas R. Kunst
articles.abstract: With global migration at an all-time high, understanding the role of family-related factors in cross-cultural adaptation is crucial yet underexplored. This paper proposes a new Migrant Family Adaptation Framework and reports a meta-analysis of the association between a large set of family-related variables and cross-cultural adaptation with data from 449 studies (Nparticipants = 308,335; neffects = 1,174) conducted between 1988 and 2022. Specifically, we tested nine broad categories of family-related variables underpinning key processes of family resilience (family cross-cultural adjustment, family functioning, lack of family-work conflict, family support, contact with family, presence of family, relationship status, family characteristics, and family attitudes towards living abroad) and three adaptation outcomes (overall, psychological, socio-cultural). Three-level models showed that family cross-cultural adjustment was the strongest and most consistent predictor of migrants’ overall, psychological, and socio-cultural adaptation. In terms of more nuanced sub-indicators, family satisfaction, spousal support, low family conflict, and positive family attitudes towards living abroad showed robust effects. Effects were comparable across migrant, refugee, student, and expatriate samples, except that the effect of family support was stronger for expatriates than migrants, whereas family presence mattered more for migrants than expatriates. Comprehensive sensitivity checks (excluding studies at risk of bias, unpublished reports, and statistical outliers) left the pattern and magnitude of effects virtually unchanged. No evidence of small-study or publication bias was observed. Theoretical implications in light of the new theoretical framework, directions for future research, and policy implications are discussed.

articles.title: Fifteen Years of Child-Centered Long-Form Recordings: Promises, Resources, and Remaining Challenges to Validity
articles.authors: Alex Eguiluz; Loann Peurey; Marvin Lavechin; Tarek Kunze; Manel Khentout; Lucas Gautheron; Emmanuel Dupoux; Alejandrina Cristia
articles.abstract: Audio-recordings collected with a child-worn device are a fundamental tool in child language research. Long-form recordings collected over whole days promise to capture children’s input and production with minimal observer bias, and therefore high validity. The sheer volume of resulting data necessitates automated analysis to extract relevant metrics for researchers and clinicians. This paper summarizes collective knowledge on this technique, providing entry points to existing resources. We also highlight various sources of error that threaten the accuracy of automated annotations and the interpretation of resulting metrics. To address this, we propose potential troubleshooting metrics to help users assess data quality. While a fully automated quality control system is not feasible, we outline practical strategies for researchers to improve data collection and contextualize their analyses.

articles.title: Morphosyntax sans sight: Development of linguistic structure in blind toddlers
articles.authors: Lillianna Righter; Erin Elizabeth Campbell; Elika Bergelson
articles.abstract:
Part of language development necessarily involves connecting sensory input
with linguistic units. We asked whether visual input in particular was differ-
entially relevant for learning words and building grammar. While substan-
tial prior work (e.g. Bates & Goodman, 1997) confirms a tight link between
grammar and the lexicon, there could in principle be different degrees of
reliance on a visual referential world across them. To begin to tackle this
large question, we examined the productive morphosyntax skills of young
blind children (N=28, 14-55mo.), each matched to a sighted child of the
same productive vocabulary size, based on a parent-reported vocabulary and
early grammar checklist. We asked whether blind children’s morphosyntactic
skills were similar, advanced, or delayed relative to sighted vocabulary-size-
matched peers. We found no differences between blind and sighted children
across 6 morphosyntax measures. Blind children did show a delay in produc-
tive morphosyntax skills relative to sighted children, and this delay (roughly
9 months) was statistically longer than the delay reported for spoken vo-
cabulary in this same group (Campbell, Casillas, & Bergelson, 2024). We
also found that both age and vocabulary strongly predicted morphosyntax
scores for sighted children, but only vocabulary size (and not age) robustly
predicted morphosyntax for blind children. These results extend seminal
research in early language development in blind and sighted children (e.g.
Landau & Gleitman, 1985), highlighting close vocabulary to syntax links in
early childhood across groups, and supporting the idea that vision does not
contribute separably to either facet of language development.

articles.title: Quantifying context-dependent meaning representations: a novel procedure
articles.authors: Elena Mainetto; Hanneke den Ouden; Danny Merkx; Lisa I. Horstman; Naomi de Haas; Mona Garvert; Andrea E. Martin; Roshan Cools; Xiaochen Zheng
articles.abstract: Our brains house representations of word meaning that are constrained by both the form and the sentence context of the word. For example, when hearing the sentence “They deposited cash at the bank”, we do not think about the bank of a river. These context-dependent meaning representations enable cognitive flexibility. Existing studies aimed at isolating such meaning representations have confounded them with operational processing requirements, due to reliance on inferential and surprisal effects during natural language comprehension. We introduce a novel symbol-based procedure for disentangling context-sensitive word meaning representations from the processing demands of word meaning inference. Participants were instructed to learn associations between sentence-constrained meanings of homonyms (“They deposited cash at the [bank]”) and symbols. Explicit word meaning representations were successfully captured by a task that required the spatial arrangement of these symbols based on their associated word meaning, with smaller distances between symbols representing the same meaning than between symbols representing different meanings. Contrary to the spatial arrangement task, in a priming task assessing implicit word meaning representations related to the same symbols, there was no evidence for semantic meaning priming of reaction times. This work provides a novel experimental procedure for measuring explicit word meaning representations in a manner that can be disentangled from changes in word meaning inference, but raises questions about the suitability of the priming task used for uncovering implicit meaning representations.

articles.title: TAIL: A Test of AI Literacy for Adolescents and Teachers
articles.authors: Tomas Lintner; Ivan Ropovik; Lukas Plch; Adam Klocek; Libor Juhaňák
articles.abstract: Most instruments that claim to measure AI literacy inquire how competent people feel rather than test what they know, and almost none has been validated for both students and teachers. We developed the Test of AI Literacy (TAIL), a multiple-choice test of AI literacy built on an established four-aspect framework and piloted with cognitive interviews and item analysis. We evaluated it among Czech secondary-school students tested in fall 2025 (n = 2,441) and six months later (n = 1,669; 897 linked across the two measurement waves), and among teachers (n = 564). In every sample the items fitted a one-factor model, whereas the four content aspects could not be distinguished as separate factors. Three weakly discriminating items were removed after the first wave, leaving a 17-item form with internal consistency of .79 to .87 and item response theory reliability of .80 to .84. Item parameters were almost identical across waves. Six-month test-retest reliability was .63, with a standard error of measurement of 2.4 points. Teachers scored .41 standard deviations above students, and teachers of information and communication technologies, grammar-school teachers, and students with a university-educated parent scored higher, as predicted. Teachers' self-rated AI self-efficacy was practically unrelated to their tested knowledge, and students who used and relied on AI more knew less about it. TAIL is a short, knowledge-based measure that places adolescents and their teachers on one scale.

articles.title: Trilingual language control – interference patterns in mixed ability speakers reveal a complex interaction between age of acquisition and proficiency
articles.authors: Maya Thille; Sophie Slaats; Alexis Hervais-Adelman
articles.abstract: A widely accepted framework in multilingual control is the inhibitory control model (ICM, Green, 1998). According to this framework, the level of inhibition required to suppress a language is dependent upon the dominance of that language, such that a more dominant language requires more inhibition. A study by de Bruin and colleagues (2023) evaluated L1 and L3 intrusions in L2 target trials in a speeded trilingual picture naming task, reporting more intrusions from L3 than L1, consistent with lower inhibition of L3. Here, we expand on this and investigate whether patterns of cross-linguistic interference and reaction times (RT) in all three languages can be accounted for by the ICM. Furthermore, we explore how proficiency and age of acquisition (AoA) influence these patterns. Sixty-nine participants with some proficiency in English (NL1=22), French (NL1=21), and German (NL1=26) completed a trilingual speeded picture naming task. Patterns of intrusions did not fully align with a dominance-based inhibitory account: L2 produced more intrusions than (expected) L3 in L1 target trials. Analysis of the role of proficiency and AoA showed that intrusions are more likely between languages with similar proficiencies and AoAs, with an interaction such that languages with mismatched profiles (early AoA/low proficiency or late AoA/high proficiency) are most likely to intrude. RT patterns revealed asymmetric switch costs and a large influence of AoA. The pattern of results points to the need for a more nuanced understanding of the factors influencing how languages are accessed and controlled, beyond the construct of an ordinal dominance hierarchy.

articles.title: When You See Is Not Always When You Move: Preview Availability Influences Movement Control and Visual Search in Human Multi-Target Foraging
articles.authors: Danilo A. Kuhn; Jan Tünnermann; Anna Schubö
articles.abstract: In real-world tasks, such as picking berries from a bush or assembling a LEGO® set, actors frequently search for multiple targets while also planning and executing movements. We investigated how a preview, that is, the availability of visual information during trial instructions, influenced target selection behavior. We hypothesized that preview availability would improve movement planning and execution compared to no preview. Participants were asked to pick LEGO® bricks of a specific color and place them into predefined areas, with the placing precision varying between trials (collect, sort, pile). We assumed that higher precision requirements would delay movement onset, especially without a preview. Interestingly, results showed a consistent impact of preview availability only for those participants who first performed the task without a preview: These participants initiated their movements faster without a preview but also reached less directly and took longer to complete a trial, suggesting greater reliance on feed-back control rather than feedforward planning. Overall, participants preferred selecting a large, more easily graspable target first when a preview was available, indicating that preview availability aided target selection. Finally, the longest delay in movement onset was observed in the pile condition regardless of preview availability. This suggests that participants considered placing precision requirements already when preparing a search-and-place sequence. In sum, we found no evidence for a general benefit of preview availability for movement preparation or execution in a real-world selection task. Instead, preview benefits emerged mainly when a preview followed prior experience without one.

articles.title: Affordance-Based Control in Driving Behavior: Integration of Perception and Action by Extending rho Coupling and Satisficing
articles.authors: Takayuki Kondoh; Hiroyuki Mishima; Nobuhiro Furuyama
articles.abstract: Action-control models in ecological psychology have evolved from pursuing a single optimal solution toward affordance-based control within safety regions. However, mathematically integrating these approaches with rho coupling theory remains insufficient. This study theoretically re-examines the "risk feeling formula (RFF)"—a linear sum of two optical variables derived from real-world driving data. Our analysis demonstrates that the RFF is structurally equivalent to rho coupling, yet its "intercept" distinctly functions as a "satisficing" threshold. Rather than representing an internal computational compromise, this threshold signifies direct perceptual attunement for initiating avoidance behavior while maintaining a safety margin. Furthermore, we propose an integrated mathematical representation of affordances as the linear sum of two action-scaled pi values, reflecting the extended body effectivities, corresponding to overt risk (rho_LF) and potential risk (rho_GF). By extending rho coupling to encompass satisficing, this framework elegantly models how actors dynamically balance contextual pressures without error-nulling. This integrated theoretical approach explains diverse human adaptive strategies and provides fundamental insights for future ecological human-centered design, including advanced driver assistance systems.

articles.title: Embodied Copresence Confers No Advantage Over Screen-Based Delivery in Robot-Facilitated Language Learning
articles.authors: Nathan Caruana; Aitor Miguel Blanco; Emily S. Cross
articles.abstract: The past decade has seen growing interest in deploying social robots as assistive technologies in educational settings. Key unresolved questions concern the extent to which, and possibly when, the embodied copresence of a robot confers benefits over screen-based alternatives. This is an issue with applied significance given the logistical and cost constraints of deploying physical robots at scale. In a preregistered between-subjects experiment, 40 adults completed a Spanish language learning task alongside a Pepper humanoid robot that was either physically co-located next to participants (Embodied, n = 20) or presented via live video feed on a large screen next to participants (Screen, n = 20). Contrary to our predictions, conditions did not differ on any objective measure of task engagement (accuracy, completion time, voluntary continuation), self-report indices (enjoyment, difficulty), attention allocation to the robot or task (subjectively coded gaze orientation), or validated measures of robot perception and affiliation (Godspeed questionnaire; Self-in-Other scale), with the exception of greater perceived task difficulty and robot awareness in the Embodied than Screen condition. Reflexive thematic analysis of post-task interviews identified three cross-condition themes: robot learning companions (1) create experiences of invigilation; (2) are expected to fulfil multiple social roles (motivational coach, tutor, and companion); and (3) are expected to interact in a human-like, intelligent, and adaptive manner. These findings suggest that, for adult learners engaged in short-duration tasks, such as the simple language-learning task explored here, screen-based delivery may be functionally equivalent to physical co-presence, with implications for the scalable deployment of social robots in educational contexts.

articles.title: Liberal paternalism: Weak-victim narratives facilitate the disempowering treatment of refugees and low-income individuals
articles.authors: Christina Bauer; Steve Rathje; Gregory M Walton
articles.abstract: Refugees, low-income individuals, and other groups that are systemically disadvantaged often show substantial strength and agency, including in contending with the adversity they face. Yet, media, politicians, and other stakeholders sometimes portray these individuals as weak and passive victims. In eight studies (Ntotal=226 newspaper articles & 1,895 participants in the UK, US, & Australia) focused primarily on refugees (Studies 1-4), and secondarily on low-income individuals (Studies 5a-b), we show that i) weak-victim narratives are common in both media portrayals and mental representations, especially in liberal (vs. conservative) media and minds (Studies 1-2c & 5a), and ii) that weak-victim narratives facilitate functionally disempowering behaviors among liberals (Studies 3, 4, & 5b).

articles.title: Adolescent anxiety and gaming: a case study of stability loops
articles.authors: Tiina Auranen; Roope Holopainen; Veli-Matti Karhulahti
articles.abstract:
This research presents two longitudinal case studies of intensively gaming adolescents who 
express clinically significant anxiety symptoms in the Finnish cultural context. By means of 
Interpretative Phenomenological Analysis, two shared themes were constructed based on in-depth 
qualitative data from both participants: self-reinforcing loop between interpersonal problems and 
gaming, and self-reinforcing loop between lacking affordances and gaming. Collectively, the themes 
point at a developmental mechanism that we call stability loops: anxiety-gaming interactions that 
minimise changes over time in socioecological systems. These exploratory findings highlight how 
individual experiences of circumstances create potentially different loop trajectories, which can both 
complicate and support age-relevant development depending on the social context. As such, the study 
offers an alternative to diagnostic gaming frameworks by modelling the activity as a part of 
psychological development in a world where technology is rapidly evolving and ubiquitous.

articles.title: Rethinking empathy in the age of AI
articles.authors: Joshua D Wenger; Daryl Cameron; Madeline G. Reinecke
articles.abstract: People increasingly turn to artificial intelligence (AI) for empathic support, often reporting feelings of being cared for and supported. Longstanding models of empathy, however, center the empathizer’s embodied emotional experience, which AI fundamentally lacks. This tension between human experience and traditional researcher-imposed empathy definitions raises important scientific questions as to what it truly means for AI to “empathize.” In the present paper, we propose an alternative definition and approach to studying empathy which eases this tension, emphasizing the multiple dissociable functions that empathy serves within various relational schemas. Taking a functional-relational approach redefines the study of empathy by centering practical meta-scientific concerns (e.g., surrounding the exploration of empathy within study contexts, foregrounding lived experience). In doing so, we seek to future-proof empathy as a construct, ensuring that our science remains relevant, generalizable across time, and responsive to lived human experience as technology advances and new forms of relationships emerge.

articles.title: From Detection to Behavioral Change: A Scoping Review of Natural Language Processing in Substance Use Research
articles.authors: Erin Prince; Sheridan Fine; Francesca Filbey
articles.abstract:
Background: Natural language processing (NLP) has emerged as a promising approach for extracting
clinically relevant information from unstructured text that would otherwise be difficult to capture
through manual review alone. Although NLP in medical settings began in the 1960s, applications have
expanded rapidly in the 2000s, with broader use of digital narrative data such as electronic health
records (EHRs), clinical notes, psychotherapy transcripts, and other language-based data sources. In
substance use research, however, the literature on NLP applications remains fragmented across data
sources, methods, and clinical domains, making it difficult to identify areas of convergence and
important gaps. Accordingly, this scoping review examined NLP applications in substance use research,
focusing on clinical screening and phenotyping, risk prediction, treatment outcomes, and psychotherapy
process.
Method: A systematic search of nine clinical and technical databases identified studies published
between 2016 and 2026 to examine NLP applications related to substance use behaviors, treatments,
and clinically meaningful outcomes. Following screening and eligibility review, 28 studies were included.
Extracted data included substance use focus, setting, data source, NLP methods, outcome domain, and
key findings.
Results: Most studies (78.6%) utilized EHR clinical notes from U.S. healthcare systems, focusing primarily
on opioid outcomes. NLP methods consistently improved substance use detection compared to
structured diagnostic coding, contributing to nuanced models of overdose risk, relapse, treatment
attrition, and opioid prescribing. Recent work focused on detection and prediction to improve
multidimensional characterization and computational phenotyping of substance use populations. Across
psychotherapy studies, semantic, syntactic, contextual, and affective language features captured
clinically meaningful behavior processes and, in recent work, predicted subsequent alcohol use
3
outcomes. However, external validation performance often declined across datasets. Few studies
examined non-opioid substances, spoken language, or community samples.
Discussion: NLP methods demonstrate potential for improving substance use detection,
characterization, and modeling of behaviors across clinical and behavioral domains. Current work
suggests a shift from simple classification towards richer representations of behavioral and psychosocial
processes with notable limitations in generalizability, data diversity, and external validation remaining
challenging for substance use research.

articles.title: Orthography Shapes L2 Stress PerceptionAcross Development: Evidence from L1 Mandarin Learners of Portuguese
articles.authors: Chao Zhou; Guilherme D. Garcia
articles.abstract: Despite growing evidence that written input shapes second-language speech learning, its role in suprasegmental acquisition remains underexplored. This study examines whether orthography facilitates lexical stress identification through syllable weight. Portuguese is well suited for this question because stress placement is strongly conditioned by syllable weight, which is transparently encoded in the writing system. A total of 186 L1 Mandarin speakers identified stress location in Portuguese pseudowords presented either auditorily or with accompanying written forms. Naïve listeners used syllable weight as a stress cue only when orthographic information was available, whereas experienced learners showed weight sensitivity from auditory input alone. For experienced learners, however, orthography did not further enhance weight sensitivity; instead, it biased responses toward the default penultimate- stress pattern. These findings suggest that orthographic effects change over L2 development, interacting with auditory cue weighting and distributional regularities in L2 stress perception.

articles.title: Near-random behavior in strategic games
articles.authors: Tal Boger; Dorsa Amir; Sami Ryan Yousif
articles.abstract: Humans struggle to produce random behavior when asked to do so, leading some to suggest that our ability to randomize is attenuated (or even absent). Here, we demonstrate that the capacity for random behavior is much greater than previously acknowledged: Humans can behave in (near) optimally random ways when the context demands it. We created a custom, online version of the game Battleship in which participants competed against one another. On each turn, one player chose a tile on a 3x3 grid to place a ship, while the other player tried to guess the ship’s location. Across six preregistered studies, this strategic context led to dramatic increases in random behavior relative to closely matched non-strategic tasks. Such random behavior was also remarkably flexible and optimal depending on context; both players readily incorporated varying information about the game (e.g., that tiles can differ in value) while simultaneously accounting for their opponents’ knowledge of that information. A computational model validated these findings and revealed nuanced differences across contexts. Contrary to decades of work finding that humans fail to randomize, we find that strategic games promote highly flexible, near-random behavior.

articles.title: Gender Differences in Self-reported Emotional Sharing in Social Interaction: A Meta Analysis
articles.authors: X. Jia; Karen Holtmaat; Y. Mo; ZIHAO Zeng; M. Kaneva; Annet Kleiboer; Sander L. Koole
articles.abstract: Through emotional sharing, individuals can make their emotional experiences available to others, creating opportunities for interpersonal emotion regulation. Although gender differences in these behaviours have been documented across various domains, findings regarding their magnitude and consistency remain inconclusive. This meta-analysis examined gender differences in emotional sharing among adults. A systematic search identified 32 articles comprising 37 independent samples, 155 effect sizes, and 13,147 participants, including 8,504 women and 4,643 men. Overall, women reported higher levels of emotional sharing than men, g = 0.31, 95% CI [0.18, 0.44]. This effect was not significantly moderated by (1) functions (emotional expression, emotional disclosure, emotional expression as coping), (2) temporal level (dispositional, situational), (3) emotional valence (negative, positive or unspecified), (4) specific negative emotion (anger, sadness, fear/anxiety, shame/guilt, and unspecified negative emotions), and (5) the interpersonal target (romantic partner, friend, other, or no partner specified). Despite the absence of significant moderation effects, pooled estimates within most subgroups remained significantly positive, indicating higher levels of expression and disclosure among women than men across a wide range of emotional contexts and interpersonal relations.

articles.title: The Modulation of Mood Through Absorption in Music Listening
articles.authors: Bradley Austin-Keiller; Frank Russo; Karina J Linnell
articles.abstract: Music listening is widely used to regulate emotion, yet the listener-level processes underlying affective change remain under-specified. This longitudinal study examined musical absorption as one such process, testing a novel Musical Absorption Training (MAT) protocol designed to scaffold absorptive engagement. Adults aged 55 and older (analytic N = 49) completed 16 listening sessions over four weeks. Participants were randomly assigned either to eight sessions of guided MAT followed by eight unguided sessions, or to unguided listening throughout. Valence and arousal were rated before and after each session, state absorption after each session, and trait absorption (AIMS) at baseline, Session 8, and Session 16. Mixed-effects models showed that greater state absorption predicted larger within-session increases in valence and arousal, driven mainly by within-person fluctuations. MAT did not raise state absorption during the guided phase, but after guidance ended, absorption was preserved in the MAT group. Trait absorption increased over time without a significant Group × Time interaction; however, higher state absorption during the maintenance phase predicted higher trait absorption at study end. These findings identify absorption as a promising listener-level correlate of music-related mood change and offer preliminary evidence that structured attentional guidance may help sustain absorptive engagement across repeated listening.

articles.title: The When, Who, Why, and How of Crocodile Tears: Manipulative Crying is Associated with Specific Situations, Traits, Motivations, and Expressive Behaviors
articles.authors: Janis Zickfeld; Monika Wróbel; Paweł Ciesielski
articles.abstract: The notion of crocodile tears suggests that crying can be used strategically to manipulate others. However, systematic evidence on manipulative crying remains limited. Here, we addressed this gap by examining the prevalence of crocodile tears, along with the contexts, motivations, individual traits, and expressive behaviors associated with this phenomenon across seven studies. In the first three studies (N = 2,036), participants from seven regions reported real-life experiences of being manipulated with crying or using crying to manipulate others. Results indicated that crocodile tears are a widespread yet relatively infrequent manipulative strategy, primarily occurring in close relationships and typically intended to evoke compassion or induce guilt. Women, younger participants, individuals scoring higher on Machiavellianism and psychopathy, and participants from lower-trust countries reported more frequent use of crocodile tears. Manipulative crying was also associated with intense expressive behaviors, including exaggerated facial expressions, face-touching, and loud vocalizations. Another set of four studies (N = 4,514), conducted across five regions, experimentally manipulated crying-related behaviors to examine how expressive cues shape perceptions of crying. Machine learning analyses revealed that crying was perceived as most “crocodile” when it involved high-intensity behaviors but no tears. Moreover, intense expressive behaviors combined with the absence of tears improved participants’ accuracy in detecting fake crying. Together, these findings provide a comprehensive empirical account of crocodile tears, highlighting how multimodal expressive cues, as well as social, individual, and cultural factors, shape the strategic use and perception of crying.

articles.title: Psychopathology-AI-interaction (PAII) framework: Disorder-specific dynamics in conversational AI
articles.authors: Alexander Diel; Niels Weber; Martin Teufel; Alexander Bäuerle
articles.abstract: Chatbots based on large language models (LLM-CBs) are increasingly used for mental health support by both individuals with and without mental health conditions. Simultaneously, potential risks and harms of LLM-CB use for mental health are widely discussed, typically in disorder-unspecific terms, evaluated through single-turn benchmark and vignette designs, and rarely linked to established models of psychopathology. The current work presents the Psychopathology-AI-interaction (PAII) framework, which conceptualizes harmful human-chatbot interaction as arising from three interacting components: human factors (disorder-specific pathology, individual vulnerabilities, and personality dispositions), chatbot factors (model-specific safety failures and design principles), and interaction factors. Drawing on established models of technology-associated psychopathology, LLM-CBs are presented as a new domain in which disorder-specific maladaptive patterns emerge. A roadmap for future research is presented, focusing on psychopathology-based multi-turn benchmarks, experimental induction of vulnerabilities and manipulation of chatbot risk factors, and analysis of naturalistic conversation logs.

articles.title: A Revolution in Search of an Estimand: On the Idionomic Proposal of Hayes et al. (2026)
articles.authors: Magnus Johansson; Matti Vuorre; Nils Olof Wilhelm Hentati Isacsson; Kristoffer Magnusson
articles.abstract:
Hayes et al. (2026) argue that clinical psychology is stalled by an “ergodic error”, the application
of group-level statistics to individuals, and propose idionomic analysis as the remedy. We agree
that pooled associations do not need to describe individuals and that treatment effects vary
between people, but the proposed remedy does not answer the clinical question. Personalizing
treatment is a causal problem, yet Hayes et al. never state which causal quantity, or estimand,
they target. Their evidence consists of observational within-person associations, which cannot
separate effects from confounding that varies over time. Applied to observational data, none of
the recommended methods can identify a causal effect. Non-ergodicity shows only that pooled
and individual associations may differ, not that causal effects do. The reported heterogeneity is
also questionable, in part because person-level estimates from short series are imprecise. The
reliability Hayes et al. cite against this concern describes person means rather than within-
person variation, and the statistics summarizing heterogeneity have not been adequately
checked against simulated data in which there is no heterogeneity. Designs that randomize
treatment within or between persons can target person-level and conditional effects, within
limits set by carryover and irreversible change. Rather than the proposed idionomic revolution,
clinical psychology needs to join the causal revolution, in which the estimand is stated before
the data are analyzed.

articles.title: Do God Primes Prime God? Converging Evidence Against the Efficacy of Experimental Religious Priming
articles.authors: Will M Gervais; Meara Geraty; Aiyana Koka Willard
articles.abstract:
How does religion change people? Religious priming has been used to scientifically ask this question for nearly two
decades, linking religious cognition to varied outcomes – especially prosociality. Priming research has proliferated
in the absence of direct evidence that religious priming tools work as implicitly assumed: by activating religious
cognition. Here, we evaluate this assumption. Across a bias-adjusted meta-analysis (k = 66) and two experiments
(total N = 2960), we report strong and converging evidence: 1) against the validity of the most commonly used priming
methodology, 2) against even overt primes’ abilities to robustly affect prosocial cognition or behavior, 3) against a
meaningful relationship between cognitive activation of religion and prosocial behavior; further, evidence was 4) in
favor of even ineffective primes nonetheless inviting participant suspicion. Combined, this suggests that the evidential
strength of existing priming research is likely overstated, with critical assumptions now contradicted by evidence.

articles.title: Perceived and evidenced benefits of videogame play amongst neurodivergent populations: A scoping review
articles.authors: Emily J Smith; Jonathan Farnell; Lacey-ann Carter; Roshan Rai; Benjamin Gibson
articles.abstract: There are meaningful concerns that videogame play is harmful for neurodivergent populations, including people with autism spectrum disorders. However, there is a disproportionate focus in the literature on dangers, and there are fewer efforts to consider why such populations may be more likely to play videogames in the first place. In considering benefits to play, this scoping review attempts to map out a more balanced view of videogame engagement amongst a range of neurodivergent populations. A search of academic databases identified 9 articles comprising a mix of qualitative and quantitative studies. Using a narrative synthesis, we found that benefits to play included (1) friendship and belonging, (2) immersion, escapism, and emotional regulation, and (3) development, growth, and autonomy. In the future, we recommend a pivot away from a deficit-focused approach to investigations, and a larger investment in research that considers motivations, attitudes, and consequences of play from a lived-experience perspective.

articles.title: Psychological inoculation against deepfakes
articles.authors: Cambridge Social Decision-Making Lab; Liana Cheetham; Kelly Wong Kar Yee; Sander van der Linden
articles.abstract: Despite growing interest in countering the threat of deepfake misinformation, most interventions aimed at enhancing human detection have thus far proven unsuccessful. In the current study we explore the potential of a popular psychological intervention: cognitive inoculation—which to our knowledge—has not been tested in the context of deepfakes. In a pre-registered between-subjects experiment (N = 297), we evaluate whether an inoculation-based video intervention improves people’s deepfake detection skills compared to a control intervention. The inoculation intervention forewarned participants they may be manipulated by deepfake content and prebunked it by deconstructing deepfake misinformation in weakened form. Following the intervention, participants were asked to classify a series of 10 videos as either real or deepfaked. We find that mean detection accuracy of deepfakes was significantly higher in the inoculation compared to the control group (d = 0.625, 95% CI [0.39, 0.86]) without shifting response bias, indicating that the inoculation intervention substantially improved deepfake discernment. Further investigation of the mechanisms behind the inoculation process finds that both motivation to resist deepfakes and self-reported ability to recognize them increased following the intervention. Overall, our findings highlight the potential of inoculation interventions to build resistance to deepfake misinformation.

articles.title: Cross-cultural and Indigenous perspectives on music and social bonding
articles.authors: Danya Vivianne Pavlovich; Patricia Opondo; Juan David Leongómez; Yuto Ozaki; Zixuan Jia; Suzanne Purdy; Patrick E. Savage
articles.abstract: Experimental studies of primarily Western participants have suggested that musical synchrony facilitates social bonding. Critics question the validity and cross-cultural generality of synchrony-bonding relationships, as well as the causal role of music. Drawing on new data from large-scale Registered Reports co-designed and implemented with over 100 collaborators (“Many Voices”), we show that group singing enhances social bonding significantly more than speaking, across 901 participants speaking 30 languages. We share lessons from this collaboration regarding evolutionary hypotheses about the origins of music and language, as well as the importance of collaborating with Indigenous and non-Western researchers. By making the psychology of music research more inclusive, we may broaden our understanding of music and social bonding in humans and beyond. Indigenous knowledge does not oppose science: it improves science.

articles.title: Examining the Role of Working Memory in Reasoning and Meta-reasoning:  A Fuzzy-trace approach
articles.authors: Leili Rouhi; Zuleykha Gasimova; Valerie A Thompson
articles.abstract: Monitoring processes, such as confidence, are assumed to guide control processes, such as whether to change or persist with a response. Yet whether this monitoring–control link depends on the same working memory (WM) resources implicated in reasoning itself remains unclear. Fuzzy-trace theory (FTT) holds that reasoning relies primarily on low-effort gist representations and that errors arise when a salient but inappropriate gist interferes with the appropriate one. Drawing on FTT and the meta-reasoning framework the role of WM in reasoning, monitoring and control. Participants (N = 998) solved belief-bias syllogisms with and without conflict between validity and believability in a two-response paradigm. They gave an initial answer under a concurrent WM load, a response deadline, or both, followed by a confidence rating and a final answer. Accuracy declined only when load and deadline were combined, and this decline was similar for conflict and non-conflict problems. Confidence was reliably lower on conflict than on non-conflict problems across all conditions, and confidence reliably predicted answer changes and rethinking time regardless of WM constraints. Monitoring resolution, however, was low even without constraints. These results suggest that WM constraints impair reasoning generally but leave conflict detection and control sensitivity largely intact. Reasoners’ limited ability to discriminate their own correct from incorrect responses appears to reflect a more general limitation of monitoring rather than a consequence of constrained resources.

articles.title: Assistive AI in Counseling Psychology for Dyslexia (AAIC-D): A Conceptual Framework for Enhancing the Therapeutic Alliance
articles.authors: KHAIRUL KORAI
articles.abstract:
Individual with dyslexia frequently experience persistent reading difficulties that extend far beyond academic environments, contributing to heightened anxiety, low self-esteem, and chronic psychological distress. In traditional mental health counseling, literacy-heavy tools such as written intake questionnaires, thought journals, and dense psychoeducational handouts impose a heavy extraneous cognitive load. This load exhausts working memory and triggers reading anxiety, effectively diverting mental bandwidth away from core therapeutic processing. To address this barrier, this paper introduces a conceptual framework: Assistive AI in Counseling Psychology for Dyslexia (AAIC-D). Grounded in a narrative synthesis of existing literature, this model positions artificial intelligence not as a replacement for human clinicians, but as an accessible cognitive scaffold managed under ethical oversight. The framework synthesizes Cognitive Load Theory, the Triadic Therapeutic Alliance model (Client, Therapist, and AI), and Universal Design for Learning (UDL) principles. By leveraging Generative AI summaries, speech-to-text journaling, and multimodal text-to-speech presentation, AAIC-D offloads reading and writing effort, restoring the client's emotional capacity for therapeutic engagement. Finally, we address critical counseling practice governance concerns including algorithmic bias, data privacy under HIPAA/GDPR, and client over-reliance offering actionable guidelines to humanize and democratize psychological care. 

Keywords: Dyslexia, Assistive AI, Therapeutic Alliance, Cognitive Load Theory, Universal Design for Learning, Counseling Psychology, Cyberpsychology

articles.title: “It's my destiny.”: A Qualitative Exploration of Motivating Factors for submissives who Hold BDSM and Kink Identities
articles.authors: Briana Louise Kunstman; Jaime Derringer
articles.abstract: Although Dominant-submissive dynamics are among the most widely recognized forms of BDSM and kink, popular media often portray these relationships as inherently abusive or exploitative. Such representations contrast with growing evidence that BDSM identities and practices emerge through diverse developmental, social, and personal pathways. Building on prior research calling for greater attention to role-specific experiences within BDSM communities,the current study evaluated the themes present among 52 participants reporting submissive identities. We found that participants’ descriptions of their motivations for being a submissive consistently referred to the following themes: upbringing and past experience; submission as an identity; control and power exchange; positive mental health outcomes; and feelings of shame associated with stigma. Apart from stigma concerns, participants overwhelmingly discussed positive aspects of their experiences. This shows that there are complex motivating factors for participants to engage with or identify as submissive, opening up potential directions of exploration to understand the development of kink and BDSM identities and experiences. These findings specific to submissive motivations and BDSM identities will help work towards the destigmatization and depathologizing of kink and BDSM through increased understanding. In turn, this will allow for better mental health outcomes for community members, informed safe practice, and improved general understanding of BDSM and kink identities in our society.

articles.title: Can Accurate Information Change Identity-Linked Political Beliefs? Evidence From Republicans’ Attitudes Towards Election Integrity
articles.authors: Michael Nicholas Stagnaro; Eran Amsalem; Andrea B Mullin; Hause Lin; Adam J. Berinsky; David Gertler Rand
articles.abstract: Psychological research suggests that identity shapes beliefs and impedes updating in response to contrary evidence. A prominent example is many Republicans’ persistence in believing that the 2020 election was stolen. We test whether credible factual information can shift Republicans' beliefs about election integrity. Immediately before the 2024 presidential election, we randomly assigned 861 conservative Republicans to an intensive informational intervention or a control matched with civic content. The intervention presented extensive, accurate, politically balanced evidence and encouraged sustained engagement. Treated participants reported stronger beliefs in US election integrity overall, greater confidence in the 2020 election, and more positive expectations for the 2024 election (.5 < ds < .8), including those who started lower in electoral confidence (.5 < ds < .97). Effects were still detectable two weeks later, after Trump’s victory. Though learning was incentivized, belief reporting was not – showing that when attended to, credible balanced evidence can change minds.

articles.title: Displayed judgment certainty reorganizes source selection in self-formed networks
articles.authors: Gaël Carniel; Frédéric Moisan; Alain Barrat; Jean-Claude Dreher
articles.abstract: Collective intelligence in self-formed networks depends on which judgments people choose to observe, as well as on how they integrate those judgments. We tested whether displaying judgment certainty reorganizes source selection and improves subsequent accuracy. Across eight online sessions, 273 participants evaluated 14 true and false news headlines, formed costly directed observation networks, and revised their beliefs over five updates. During network formation, we manipulated the visibility of certainty, defined by the extremity of each source's private probability judgment, while belief direction and source accuracy remained hidden. Displaying certainty produced denser networks and redirected links toward more certain sources; current popularity also predicted selection. Visibility increased exposure to highly certain but incorrect judgments, without a clear improvement in the relative accuracy of selected sources. Accuracy increased across repeated judgments, but certainty visibility did not detectably increase this improvement and reduced reconstructed net scores under the task's payoff structure. Observations with selected sources showed greater improvement than those without, and improvement was associated with selected sources' initial accuracy. Belief revisions moved toward selected sources and decreased with participants' own certainty. Among six compact predictive models, certainty-reinforcing DeGroot provided the best penalized and aggregate held-out prediction, although it did not capture the large first update. These findings distinguish a cue's ability to attract attention from its ability to identify useful information: displayed certainty can reorganize costly information acquisition without a detectable average accuracy benefit.

articles.title: Conversation as data: Extracting features from naturalistic conversation datasets
articles.authors: Emma Templeton; Luke J. Chang
articles.abstract: In this chapter, we outline important considerations for designing and analyzing conversation studies. We first advocate for the use of representative designs to ensure that datasets adequately reflect the complexity inherent in conversation. We then focus on how behavior in conversation recordings can be quantified through a process of feature extraction, and discuss strategies to assess the validity of feature extraction pipelines. Finally, we discuss analytical considerations specific to working with conversation data. Being able to rigorously collect, operationalize, and analyze natural conversation data will lead to robust results that the entire field can build upon, advancing our understanding of exactly how conversation allows us to achieve our social goals.

articles.title: A Megastudy of Behavioral Interventions to Increase Voter Registration Ahead of the 2024 U.S. Presidential Election
articles.authors: Katherine Anne Mason; Kayley Okst; Don Green; Robb Willer; James Druckman; Jan G. Voelkel; Yash Patel; Claire Robertson; Wooyoung Choi; Jasmine Sanchez
articles.abstract: In the United States, in nearly all cases, one must register in order to vote—yet, a substantial portion of the eligible electorate remains unregistered. Despite this, relatively little is known about how to increase the likelihood that a voter registers. Here, we tested the impact of 10 expert-crowdsourced, theoretically-based psychological interventions on a sample of eligible, yet unregistered, U.S. voters ahead of the 2024 presidential election (N = 12,896). Eight of the interventions increased intentions to vote, and five led individuals to click on the voter registration website. Escalating Commitment, which sequentially employed several social pressure strategies, was the strongest intervention across these outcomes. However, none of the interventions had a significant effect on actual voter registration or voter turnout. The results highlight a substantial disconnect between voters’ intentions and their ultimate behaviors. We discuss potential structural and psychological barriers that undermine the translation of intent into action.

articles.title: Weak Links between Speech Perception and Speech Production at the Subphonemic Level
articles.authors: Brian W. L. Wong; Arthur G. Samuel; Efthymia C Kapnoula
articles.abstract: Recent research has shown individual differences in gradiency, defined as sensitivity to fine-grained acoustic differences at the subphonemic level. Consistency also varies, with some listeners providing more stable responses than others to repeated presentations of the same stimuli. However, it remains unclear whether gradiency and consistency are linked between perception and production. Across two experiments, 160 Spanish speakers completed a Visual Analogue Scale (VAS) task measuring perceptual gradiency and consistency along a Spanish /ba/–/pa/ continuum manipulated in 7–8 ms steps of voice onset time (VOT). The same participants also performed an explicit imitation task using the same stimuli. Results revealed only weak relationships between perceptual gradiency and imitation accuracy, as well as between perceptual consistency and imitation consistency, even after accounting for other factors related to speech perception and imitation. These findings suggest that models proposing strong perception–production coupling may not extend to the subphonemic level.

articles.title: Mapping Behavioural and Psychological Factors Associated with Engagement in Online Activism: A Critical Scoping Review
articles.authors: Benjamin Gibson; Jekaterina Schneider; Mark J. Forshaw
articles.abstract: Online activism can be a powerful means of supporting social and political engagement. However, there are genuine concerns that online behaviours do not translate into social and political action, while nascent research suggests that online activism may affect well-being and feelings of identity more negatively compared to traditional (i.e., in-person) forms of activism. This scoping review attempted to map out the evidence so that the reader may better understand the psychological and behavioural factors associated with engagement in online activism. A search of academic databases and registers identified 24 articles comprising 28 studies and examined various forms of online activism including hashtag campaigns, online petitions, and social media engagement. Online engagement was shown to support a range of (further) online and offline activist behaviours, to foster collective identities, and to provide psychological benefits such as increased self-efficacy and feelings of empowerment (which in turn encouraged further political action). However, contextual and individual factors likely influence both behaviours and opportunities for psychological benefits. This review highlights the blurred boundaries between online and offline activism, while evidencing that even “passive” digital engagement may serve as a gateway to broader civic participation.

articles.title: “Who Will Marry a Mad Doctor?”: A Qualitative Study of Associative Stigma Among Mental Health Professionals in India
articles.authors: Deepti Dilip Moar; Rajat Kanti Mitra; Sunil Mittal
articles.abstract: Mental health professionals (MHPs) can experience stigma through their professional association with mental illness and mental healthcare. Existing studies have often focused on particular professions, service populations, or specific aspects of associative stigma, making it difficult to identify recurring patterns across professions and beyond the workplace. This study explored associative stigma among MHPs in India across professional, family, and wider social contexts. Semi-structured interviews with 22 MHPs, including psychiatrists, clinical psychologists, counsellors, psychiatric social workers, and psychiatric nurses, were analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis within a constructivist framework. Eight themes were developed, spanning misconceptions about MHP roles and abilities, mistrust of expertise and motives, concerns about how mental health work might affect them, devaluation of mental health work, exclusion involving social distancing and concealment, role expectations extending beyond work, ambivalent responses in which admiration or reliance coexisted with misunderstanding, avoidance, or devaluation, and differences in professional standing. Across the analysis, experiences that might otherwise appear separate were connected by recurring meanings attached to mental illness and mental healthcare. The study broadens understanding of the social and professional reach of stigma surrounding mental illness. Through professional association, these meanings can shape how MHPs, their expertise, and mental health work are understood and valued.

articles.title: Can Large Language Models Code Reality Criteria in Autobiographical Statements? Reliability and Validity of an Artificial Intelligence–Based Tool for Criteria-Based Content Analysis
articles.authors: Elsa Gewehr; Laureen Gräflich; Johannes Zimmermann; Renate Volbert
articles.abstract: Objective: Coding for Criteria-Based Content Analysis (CBCA) to differentiate fabricated from experience-based autobiographical statements is slow and depends on trained coders whose agreement is imperfect. We developed the large language model (LLM) based system CBC-AID and evaluate its reliability and validity in coding CBCA. Hypotheses: As preregistered, AI–human consistency is non-inferior to the interrater reliability of trained coders (H1: total score; H2: each criterion), and AI-based scores discriminate between experience-based and fabricated statements at least as well as human scores (H3: total score; H4: each criterion). Method: Two versions of an LLM-based coding tool (CBC-AID), a single-prompt and a multi-agent system, coded 957 transcripts from 399 persons in nine laboratory studies with human CBCA codings and known truth status. Bivariate Bayesian multilevel models estimated within-study correlations and standardized truth effects under global rating and weighted frequency. Results: AI–human correlations of the total scores (ρ = .53–.67) fell short of the benchmark of .66 in all four combinations of version and scoring scheme; Version 1 under global rating came closest (ρ = .67, 95% CrI [.62, .72]). The AI assigned higher scores than human coders (0.7–2.7 SD). Truth effects were similar for AI-based (δ = 0.17–0.32) and human coding (0.16–0.24; Δδ = −0.06 to 0.12); non-inferiority was supported for one of four combinations, and human coding itself discriminated weakly. Conclusions: LLM-based coding approximated but did not reach the consistency of trained coders and preserved their modest discriminative validity. It may serve as a traceable supplement to human coding in research; forensic use requires field validation and human oversight.

articles.title: When the Same Leader Helps and Harms: Inconsistent Leadership Behavior in Team Meetings
articles.authors: Amelie Verena Güntner; Kai N. Klasmeier; Catrin Millhoff; Nora Gosch; Simone Kauffeld
articles.abstract:
Purpose: The same leader often displays constructive and destructive behaviors at once, a
phenomenon known as inconsistent leadership. Inconsistency has been linked to negative
follower outcomes, yet it has almost exclusively been studied as a follower perception. This
study examines inconsistent leadership as enacted behavior, asking how and under what
conditions the co-occurrence of instrumental and destructive leadership shapes team behavior in
meetings.
Design/methodology/approach: Using a multilevel moderated mediation model, we tested our
model on 30 videotaped team meetings (5,430 coded behaviors), rating leaders' instrumental and
destructive behavior and coding leaders' action planning and team members' conflict-related
communication.
Findings: Instrumental leadership was associated with more action planning, which in turn
reduced conflict-related communication, but only when destructive leadership was low. When
leaders behaved destructively alongside instrumental leadership, this indirect effect disappeared.
Practical implications: Occasional destructive behavior can undo the benefits of otherwise
constructive leadership, so what matters for teams is not only what leaders do well but whether
they do it consistently. Organizations can address this through leadership development that helps
leaders recognize and reduce inconsistent behavior in meetings.
Originality/value: Inconsistency has almost always been studied as a follower perception. This
study extends its consequences beyond follower attitudes to observable team communication and
to the leader's own planning, showing that inconsistency also shapes the enacting leader. It offers
a behavioral, micro-level operationalization that complements existing perception-based
measures.

articles.title: Perceptions of Profit Motive: For-Profit Companies are Judged Less Favourably Than Non-Profits Even When the Societal Benefits of Profit-Seeking are Made Salient
articles.authors: Zuleykha Gasimova; Martin Harry Turpin; Alexander C. Walker; Jonathan Albert Fugelsang; Derek J. Koehler
articles.abstract: People tend to view profit-seeking businesses more negatively than otherwise equivalent non-profit businesses or organizations. This tendency puts people at risk of missing out on the potential societal benefit that can emerge when profit-seeking motivations are aligned with prosocial goals. When making judgments about firms and businesses, people may simply neglect the possibility that profit-seeking could result in gains for society. The current research finds that people’s attitudes are more ambivalent (as opposed to strictly negative) when they consider, in a broader sense, examples of how profit-seeking companies could positively or negatively affect society (e.g., consumer and employee welfare, technological advances, etc.). Study 1 (N = 101) showed that people are open to endorsing both general (pro-profit) statements about how profit-seeking businesses may produce socially beneficial outcomes and general (anti-profit) statements about how profit-seeking businesses may produce socially harmful outcomes. In Study 2 (N = 301), we examined whether exposure to such statements highlighting the potential positive (or negative) societal impacts of profit-seeking affected participant’s judgements of for- and non-profit firms. Exposure to pro-profit and anti-profit statements did not impact people’s judgments of profit-seeking businesses. Instead, people consistently exhibited a tendency to judge for-profit companies as having a less positive societal impact in comparison with their non-profit counterparts. This anti-profit bias persisted even among participants who had expressed agreement with general statements about the ways in which profit-seeking companies can deliver societal benefits.

articles.title: Historical Trends in Associations of Caregiver Knowledge of Whereabouts and Perceived Cannabis Use Among Friends With Cannabis Use Frequency Among Chilean Adolescents
articles.authors: Mauro P. Olivera; Diego Manríquez-Robles; Luis Sáenz-Herrera
articles.abstract: Adolescent cannabis use is associated with family and peer contexts, but whether these associations vary across historical periods is uncertain. We analyzed 12 repeated cross-sectional waves of the Chilean National School Population Survey on Drug Use (2001-2023; 636,008 records). Wave-specific Spearman correlations were estimated using complete cases, with sampling variances and within-wave covariance matrices obtained from 5,000 stratified course-cluster bootstrap replicates. Random-effects meta-analysis and meta-regression used Hartung-Knapp small-sample inference; subgroup interactions used wave-delete jackknife tests. Complete-series unweighted estimates were primary because final expansion weights were unavailable for three waves; supported-wave weighted analyses were sensitivity checks. Caregiver knowledge of whereabouts was inversely associated with cannabis use frequency (pooled ρ = -.200, 95% CI [-.212, -.189]), while perceived regular cannabis use among friends was more strongly and positively associated (pooled ρ = .427, 95% CI [.408, .445]). Neither overall historical trend was significant under small-sample inference (knowledge: β = .0014, p = .065; friends: β = -.0027, p = .109). Weighted sensitivity supported attenuation for knowledge (β = .0027, p = .007). Peer-use trends differed by sex and family structure, whereas knowledge trends did not. These repeated cross-sectional findings indicate strong, persistent associations but limited evidence for a uniform historical change. The subgroup variation and sensitivity dependence emphasize cautious interpretation.

articles.title: Relationships Between Auditory Statistical Learning and Reading Skills in Children with Reading Difficulties
articles.authors: Anqi Hu; Brynn Siles; Monique Montoute; Kelly Hay Yee Chan; Sarah Young-Hong; Amanda Van Horne; Morten H. Christiansen; Zhenghan Qi
articles.abstract:
Purpose. This study evaluated the psychometric implications of a novel gamified SL task for school-aged children with reading difficulties and examined the relationships between auditory syllable-based statistical learning (SL) and literacy skills.

Methods. Two groups of children aged 7–11 with reading difficulty were recruited. In Experiment 1, 13 children piloted a child-friendly, non-gamified auditory SL task at two timepoints, with learning assessed via a two-alternative forced-choice (2AFC) test at both timepoints and a statistically induced chunking recall (SICR) test at Timepoint 2. In Experiment 2, 22 children completed a gamified version of the SL task, with learning assessed via 2AFC and SICR at both timepoints and reading skills (nonword and sight-word fluency) assessed at Timepoint 1.

Results. Children showed learning at the group level across timepoints, as measured by SICR in both gamified and non-gamified tasks, and as measured by 2AFC in the gamified task only. SICR showed higher internal consistency than 2AFC across tasks. Test-retest reliability for 2AFC was higher for the gamified (r = .64) than non-gamified (r = .14) task.  Children’s performance on 2AFC and SICR in the gamified task were significantly associated with their nonword and sight-word reading fluency.

Conclusions. Gamification and the use of a statistically induced chunking recall task in an auditory SL task improved the task’s psychometric properties in school-aged children with reading difficulties. Auditory SL was also associated with concurrent reading skills in these children, suggesting that the implicit learning of regularities in spoken language input may additionally support reading development.

articles.title: Questionable prospective effects between shame, loneliness, and non-suicidal self-injury among Chinese adolescents: A reassessment of Chen et al. (2026)
articles.authors: Kimmo Sorjonen; Bo Melin; Marika Melin
articles.abstract: Chen et al. argued that shame and loneliness play a role in the longitudinal emergence of non-suicidal self-injury among adolescents. However, significant cross-lagged parameters do not by themselves establish genuine prospective influence because similar estimates may arise through alternative statistical processes. Using simulated data that reproduced the sample size and correlation matrix reported by Chen et al., we examined whether their conclusions were robust across several defensible analytic specifications. The pattern of results depended strongly on analytic choice: some models suggested positive prospective associations, whereas others indicated negative or null effects. When estimates from all specifications were combined using meta-analytic methods, no overall effect reached statistical significance. Accordingly, the available evidence does not provide a firm basis for concluding that shame, loneliness, and non-suicidal self-injury exert reciprocal prospective influences on one another. In line with multiverse-analysis recommendations, conclusions should be drawn from the collective pattern across reasonable analytical alternatives rather than from a single model.

articles.title: Neuroscience-Informed Psychoeducation for Dementia
articles.authors: William Goette
articles.abstract: Dementia is a progressive syndrome characterized by neurodegeneration across distributed brain networks that results in cognitive, behavioral, and functional declines. Conventional psychoeducation provides disease facts and resources but often lacks the mechanistic grounding needed to translate knowledge into durable caregiver skills. Neuroscience-informed psychoeducation (NIPE) extends traditional approaches by offering brain-based explanations of symptoms and caregiving challenges, paired with learning principles optimized for stressed learners. This chapter proposes a dementia-specific NIPE framework grounded in network-level neuroscience and cognitive reserve, specifying core content domains across the disease course, delivery structures, and mechanism of efficacy. The chapter synthesizes evidence for effectiveness, cost-effectiveness, cultural adaptation, clinician training, and outcome measurement, presenting NIPE as a pragmatic approach to strengthening person-centered dementia care.

articles.title: STORM: Study of Open Research Methods in Undergraduate Psychology Students
articles.authors: Marta Topor; Charlotte Bradley; Kait Clark; Emily Kate Farran; Adele Lindsay; Su Morris; Bertil Wegmann; Ashley Yvette Williams; Priya Silverstein; Katie Anne Gilligan-Lee
articles.abstract: The open research movement reflects an ongoing research culture change that aims to tackle issues of research replicability, reduce the use of questionable research practices, and improve the quality of research. We argue that a cornerstone of changing research culture in the psychological sciences and increasing the use and implementation of open research practices is through the training and development of junior researchers, i.e., undergraduate/bachelor students. In this paper, we present findings from the Study of Open Research Methods (STORM), which investigated understanding (contextual and situational perceptions, awareness, and experience) of the replication crisis and open research in undergraduate psychology students in the UK for the first time. Cross-sectional data were collected over three waves (2020-2022) with a total of 2,063 student responses. Our findings provide benchmarks of psychology student understanding of the replication crisis and open research across the UK. The most consistent predictor was students’ year of study, reflecting increasing open research knowledge and experience over the course of their psychology programmes. In Wave 1, this predictor showed evidence of an effect only for universities with a local UKRN lead, whilst in Wave 2 evidence of an effect was present for the other universities on some of the outcome measures. Our exploratory findings reflect a likely increase in open research teaching between 2020 and 2022 in universities with a local UKRN lead. This paper highlights areas for student improvement in open research understanding and teaching gaps in undergraduate research methods training.

articles.title: The precision hierarchy hypothesis: A unifying framework to explain opposing serial effects
articles.authors: Carina Ufer; Helen Blank
articles.abstract: Serial dependence, the phenomenon where current perception is biased toward the previous stimulus, has been interpreted as a mechanism for perceptual stability, smoothing variability in sensory input. However, analyses that include both the previous stimulus and previous response unmasked repulsive effects at the sensory level that were otherwise concealed. Moreover, attractive serial biases fail to scale with environmental correlations, challenging their primary role in maintaining stability. We propose the Precision hierarchy hypothesis, grounded in predictive processing, as a unifying framework for these seemingly contradictory findings. Repulsive effects naturally emerge when priors - shaped by recent trials - are highly precise, making small deviations in incoming input more probable under alternative priors. We further propose that prior precision decreases across hierarchical levels. A higher precision at lower sensory levels leads to repulsive effects, as even small deviations in incoming signal are in conflict with the prior. In contrast, attractive biases emerge at higher, more abstract levels, where deviations are integrated with broader conceptual priors. By dynamically shaping prior precision according to environmental correlations, perception remains adaptive, balancing the need for stability with the sensitivity to detect meaningful changes in the environment. This framework reconciles diverse findings on serial effects and provides testable predictions for future research.

articles.title: Truth Bias in Human Reinforcement Learning
articles.authors: Juan Vidal-Perez; Raymond J Dolan; Rani Moran
articles.abstract: Humans display a truth bias, a default tendency to treat incoming information as true unless there is reason to doubt its veracity.  Whether this bias is confined to the evaluation and recollection of declarative information, or extends to  how  we learn and make decisions, remains unknown. Here, we introduce a computational reinforcement-learning framework in which participants receive choice-outcome feedback from sources explicitly identified as truthful or untruthful. Because truthful and untruthful feedback are matched in their objective informational value, the task isolates asymmetries in how feedback truthfulness shapes learning. Across two behavioural studies (total n = 403; Study 2 pre-registered), truthful feedback exerted a greater influence on learning and subsequent choice than equally informative untruthful feedback. This learning asymmetry deviated from optimal statistical learning and persisted when we manipulated the prevalence of untruthful sources. The asymmetry also extended beyond reinforcement learning. Participants showed a corresponding truth bias in explicit inference, and individual differences in explicit and reinforcement-learning truth biases were positively correlated. Moreover, combining reinforcement learning with evidence-accumulation modelling revealed that merely anticipating feedback from an untruthful source reduced the efficiency with which learned values guided evidence accumulation, producing slower and less accurate choices before any feedback was received. Thus, truth asymmetries span multiple facets of cognitive processing, from learning and explicit inference through to value-based decision making. Together, these findings show that truthful and untruthful information are not cognitively equivalent even when they carry the same objective information.

articles.title: Large Language Models for Test-Enhanced Learning: A Tutorial and Proof of Concept
articles.authors: Ariana Modirrousta-Galian; Daryl Yu Heng Lee; Frederic Dick; Eva Lash; David Shanks
articles.abstract: Practice tests improve retention of studied information and enhance learning and retrieval of new information (test-enhanced learning; TEL). In five preregistered studies (total N = 623)—four online randomized experiments and one correlational classroom study with final-year psychology undergraduates—we examined whether large language models (LLMs; Gemini and ChatGPT) can generate practice tests that promote TEL and whether this use of LLMs can be feasibly incorporated into a classroom setting. LLM-generated multiple-choice tests with fixed feedback did not improve 2-day recall of a TED Talk relative to a control (Studies 1 and 2). In contrast, LLM-generated short-answer tests with personalized feedback significantly improved 7-day recall of an educational video relative to rewatching it (Studies 3 and 4), regardless of whether final test format matched that of the practice test. In the classroom study, participation in fortnightly LLM-generated short-answer tests (with personalized feedback) on lecture content was positively associated with graded assessment performance, and students’ attitudes towards this use of LLMs were generally favorable. Overall, we demonstrate that LLMs can substantially reduce the practical burden of implementing TEL, while maintaining sufficiently good question quality and enabling automated personalized feedback, and that this approach can be feasibly deployed in an undergraduate psychology class.

articles.title: Eye Tracking and NLP: A Survey and an Outlook
articles.authors: Yevgeni Berzak; David Robert Reich; Omer Shubi; Lena A. Jäger
articles.abstract: With the rise of LLMs, NLP has been redefining itself as a field of study, with an increasing interest shift towards areas such as NLP for science, model analysis, human-centered AI and user-facing applications. As part of this transformation, in recent years, a new area of NLP which combines text processing with eye movements in reading has been emerging. Recent work has demonstrated that this area has a strong potential for driving innovation in NLP and enhancing its scientific and societal impact. In this survey, we characterize the main streams of work on the intersection of eye tracking for reading and NLP, provide critical commentary on promises and challenges, and identify key open directions that can guide future work in this area.

articles.title: Identifying people with psychotic illnesses who could reduce or discontinue antipsychotic medications with a lower risk of relapse: a scoping review
articles.authors: Anna Liguori; Sarah Markham; Elen Williams; Firoza Davies; Anna Ferguson Montague; Alexandra Burton; Natalie Shoham
articles.abstract:
Background: Psychotic disorders can confer a substantial illness burden. Whilst Antipsychotic Medications (APMs) are effective in preventing relapse, they are associated with significant adverse effects, leading some patients to consider APM dose reduction or discontinuation.
Aim: We aimed to synthesise evidence on factors associated with relapse vs no relapse following APM dose reduction or discontinuation in patients with psychotic disorders.
