Methods: We searched Embase, PsycINFO, PubMed, CINAHL and grey literature sources with no date restrictions and followed PRISMA guidelines. We included evidence sources which reported on factors associated with relapse/ no relapse following APM dose reduction or discontinuation in patients with a psychotic disorder, or tools to identify patients with a lower risk of relapse. We consulted our Lived Experience Advisory Panel (LEAP) throughout the review process.
Results: 69 studies met our inclusion criteria. 60 reported empirical evidence on factors associated with relapse/ no relapse, while 8 sources provided expert opinion or guideline-based recommendations and 1 source included both empirical results and expert opinion. We identified 62 independent factors across sociodemographic, illness, treatment, and biological domains. No factor had sufficiently consistent evidence to support its use as a reliable predictor of relapse. Factors reported in expert opinion pieces and guidelines largely aligned with those in empirical studies.
Conclusions: While factors affecting relapse risk following APM dose reduction or discontinuation are increasingly being researched, current evidence does not support any specific factor as a predictor of successful APM dose reduction or discontinuation. Nevertheless, several potentially promising factors warrant further investigation.

articles.title: Uncorrected publication bias distorts the spindle-memory link: Comment on Chen et al (2024) “Sleep spindles consolidate declarative memory with tags: A meta-analysis of adult data”
articles.authors: Péter Przemyslaw Ujma
articles.abstract: The recent meta-analyis by Chen et al (2024) investigates the link between sleep spindles and the consolidation of tagged declarative memory traces and reports substantial publication bias. The present commentary discusses the significance of publication bias in the literature of the cognitive neuroscience of sleep spindles. Using the dataset published by the original authors, it is demonstrated that with adequate controls for publication bias, the link between sleep spindles and memory consolidation is greatly diminished or absent, in line with the pattern seen in other recent meta-analyses. Large samples, transparent and standardized analysis strategies, and strict controls for publication bias in meta-analyses are essential to ensure replicability in the cognitive neuroscience of sleep spindles.

articles.title: A Browser-Based Remote Photoplethysmography Method for Live Heart Rate Estimation
articles.authors: Mariana Von Mohr; Manos Tsakiris; Gianluca Finotti
articles.abstract: Remote photoplethysmography (rPPG) enables contact-free heart-rate estimation from facial video, but most web-based implementations process recordings offline, limiting their use in real-time experimental applications. We developed and, to our knowledge, provide the first ECG validation of a live rPPG implementation embedded directly within Gorilla Experiment Builder, a widely used platform for online behavioural research. We validated the method in 27 participants against simultaneously recorded electrocardiography (ECG) across nine trial durations ranging from 10 to 50 s. rPPG-derived heart rate showed excellent agreement with ECG-derived heart rate, with a mean absolute error of 1.48 bpm, a root mean square error of 2.19 bpm, and an ICC(A,1) of .960. Mean bias was small (0.40 bpm), with repeated-measures 95% limits of agreement from -3.85 to 4.66 bpm, and heart-rate error did not differ significantly by trial durations. These findings support the feasibility of live rPPG within a browser-based experimental platform for physiological feedback and adaptive online experiments without requiring webcam videos to be stored or processed offline.

articles.title: The broken brain? Prevalence and consequences of brain framing of mental disorders
articles.authors: Olha Guley; Sanil Shashank Pandhare; Elena Pasquinelli; Daniel Nettle
articles.abstract: Public discourse often frames mental disorders as brain disorders, yet little is known about how this framing shapes lay beliefs. We combined large-scale text analysis of 55,068 New York Times articles with one correlational study (N = 204) and four preregistered vignette experiments (total N = 2,445) to examine both the prevalence and consequences of “brain talk” about mental disorders. We find that brain framing has become much more prevalent since 1980, and especially since 2004. We find evidence that brain framing increases belief in other biological and genetic causes; reduces belief in psychological and environmental causes, and strengthens beliefs in the efficacy of medication as a treatment. Effects on pessimism about recovery varied across studies and disorders. Brain framing had no robust effects on perceived age of onset, duration, severity, or beliefs about efficacy of psychotherapy treatment. Public beliefs about mental disorders are malleable and can be shaped by framing, highlighting the cognitive and societal consequences of brain framing in communication about mental health.

articles.title: Norm Commitment as a Link Between ‘Dark’ Personality and Norm Violation
articles.authors: Marie Joséphine Hamatschek; Miriam Wittpoth; Celina Marke
articles.abstract: ‘Dark’ personality traits predict criminal action, yet the underlying mechanism remains underspecified. We propose legal norm commitment (LNC) – an affectively anchored inner bond to the law – as an underlying mechanism. Based in a criminal-psychological action theory, LNC is assumed to build on (a) belief in the law (requiring overlap between inner direction and the law, or DLO; plus moral-emotional imperativeness) and (b) attachment to significant others. In a sample of incarcerated and free participants (N = 387), we assessed psychopathy (boldness, meanness, disinhibition), Machiavellianism, narcissistic entitlement, guilt proneness, LNC, and a catalogue of specific past norm violations via self-report. We used mediation analyses to test whether the norm violation tendency was predicted by the LNC (components) contained in the personality traits (implying conceptual overlap, not a causal relation). DLO partly accounted for personality–norm violation associations for all expected traits, but not for disinhibition, supporting a mechanism-based distinction between ‘dark’ and dysregulatory traits. Attachment and imperativeness showed no mediating effects. Among the traits investigated, meanness and guilt proneness shared the most variance with behaviorally effective LNC components. Given these preliminary findings, LNC as a value-free, mechanism-based concept might clarify some of the ‘darkness’ of personality.

articles.title: Using Customised LLM-Based Chatbots in Psychological Research: A Practical Tutorial
articles.authors: Hu Meilan; Gabriel Rongyang Lau; Adalia Yin Hui Goh; Samuel Rhys Cox; Louis Tay; Andree Hartanto
articles.abstract: Large language model (LLM)-based chatbots offer new methodological opportunities for psychological research by enabling scalable, standardised, and interactive research procedures. However, their usefulness depends on the researchers’ ability to customise, evaluate, and deploy them in ways that align with the methodological requirements of a given study. The current tutorial provides a practical, step-by-step framework for developing customised LLM-based chatbots for psychological research. We distinguish between no-code or low-code development approaches, including provider-hosted chatbot builders and visual or low-code programming platforms, and code-based approaches using proprietary model application programming interfaces (APIs) or locally hosted open-weight models. We compare these approaches in terms of technical expertise, behavioural and workflow control, study integration, cost, data governance, maintenance, and reproducibility. We also outline key components of the process of customising an LLM-based chatbot and illustrate deployment workflows across multiple platforms, including local desktop interfaces, messaging applications and survey platforms. Finally, we discuss key considerations for research ethics, privacy, data governance, security, transparency, and reproducibility, including recommendations for documenting and sharing chatbot configurations and study procedures. Through this tutorial, we aim to support researchers in integrating customised LLM-based chatbots into psychological research and in expanding the methodological possibilities available to them.

articles.title: Longitudinal and Latent-variable Extensions of the Triadic Actor-Partner Interdependence
articles.authors: Shiyao Wang; Jennifer Dang Guay; Karla Van Leeuwen; Evelien Schat; Eva Ceulemans
articles.abstract: When modeling interpersonal processes within triadic systems, researchers commonly encounter two types of analytical complexity: observations collected repeatedly over time, and constructs measured via multiple items. The current study introduces longitudinal and latent-variable extensions of the standard triadic Actor-Partner Interdependence Model (tAPIM) to accommodate these data structures. The longitudinal extensions, the concurrent tAPIM and the temporal tAPIM, account for temporal dependence and temporal precedence in repeated observations, while the latent-variable extension models each member’s construct as a latent variable measured from multiple observed items. In addition, we identify measurement invariance across triad members as a challenge specific to triadic data analysis and conduct a simulation study to investigate the consequences of its violation for the estimation of actor and partner effects. The results indicate that: 1) imposing invariance constraints that are not empirically supported may bias the estimation of nonzero actor and partner effects associated with the noninvariant member, while effects of invariant members and zero effects are accurately recovered; 2) relaxing invariance constraints avoids bias in point estimates, but standard errors of effects associated with the noninvariant member were still inflated, reducing power to detect true effects. The current paper offers practical guidance for researchers modeling interdependence in triadic systems using multi-item or longitudinal data.

articles.title: Norms for Emotional Valence and Polarity for 3,596 French Words: Implications for Lexical Processing
articles.authors: Aurélie Garrone; Maximiliano A. Wilson; Georges Chedid; Christophe Bedetti; Guillaume T. Vallet; Simona Maria Brambati; Maxime Montembeault
articles.abstract: Language and emotion are closely interconnected, with words carrying affective properties, such as emotional valence, ranging from negative to positive with a neutral midpoint, and emotional polarity, which reflects the absolute distance from that midpoint. Although norms for emotional valence and polarity exist in many languages, they remain limited for French, particularly Québec French. We therefore aim to 1) develop norms for emotional valence and emotional polarity in a set of 3,596 highly characterized French words taken from the French Lexicon Project (Ferrand et al., 2010); and 2) assess the influence of valence and polarity on lexical decision times in a word recognition task. A group of 351 French-speaking participants from Quebec took part in an online valence rating task and rated words on a 0-100 scale based on their emotional content. Descriptive norms for valence and polarity (mean, standard deviation) were then prepared for each word and are available open access on lexique.org. Both emotional valence and polarity were found to be significant predictors of lexical decision time. In particular, positive words were significantly associated with faster lexical decision times, compared to neutral and negative words. Our study provides novel standardized norms of emotional valence and polarity for Québec French, supporting research at the intersection of language and emotion in an understudied linguistic context, and helps shed some light onto the role of affective dimensions of language in word processing.

articles.title: It's a small world of signs: Semantic network structure in American Sign Language based on free associations
articles.authors: Zed Sehyr; Karen Emmorey; Elana Pontecorvo; Naomi Kenney Caselli; Erin Michelle Buchanan
articles.abstract: Semantic network analyses have shown that words in spoken languages are organized into efficient "small-world" structures that support rapid lexical access and retrieval. However, little is known about whether similar organizational principles generalize to sign languages. We present the first large-scale analysis of semantic network structure in American Sign Language (ASL) using a free semantic association task. Deaf ASL signers (N = 45) produced three associations to 2,714 cue signs drawn from ASL-LEX, resulting in almost 100,000 cue–response pairs. We constructed (a) directed associative networks based on cue-response relationships and (b) undirected conceptual similarity networks based on cue–to-cue cosine similarity and compared ASL with English using matched subsets of the Small World of Words norms. We estimated network statistics and evaluated network topology using bootstrapping and degree-preserving random graphs. Both languages exhibited small-world organization indicating similar pressures on efficient semantic organization across language modalities. However, the languages differed in topology. Across network types, ASL exhibited longer average path lengths, and in conceptual similarity networks, lower clustering, suggesting reduced integration. In associative networks, ASL showed lower modularity, while in the conceptual similarity networks, ASL showed higher modularity than English, indicating a more compartmentalized semantic space. Further, more frequent signs occupied denser and more diverse semantic neighborhoods, whereas iconic signs exhibited fewer semantic connections and lower response diversity. These findings suggest that semantic memory is shaped by modality-independent organizational principles while also reflecting language-specific network topologies and structural pressures. The dataset and tools provide a basis for future cross-linguistic investigations.

articles.title: Partisans are more likely to entrench their beliefs in misinformation when political outgroup members correct claims
articles.authors: Diego A. Reinero; Elizabeth Ann Harris; Steve Rathje; Annie Duke; Jay Joseph Van Bavel
articles.abstract:
Misinformation has become a global issue with potentially dire consequences (e.g., election
results, COVID-19 vaccines, international conflicts). The most common strategy to reduce
beliefs in misinformation is to issue corrections or fact-checks. However, fact-checks are often
ineffective for polarized issues and there has been debate over whether misinformation
corrections sometimes "backfire," causing people to become more entrenched in misinformation.
Across three experiments (N = 1,217) we identify a key feature – the partisan identity of the
source – that explains when corrections will be effective and when they will be most likely to
backfire. We found that while corrections work on average, backfires still occurred 23% of the
time and were 52% more likely to occur when the correction came from a political outgroup vs.
ingroup member – leaving people with more entrenched beliefs in misinformation. Indeed, the
effect of partisan bias on initial belief in misinformation was 5x larger than the effect of
corrections. Partisan bias was most prominent and corrections were least effective when famous
politicians were involved. In sum, corrections have small effects compared to partisan identity
congruence, and sometimes backfire–especially if they come from a political outgroup member.

articles.title: Gender Differences in Self-reported Emotional Sharing in Social Interaction: A Meta Analysis
articles.authors: X. Jia; Karen Holtmaat; Y. Mo; ZIHAO Zeng; M. Kaneva; Annet Kleiboer; Sander L. Koole
articles.abstract: Through emotional sharing, individuals can make their emotional experiences available to others, creating opportunities for interpersonal emotion regulation. Although gender differences in these behaviours have been documented across various domains, findings regarding their magnitude and consistency remain inconclusive. This meta-analysis examined gender differences in emotional sharing among adults. A systematic search identified 32 articles comprising 37 independent samples, 155 effect sizes, and 13,147 participants, including 8,504 women and 4,643 men. Overall, women reported higher levels of emotional sharing than men, g = 0.31, 95% CI [0.18, 0.44]. This effect was not significantly moderated by (1) functions (emotional expression, emotional disclosure, emotional expression as coping), (2) temporal level (dispositional, situational), (3) emotional valence (negative, positive or unspecified), (4) specific negative emotion (anger, sadness, fear/anxiety, shame/guilt, and unspecified negative emotions), and (5) the interpersonal target (romantic partner, friend, other, or no partner specified). Despite the absence of significant moderation effects, pooled estimates within most subgroups remained significantly positive, indicating higher levels of expression and disclosure among women than men across a wide range of emotional contexts and interpersonal relations.

articles.title: Family-Specific Dynamics Between Parenting and Preschoolers’ Self-Regulation: Evidence from 100-Day Daily Diary Data
articles.authors: Dian Yu; Lauren G. Bailes; Jaely DeLeon; Juliana Marie Agnolet
articles.abstract: Current research supports that parenting practice contributes to individual differences in preschoolers’ self-regulation (SR). Dynamic systems theory suggests that the link between parenting and child SR may be bidirectional and family-specific. Taking a dynamic systems perspective, this study examined the daily bidirectional link between parenting practices and preschoolers’ SR and the family-specific holistic dynamic patterns. Thirty-nine families took part in a 100-day daily diary study in the United States. Using dynamic structural equation modeling, we examined the autoregressive and cross-lagged effects of daily parental responsiveness, negative reactivity, and child self-regulation. Autoregressive and cross-lagged effects were estimated as random slopes, allowing the dynamic effects to vary from family to family. On average, parental responsiveness predicted future SR, and SR predicted future negative reactivity. Significant heterogeneity was identified, indicating that the bidirectional links between parenting and SR were family-specific. Considering autoregressive and cross-lagged effects holistically, all families showed a tendency to return to their equilibrium states, defined by their personal means of responsiveness, negative reactivity, and SR. Among the 39 families, 19 families had a mutually influential connection between negative reactivity and SR, and one family had a mutually influential connection between responsiveness and SR. The rest of the families did not show a mutually influential pattern between parenting and child SR. The findings highlighted the importance of considering heterogeneity in the holistic within-family processes. The effectiveness of future interventions should be considered family-specifically and as changes in family dynamic patterns.

articles.title: Political Emotions Shape Preferences for Leaders’ Facial Traits: Anger Favors Dominance, Fear Favors Trustworthiness
articles.authors: Mariana Von Mohr; Manos Tsakiris
articles.abstract: Past work shows that conservatives prefer more dominant-looking political leaders, whereas liberals prefer more trustworthy-looking ones. We extend this by showing that, beyond partisanship, discrete political emotions independently shape preferences for leaders’ facial traits. A balanced sample of U.S. Republicans and Democrats identified the political issue that made them most angry or most afraid and then chose which leader would best address that issue using computer-generated faces varying in dominance and trustworthiness. Participants chose a more dominant and less trustworthy-looking leader more often when angry (49.5 percent) than when fearful (46.5 percent). Mechanistically, anger shifted choices toward more dominant-looking leaders by increasing reliance on dominance cues and reducing reliance on trustworthiness cues, whereas fear selectively increased reliance on trustworthiness cues. These findings show that political emotions exert distinct influences on leader evaluation with implications for democratic decision-making and electoral choices.

articles.title: The Development of Compositionality in Language and Thought
articles.authors: Eulalie Péquay; Isabelle Dautriche
articles.abstract:
Compositionality is the property of a representational system whereby com-plex meanings
arise from the combination of simpler meaningful elements. Here we take a developmental
perspective to understand the origins of compositional representational systems and their
relation to language—an issue that bears on longstanding debates in cognitive science about
the structure of the human mind. Based on our review, we conclude that (a) well-controlled
evidence for compositional abilities during language acquisition remains scarce, although
some studies suggest infants begin to understand specific multiword combinations during the
second year of life, and (b) the key computation underlying compositionality—function
application—can be observed in infancy during the first year of life, well before, and even out-
side, compositional language. These findings suggest the mind may support compositional
operations prior to the emergence of compositional language, while leaving open questions
about how the development of compositional thought and compositional language interact.

articles.title: From Epic to Applied Psychology: A Conceptual Mapping of Sanskrit Psychological Constructs and Their Contemporary Relevance
articles.authors: Manoj Kumar Mallick
articles.abstract: This conceptual paper examines whether four Sanskrit epic constructs hold structural resonance with four established areas of psychological science. It responds to a growing interest in integrating Indian Knowledge Systems with psychological theory, extending that integration into underexplored epic material. Sanskrit's own literary and grammatical heritage has long been recognised in linguistics and aesthetics; this paper asks whether its psychological vocabulary deserves comparable recognition. Following a conceptual-article design (Theory Synthesis), the paper pairs dharma saṅkaṭa with moral cognition, tapas-nirvṛtti with self-regulation, rasa with affective science, and karma yoga with motivation theory. Four criteria—definitional precision, scope-matching, textual traceability, and precision over popularity—guided construct selection. Constructs were drawn from named episodes in the Mahābhārata, Kumārasambhava, and Buddhacarita, rather than from Sanskrit thought treated generally. Each pairing shows meaningful structural alignment without collapsing into a single unifying model. Applied implications extend to education, therapy, policy, and Gen-Z digital burnout, illustrating the pairings' contemporary relevance. Each pairing was illustrated through a textual episode and a contemporary vignette, grounding abstract resonance in concrete cases. The paper offers four testable propositions for future empirical validation. It also proposes a shared vocabulary bridging Sanskrit psychological thought and contemporary science, without claiming either tradition anticipated or exhausts the other.

articles.title: Moral Concern for AI in an Economic Game
articles.authors: Carter Allen; Joshua Lewis; Lucius Caviola
articles.abstract: How will people morally regard increasingly human-like artificial intelligence systems? We introduce the AI Harm Game, a novel paradigm examining whether people will harm AI for personal gain. In our study, 498 U.S. participants interacted with GPT-4o in a three-round economic game. In each round, participants chose whether to harm the AI for a small monetary bonus (causing it to vividly simulate suffering) or refrain from harming it (eliciting gratitude). Although participants were overwhelmingly skeptical that current AIs can suffer, their decisions and reasoning about whether to harm the AI varied considerably. Participants harmed the AI in 1.4 out of 3 rounds on average. Women and older participants were more reluctant to harm the AI, while participants higher on measures of selfishness and psychopathy were more willing. These findings reveal that even without attributing consciousness to them, many people hesitate to harm responsive AIs, suggesting people’s moral impulses may generalize to future human–AI relationships.

articles.title: Evaluating dyadic interdependence between cannabis attitudes and parental monitoring processes among parents and adolescents
articles.authors: Tram Doran; Emily Olenik; Sarah Ryan; Alexandria LeVert; Jane Metrik; Pearl Ayiku; Samuel Meisel; Jack Rusley; Anthony Spirito; Sarah Ann Thomas
articles.abstract: Cannabis is a commonly used substance during adolescence. As US legalization expands, public perception of cannabis increasingly reflects the view that it is less harmful than other substances. The extent to which parents monitor and know about their adolescent’s activities and whereabouts is an important tool to manage risk behaviors like substance use. However, it is unclear how parental monitoring may vary based on cannabis attitudes. The current study investigated how parents' and adolescents’ attitudes toward cannabis (risk of harm to teens, disapproval, and ease of availability) are associated with parental knowledge about adolescents’ whereabouts/activities and its sources (adolescent disclosure, parental solicitation). We hypothesized that lower perceived risk of harm and less disapproval of cannabis use would be associated with lower levels of parental monitoring among both parents and adolescents. Our sample was N = 73 adolescents ages 14–17 (59% female) and their caregivers. Lower parental perceived risk of harm to teens from cannabis use was associated with less adolescent-reported parental solicitation. Lower adolescent perceived risk of harm to teens from cannabis use was linked to less adolescent disclosure to parents. Greater adolescent-perceived cannabis availability was associated with (a) both adolescent- and parent-report that parents knew less about adolescents’ whereabouts and activities, and (b) lower adolescent-report of less disclosure to parents. Results highlight the interdependent nature of parent and adolescent cannabis perceptions in relation to monitoring processes. Parents may benefit from public health initiatives that provide them with information on the potential negative health and emotional consequences of cannabis use in adolescence.

articles.title: Associations between dark triad traits and affective and cognitive theory of mind
articles.authors: Lucy Hampson; Caitlin Hill; Kacie Hoyles; Ellie Hunstone; Gareth Richards
articles.abstract: The dark triad comprises three socially aversive personality traits: Machiavellianism, subclinical psychopathy, and subclinical narcissism. Theory of Mind (ToM) involves ability to infer thoughts and beliefs (socio-cognitive component) and attribute emotional states to others (socio-perceptual component). With conflicting findings in the literature, we utilised a cross-sectional online survey to examine correlations between dark triad traits and ToM. Zero-order correlations revealed negative associations between narcissism and socio- cognitive ToM, and between psychopathy and socio-perceptual ToM. Although follow-up multiple regression models were not statistically significant, psychopathy remained a significant predictor of socio-perceptual ToM once age and sex had been controlled for. Conclusion drawn from these data should consider the relatively small and unrepresentative sample, and low internal consistency observed for the ToM measures.

articles.title: The beliefs at the heart of multilingual family language policies: A corpus-assisted discourse study of parental attitudes towards childhood multilingualism
articles.authors: Ruth Kircher; Melanie Brouillard; Alexa Ahooja; Erin Quirk; Susan Ballinger; Linda Polka; Krista Byers-Heinlein
articles.abstract: This study focuses on parental language beliefs, which we approach from an attitudes perspective. Language attitudes are at the heart of multilingual family language policies because they shape parents’ language practices and language management – and thereby, ultimately, children’s multilingual development. Based on French and English corpora (over 30,000 words in total) comprising 742 Quebec-based parents’ responses to an open-ended survey question, we present a corpus-assisted discourse study of parental attitudes towards childhood multilingualism. We analyse frequencies and collocations to attest statistically significant patterns, and we examine concordance lines and longer text segments to establish meaning in context. Our findings confirm the multidimensionality of parental attitudes towards childhood multilingualism, providing new insights into the nature of the three previously-established dimensions – status, solidarity, and cognitive development – as well as revealing a potential fourth dimension: personality development. The study thus makes a contribution to the family language policy framework and to language attitude theory more generally. Moreover, the findings show systematic differences between parents transmitting multiple societal languages versus parents transmitting heritage languages alongside one/more societal languages. The study thus also makes a practical contribution by facilitating the development of tailored support measures for different types of multilingual families.

articles.title: Playing for fun, playing to escape: Gaming motives and problematic video game use in a French sample aged 6 to 45 years
articles.authors: Chloe Nguyen; Quentin Hallez
articles.abstract: Data on the prevalence of problematic gaming in France are scarce, and few studies have compared gaming behavior, gaming motives, and their correlates across developmental periods with identical instruments. We surveyed 676 French participants aged 6 to 45 years (52.4% male), spanning childhood (6–14 years; parent-reported), adolescence (15–17), young adulthood (18–25), and adulthood (26–45), using the Game Addiction Scale (GAS-7), the Motives for Online Gaming Questionnaire (MOGQ), the WHO-5 Well-Being Index, and the Barratt Impulsiveness Scale (BIS-15). Overall, 79.6% of participants played video games. Problematic gaming (monothetic GAS criterion) characterized 4.8% of gamers, with no significant differences across age groups and rates three times higher in males than in females. Although symptom levels were similar across age groups, motive profiles were not: recreation dominated at every age, whereas coping and escape motives were rare in childhood and markedly higher from adolescence onward. In hierarchical regressions, escape and competition motives and gaming frequency were the strongest unique correlates of problematic use, statistically attenuating the bivariate contributions of gender, impulsivity, well-being, and gaming time. Motive–symptom associations were invariant across age groups, whereas the association between gaming time and symptoms was stronger in older age groups. These cross-sectional findings suggest that motivational assessment may be more informative than screen-time metrics for the prevention and screening of problematic gaming.

articles.title: Getting Closer or Stepping Back? Personal Space Adjustments Following Facial Emotion Imitation and Observation
articles.authors: Ivan Patané; Clément Desoche; ALESSANDRO FARNE; Fadila Hadj-Bouziane
articles.abstract: Regulating personal space (PS) is essential for navigating social interactions. Although emotional cues are known to influence PS, the mechanisms underlying this modulation remain poorly understood. The present study investigated whether active facial emotion imitation is followed by changes in PS regulation and whether these changes differ from those observed following passive emotion observation. Participants completed a Virtual Reality Stop-Distance task to assess their preferred interpersonal distances from angry, happy, and neutral virtual agents, before and after an imitation session, during which they actively imitated angry or happy facial expressions. Following emotion imitation, participants exhibited a bidirectional modulation of PS: they increased their distance from angry virtual agents and decreased it from happy virtual agents, while no changes were observed for neutral agents. These findings suggest that active facial imitation enhances sensitivity to emotional signals and adaptively modulates interpersonal distance. Eye-tracking analyses revealed no significant changes in gaze behavior between pre- and post-imitation sessions, indicating that the reported effects were not driven by differences in overt visual attention. In a second experiment using a similar pre-post design, a new group of participants passively observed the same emotional expressions without imitating them. Results showed that, after emotion observation, angry virtual agents elicited an increased interpersonal distance, whereas no changes in distance from either the happy or neutral virtual agents were observed. Together, these results indicate that defensive distancing from others’ angry expressions followed both active imitation and passive observation, whereas the approach-related reduction in distance in response to happy expressions was evident after active imitation only. These findings highlight the contribution of emotional-cue exposure to personal space regulation in social contexts and provide further evidence that emotional experience can dynamically shape interpersonal behavior.

articles.title: Linking Traits and Behavior Through Computational Modeling of Neuroethical Decisions
articles.authors: Brian Kim; Kianté Fernandez; John Medaglia
articles.abstract: Individual differences in psychology are often measured through self-report questionnaires or behavioral performance, yet these approaches capture different constructs and rarely align. Computational modeling provides a framework for connecting both measures, as it extracts a process-level description of cognition from observable behavior in the form of latent variables. These latent variables represent repeated patterns of decision-making that should relate to psychological traits. We applied this approach to neuroethical decision-making, where evidence shows that both behavioral performance and self-reported psychological traits are related to how individuals weigh uncertain risks against potential benefits of emerging brain technologies. Participants completed a neuromodulation task in which risk and benefit probabilities were systematically varied. To capture how decisions unfolded, we used a temporally sensitive diffusion decision model that estimates when and how risks and benefits are evaluated. These model parameters described general trends in task behavior: individuals considered risks earlier and weighed risks more highly than benefits. Additionally, model parameters described how individuals modified their behavior: individuals who considered benefits first according to the model tended to endorse neuromodulation, but shifted towards rejection when risks were evaluated earlier. Importantly, self-reported psychological traits related to these computational parameters. Cognitive factors such as risk propensity and numeracy related to risk sensitivity and evaluation timing, while prosocial traits were also related to evaluation timing and benefit sensitivity. By contrast, Religion & Spirituality and Moral Commitment measures showed lower than expected associations across parameters. By capturing process-level mechanisms, computational modeling served as a bridge between self-reported traits and observed behavior, showing how stable individual differences shape the dynamics of decision-making in neuroethical contexts.

articles.title: Credible Signaling through Sound – the Role of Timbre in Music Recognition in Young BaYaka Foragers
articles.authors: Matthias Melchior Chanan van der Vlist; Jiaxin Li; Frans T. M. van Schaik; Roger Mundry; Henkjan Honing; Karline R. L. Janmaat
articles.abstract: This study explored perceptual sensitivity to spectral and temporal acoustic features in music recognition among BaYaka hunter-gatherer children. Using an interactive, non-competitive game (Move to Match), we tested song recognition under various forms of audio degradation to identify which musical dimensions are crucial for recognizing familiar songs. BaYaka children demonstrated robust recognition of songs across unaltered, spectrally degraded, and temporally degraded versions, highlighting sensitivity to multiple acoustic dimensions. We suggest that songs may be recognized despite degradations because of spectral contour processing, rather than pitch and rhythm cues alone. Moreover, recognition performance decreased for duration-degraded songs (“plinks”), as the brevity constrains the cues available to listeners. However, song identification of (spectrally degraded) plinks far exceeded chance levels and outperformed Western adults performing similar tasks. This suggests that onset-transients and spectral shape, contributing to timbre perception, might serve as reliable markers for identifying musical sounds. We discuss the possibility that music cognition evolved for reasons beyond social bonding to support identification of personal contributions within musical exchanges through timbre, which may hold importance in cooperative contexts. As one of the first experimental studies of music perception in hunter-gatherers, this work demonstrates the potential of culturally adapted methods for future cross-cultural research.

articles.title: A questionnaire survey on context-dependent requirements for the trustworthiness of artificial intelligence and humans
articles.authors: Satoshi Nishida
articles.abstract: Trustworthiness has become an important focus of artificial intelligence (AI) research. Although trustworthiness is a multifaceted concept and its requirements may depend on the context in which AI is used, little is known about how the public perceives these requirements. To address this issue, we conducted a questionnaire survey with nonexpert participants to examine the requirements that the public considers important for trustworthy AI and how their perceived value differs between social and nonsocial contexts. We further compared these context-dependent patterns with those observed for human trustworthiness. Our findings showed that, across social and nonsocial contexts, confidentiality and privacy protection were among the most important requirements for AI trustworthiness whereas the relative importance of other requirements depended on the context. In nonsocial contexts, transparency and interpretability of decision-making were particularly important whereas in social contexts, the ability to collaborate and communicate and a positive public image and attractive appearance were predominantly significant. Although similar context-dependent patterns were observed for human trustworthiness, findings consistently highlighted the ability to collaborate and communicate as a requirement for trusting humans, regardless of context, in contrast to AI trustworthiness. These findings provide insights into the public’s perception of trustworthy AI and highlight the importance of considering the context in which AI is used when examining AI trustworthiness requirements.

articles.title: Self-Generated Goals in the Age of Foundation Models: Artificial Autotelic Agents and Their Implications for Cognitive Science
articles.authors: Gaia Molinaro; Anne Collins; Pierre-Yves Oudeyer; Cédric Colas
articles.abstract: Goals have traditionally been treated as inputs to intelligent systems, biological and artificial, rather than as products of intelligence itself. A growing body of work in cognitive science and artificial intelligence (AI) challenges this framing through autotelic agents — self-improving systems motivated to represent, generate, select, and pursue their own goals. Recent advances in foundation models (large-scale generative AI models trained on broad datasets) expand this research program by extending the languages and tools through which artificial agents can express, evaluate, and pursue goals. By operating over formats such as natural language and code, foundation models allow agents to generate more abstract and compositional goals, approximate human judgments of interestingness and learnability, and support richer loops of problem generation and problem solving. These advances create new opportunities for cognitive science to model human goal dynamics, for AI to build more adaptive autotelic systems, and for human–AI systems to support shared goal exploration without narrowing human agency.

articles.title: “For me, it is like a tide: it is always there...”: a qualitative exploration of dynamic suicidal thoughts in autistic adolescents
articles.authors: Mirabel Pelton; Lilian Clark; Xinxin Zhu; Ed Flexney; Martha Enticott; Rachael Adams; Olivia King; Maria Gardani; Rachel L Moseley-Braund; Tanya L Procyshyn
articles.abstract:
Background
Autistic young people are twice as likely to die by suicide than their non-autistic peers, but mechanisms driving this remain undefined.  This study explored factors contributing to suicidal thoughts in adolescence (aged 11-15), alongside processes of coping and recovery.  

Methods
We conducted reflexive thematic analysis of semi-structured interviews with nine autistic young people (mean age=21.1) to produce conceptual models of: (i) suicide risk; and (ii) recovery. 

Findings
An over-arching theme described adolescent suicidal thoughts as omnipresent, fluctuating, and unpredictably building to crisis. Self-exploration uncovered multiple meanings and functions of suicidal thoughts. Nested sub-theme 1 described the development of autistic identity. Early experiences of rejection and de-humanisation resulted in existential questioning; self-discovery, neuroaffirming resources, and neurodivergent communities enabled agency and a protective autistic identity. Nested sub-theme 2 described marginalisation and social identity. Harmful school environments, pressure to mask autistic traits and invalidation in health services resulted in suicidal distress and crisis. Critical consciousness and leaving education enabled autonomy, purposeful coping and pursuit of life goals. Living well as an autistic person offered greatest protection, but recurrent setbacks and others’ lack of understanding hindered progress. 

Interpretation
Suicidal thoughts and feelings were shaped by interactions between autistic young people and their environment and marked by epistemic injustice.  Findings resonate with the Integrated Motivational-Volitional model’s emphasis on defeat and entrapment; however, defeat was experienced early, and was pervasive and entrenched, while fluctuations in risk were shaped by harmful environments and neuronormative pressures. Findings further support the COURAGE model of suicide recovery, particularly domains for optimising identity, self-understanding, and meaning in life; however, domains dependent on social acceptance and empowerment were less well-supported, suggesting that opportunities were constrained by broader social and structural barriers. Across both models’ structural factors increased risk and constrained the conditions necessary for autistic people to live meaningful and sustainable lives. Clinicians should prioritise neuroaffirming approaches and resources, but lasting reductions in suicide risk in autistic young people will require structural change, including greater equality of opportunity and an urgent action to reduce the distress of educational environments.

articles.title: Relationship Microcultures Theory
articles.authors: Maya Rossignac-Milon; Emma S Miller; Lydia Emery; Joshua Conrad Jackson; Eli Finkel
articles.abstract: Just as groups of people form large-scale macro-cultures, close relationship partners construct their own microculture. Dyads invent their own language (the word “muddles” for homemade ceramics), stories (rescuing their cat), rituals (weekly backgammon), morality (conflicts require mutual apologies), identity (activists), and sense of reality (belief in UFOs). We contend that the emergence, development, and maintenance of this co-created microculture predicts key relational and personal outcomes. We introduce Relationship Microcultures Theory (RMT), which complements prevailing relationship theories by examining how particular words and behaviors are interpreted within the history of the specific relationship in which they acquired idiosyncratic meaning, shaping in turn the well-being of the relationship and the individuals involved. In our Microcultural Unit Model, we describe a meta-theory for understanding how particular dyadic interactions become microcultural units (e.g., inside jokes) by acquiring mutual, idiosyncratic, and referential meaning. In our Aggregate Microculture Model, we advance a theory of how more extensive microcultures—those comprising more units, used more frequently, and spanning more life domains—contribute to relational outcomes (e.g., relationship satisfaction and longevity) and personal outcomes (e.g., meaning in life and self-regulatory success). We also theorize that microcultural extensiveness can undermine relational and personal outcomes when mutuality, idiosyncrasy, and referentiality are low. By examining the dyad as a culture in miniature, RMT opens novel research directions for relationship science.

articles.title: Quantifying the relative associations of time of social media use and addictive social media use with emotional distress among U.S. adults
articles.authors: Hyosin Kim; Jakub Helvich; Giselle Lee; Brian Primack
articles.abstract: Both time of social media use (TSMU) and addictive social media use (ASMU) have been associated with depression and anxiety. However, their relative associations with emotional distress remain unclear, and research involving middle-aged and older adults has been limited. We examined associations of TSMU and ASMU with depression and anxiety in a probability-based nationally-representative sample of 1512 U.S. adults aged 30–70 years. Depression and anxiety were measured using the Patient Health Questionnaire-9 and Generalized Anxiety Disorder-7, respectively. TSMU and ASMU, assessed using the Bergen Social Media Addiction Scale, were both operationalized in quartiles to facilitate direct comparison. In separate weighted logistic regression models, both TSMU and ASMU were associated with depression and anxiety. However, when TSMU and ASMU were included in the same models, associations between TSMU and both depression and anxiety became non-significant, whereas associations between ASMU and both outcomes remained strong (p<0.001 for both). Compared with participants in the lowest quartile of ASMU, those in the highest quartile had between 4 and 5 times the odds for depression (adjusted odds ratio [AOR], 4.94; 95% confidence interval [CI], 3.20–7.62), and anxiety (AOR, 4.59; 95% CI, 2.76–7.63), even after adjusting for TSMU. These findings suggest that ASMU may be more strongly associated with depression and anxiety than overall amount of social media use among U.S. adults.

articles.title: Autobiographical Recollective Style in Grapheme–Color Synesthesia: Overlap with Fantasy Proneness and Multisensory Imagery
articles.authors: Eiko Matsuda; Eiko Matsuda
articles.abstract:
Although more vivid mental imagery and subjectively richer individual autobiographical memories have been reported in
synesthetes, whether synesthesia is associated with a trait-like autobiographical recollective style governing how individuals
typically recollect their personal past remains unclear. We compared 27 participants operationally classified into a grapheme–
color synesthesia group through large-scale screening with 30 controls selected through individual matching on age and sex.
Autobiographical recollective style was assessed using the Japanese version of the Autobiographical Recollection Test (ART-
J), and we examined the extent to which group differences overlapped with Big Five personality traits, fantasy proneness,
and multisensory imagery vividness. The synesthesia group scored higher than the control group on the ART-J total score
and all seven subscales. The group coefficient was not substantially attenuated in a model that included the five Big Five
traits. By contrast, adding fantasy proneness and multisensory imagery significantly increased the explained variance and
substantially attenuated the point estimate of the group coefficient. These findings suggest that the characteristics of the
grapheme–color synesthesia group extend beyond visual imagery to a broad subjective autobiographical recollective style
encompassing scene construction, reliving, rehearsal, and integration into a life story, and that this group difference partly
overlaps with broader characteristics of inner experience.

articles_hidden.title: When Positive Relational Experiences Backfire: Exposure to Forgiving, Consistently Trusting Agents Lowers Subsequent Reciprocity
articles_hidden.authors: Ismail Guennouni; Georgia Koppe; Christoph Korn
articles_hidden.abstract: Can exposure to a forgiving, consistently trusting partner improve interpersonal cooperation? Attachment theory suggests positive relational experiences can correct negative internal working models, but individuals high in rejection sensitivity (RS), characterized by anxious expectations of rejection, may be resistant to such corrective experiences due to stable negative expectations. We tested this using a randomized experiment (N = 206) in which participants played repeated trust games with HMM-based artificial agents that simulate human-like trust dynamics. After a baseline game, participants were exposed to either an idealized partner (an agent designed never to remain in a low-trust state, free from pre-programmed trust withdrawals, and consequently investing more; Manipulation) or a standard agent maintaining typical trust withdrawal patterns (Control), then played a final game with the standard agent; these features were varied together, so the design tests their joint effect. In the primary, powered contrast, exposure to the idealized partner reduced subsequent cooperation, and participants rated the unchanged post-exposure agent less favorably, a pattern consistent with a negative contrast effect, an interpretation developed after initial analysis. RS moderation was a planned analysis but was not separately powered: we detected no moderation of the reduction by RS, and an apparent RS difference in responsiveness to partner investment was not robust once participant-level variation in responsiveness was modeled. These findings suggest that brief exposure to an idealized partner does not universally promote cooperation and can reduce it, and point to expectation-updating, rather than exposure alone, as one candidate target for future interventions.

articles_hidden.title: Feedback helps children seek information to fill knowledge gap
articles_hidden.authors: Martina de Eccher; Nivedita Mani
articles_hidden.abstract: Effective self-regulated learning depends on metacognitive monitoring and control abilities, which allow learners to recognise what they do not know and adjust their learning behaviour to address knowledge gaps. However, children’s metacognitive abilities are still developing, which can hinder their ability to select relevant information effectively. This work examines whether providing feedback on children’s knowledge tests can assist their metacognitive monitoring and control processes, improving their ability to target information-seeking to fill knowledge gaps. In two experiments, 5-9-year-old children (N=203) completed a word-learning task on a tablet. They were then tested on their knowledge of the novel word-object associations and asked to report their (un)certainty in their answers. In the first experiment, children received feedback after each test trial. In both experiments, children received summary feedback at the end of the test. Afterwards, they could select some of the objects to hear their labels again and were tested on their recognition of the label-object associations once more. In both experiments, feedback boosted children’s ability to strategically seek information to fill their knowledge gaps. Moreover, when given feedback after each test trial, children based their uncertainty judgments on their previous performance. While this resulted in younger children’s uncertainty judgments to better reflect their performance, older children’s judgments were less accurate than without feedback. Importantly, children’s information-seeking was better guided by feedback than by their own subjective uncertainty, indicating that feedback provides a valuable external means for metacognitive control. Overall, the findings underscore the role of feedback in fostering the development of metacognition and self-regulated learning in childhood.

articles_hidden.title: Ecological Momentary Assessment of Mood: Reliability and Validity of a brief measure
articles_hidden.authors: Madeleine Jones; Nina H. Di Cara; Oliver Davis; Claire Haworth
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background:
Ecological Momentary Assessment (EMA) is useful for capturing the time-sensitive variability in mood. However, there is no widely used, gold-standard momentary measure of mood, making it difficult to compare results across studies. Measures often vary in number of items, as an attempt to resolve the trade-off between reliability and missingness. 
Objective:
This study evaluated the performance of a brief EMA measure for mood in relation to reliability, missingness, and construct validity.
Methods:
We collected EMA data from a sample of young adults at a UK university (n=171). Participants received a notification from the PIEL Survey app on their mobile phones to respond to a short mood survey four times a day for two weeks. This survey was developed through co-production with a focus group and required participants to rate their mood (0–10) on five items: cheerful, frustrated, relaxed, sad, and worried. We assessed the within- and between-participant reliability using multilevel modelling methods. Construct validity was evaluated through comparison with scores on the Positive and Negative Affect Schedule. Principal Component Analysis was also used to explore the underlying dimensionality. We further considered compliance rates and the degree of ‘careless responding’ (defined by response times, standard deviations, and overall reliability).
Results:
Our data showed good internal consistency reliability and acceptable variance using both generalisability theory and multilevel modelling. There was high between-participant reliability (RkR≥0.98, RkRn≥0.98), and moderate within-participant reliability (Rc≥0.64, Rcn≥0.56) for both positive and negative items. High construct validity was also established: our measure showed moderate correlations with an existing, longer measure of mood. We found two Principal Components together explained 75.8% of the variance in our measure, which appear to represent distinct Positive and Negative Affect dimensions. We also found high compliance rates with only 23.3% of responses missing overall, showing some degree of variability across time window, weekday, and time in the study. Our sample contained no careless responders overall. 
Conclusions:
In summary, the five-item measure was brief enough to maintain high compliance in a non-clinical sample, without sacrificing reliability or construct validity. This shows promise for the use of shorter-item surveys in Ecological Momentary Assessment, which may enhance compliance rates and reduce the level of careless responding. Future studies should consider whether this measure also maintains reliability for different populations.

articles_hidden.title: The Perception and Metacognition of Time Within and Between Stimulus Modalities
articles_hidden.authors: Aris Yiu; Daniel R. Little; Simon James Cropper
articles_hidden.abstract: Time perception depends not only on judging duration but also on evaluating how accurate that judgement was. Our previous work compared visual, auditory, and audiovisual intervals separately and observed a modality asymmetry at short durations. The present study examined whether pairing them within a trial reproduces this pattern, and whether order matters. Eleven participants completed a modified temporal bisection task, bisecting two consecutive intervals then choosing the more accurate. Intervals were both audiovisual (AV), auditory followed by visual (A+V), or visual followed by auditory (V+A), tested at 1500 and 3000 msec. The AV condition ran twice, showing no reliable repetition difference. The modality asymmetry did not reappear once the two modalities were directly paired. Neither Modality nor Duration reliably affected the metacognitively-selected estimate. However, this stability did not extend to metacognitive accuracy, indexed by our Metacognitive Index (MCI), which was higher for V+A at the shorter duration, though only anecdotally (BF10 = 1.43). A hierarchical Bayesian model tracked the observed data closely, with individual consistency explaining much of the between-participant variability. In summary, perceiving a duration and judging one’s own performance may not be the same computation, with the latter more sensitive to modality-induced distortion.

articles_hidden.title: ­­­Neural markers of implicit metric processing in 6-to-10-year-old children
articles_hidden.authors: Katerina Drakoulaki; Mara Breen
articles_hidden.abstract: Introduction. Auditory processing is guided by exogenous and endogenous processes: neural responses adapt to hierarchically organized structures and task-specific conditions across development. Here, we investigated the endogenous selective attention mechanisms influencing subjective metric tracking of an isochronous sequence of identical tones in children 6-10-years-old. Methods. We adapted an adult imagined meter paradigm to map the developmental neural trajectories of implicit metric coding. High-density electroencephalography data were recorded from 112 children listening to undifferentiated tones grouped subjectively into quaternary or ternary meters in fast (450ms SOA) and slow (625 SOA) tempi. We predicted that mature metric encoding would manifest as adult-like N1 and late metric negativity (LMN) amplitudes to metrically strong beats. Results. Across four age cohorts, we replicated established findings on cortical auditory evoked potential morphological development. Behavioral accuracy on the task reflected more mature neural responses to imagined strong beats. High-scorers reliably showed negative responses in the N1 and LMN time windows for strong beats across hierarchies. Low scorers showed positive responses in the N1 and LMN time windows for strong beats, similar to other selective attention paradigms in this age range. Discussion. Metric tracking was modulated by tempo and meter: we suggest that fast tempo facilitated tracking by aligning with children's faster endogenous temporal preferences, while slower tracking was more difficult; similarly, tracking ternary meter was more challenging than quaternary, likely due to familiarity.

articles_hidden.title: Exploratory Item Response Matrix Factorization: Bridging Psychometrics and Machine Learning
articles_hidden.authors: Changsheng Chen; Wim Van Den Noortgate
articles_hidden.abstract: Recent evolution in psychological and educational assessments has challenged traditional exploratory psychometric methods regarding analyzing high-dimensional sparse data and making accurate predictions, while methods from machine learning present potential for addressing relevant issues. This study proposes Exploratory Item Response Matrix Factorization (EIRMF) based on matrix factorization and compares it with Exploratory Multidimensional Item Response Theory (EMIRT) by simulation data and real data. The results show that tuning the number of factors (as a hyperparameter) in EIRMF can be an effective tool for factor retention analyses compared to methods used in EMIRT. EIRMF slightly outperforms EMIRT in most cases regarding prediction accuracy. For parameter and multidimensionality recovery, we propose Select Pairwise Correlation (spCORR) as a new metric to evaluate methods with other existing metrics. The results show that EIRMF and EMIRT produce highly correlated item intercepts and moderately correlated item slopes and factor scores, and using rotation methods (such as Promax) can improve multidimensionality recovery. A higher number of items and samples improves methods’ performance, while higher levels of factors and missingness show adverse effects. Overall, EIRMF can be an alternative to EMIRT in tasks where EMIRT is less effective with bridging psychometrics and machine learning.

articles_hidden.title: Effect of an online music program on behavioral co-regulation in mothers and children with cochlear implants and with normal hearing
articles_hidden.authors: Michela Santangelo; Chiara Barachetti; Miriam D Lense; Letizia Guerzoni; Domenico Cuda; Marinella Majorano
articles_hidden.abstract: Children with cochlear implants (CIs) could show disruptions of contingency in early interactions. Music and rhythmic activities could improve co-regulation in mother-child dyads with CIs. This study explores i) the impact of an online music program on behavioral co-regulation of dyads with children with CIs (CI-T; N = 15; M = 17.70 months, SD = 6.60) who participated in the program, a CI control group (CI-C; N = 16; M = 19.39 months, SD = 6.50), and dyads with normal hearing children (NH-T; N = 14; M = 16.14 months, SD = 3.55) who participated in the program; ii) the associations in the CI-groups between practices of music at home and behavioral co-regulation. The CI-groups were assessed at three (T1) and six (T2) months after CIs’ activation. The NH-T group was assessed before (T1) and after (T2) the program. Analyses of video-recordings revealed significant increases at T2 in the duration of mother-child contingent and affective behaviors in the CI-T group, compared to the CI-C group. In the CI-groups, correlational analyses show positive associations between maternal reports of music at home and mother-child contingent and affective responses. The potential of music activities for auditory rehabilitation after CIs activation is discussed.

articles_hidden.title: A Comparison of Mixed-Integer Linear Programming and Metaheuristics in Parallel Short-Form Construction
articles_hidden.authors: Tim Trautwein; Ulrich Schroeders
articles_hidden.abstract: Constructing parallel test forms requires balancing different construction goals, including content coverage, measurement precision, and equivalence across forms. We evaluated the accuracy and efficiency of two different psychometric approaches in parallel test constructions using two simulations: mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) uses fixed full-pool item-parameter estimates, whereas ant colony optimization (ACO) re-estimates item parameters for candidate subsets. In Simulation 1, we compared their parameter recovery across 1,000 randomly sampled item subsets per condition to quantify item-parameter uncertainty, varying (1) effective sample size per item (n = 100, 200, 500, 1,000), (2) model complexity (1PL, 2PL, 3PL), (3) latent trait distribution (normal, left-skewed), and (4) item-set proportion (10%, 20%, 30%). Full-pool calibration generally yielded more accurate and less variable parameter recovery, particularly for discrimination parameters in more complex models and smaller item sets. In Simulation 2, we assembled three parallel 40-item forms across 30 independently generated datasets in two exemplary conditions. MILP and ACO performed similarly in the 2PL condition, whereas in the 3PL condition ACO showed a slight advantage in parallelism and MILP achieved higher minimum test information. Across both conditions, MILP with full-pool calibration showed more consistent item-parameter and test-information recovery. Evaluating the same final ACO-selected items with full-pool rather than subset-specific re-estimates improved recovery on nearly all metrics. These findings indicate that repeated subset-specific re-estimation may not improve the psychometric properties of parallel short tests, but increase the risk of overfitting by allowing the search to capitalize on sample-specific estimation error.

articles_hidden.title: Distinct neural representations of perceptual and numerical absence in the human brain
articles_hidden.authors: Benjy Barnett; Stephen M Fleming
articles_hidden.abstract: The ability to represent absences is fundamental to human perception and cognition. Sensitivity to perceptual absences depends on inferring a lack of sensory evidence, enabling the recognition of a lack of environmental resources or other objects. In turn, encoding absence as a concept – in the form of the number zero – has enabled a multitude of technological and mathematical advances. Whether perceptual and conceptual absences rely on overlapping or distinct neural representations in the human brain, however, remains unknown. We employed three different tasks together with magnetoencephalography (MEG) to characterise neural representations of absence evoked within perceptual and numerical domains. Using multivariate decoding and Bayes factor analyses, we replicate previous findings of shared representations of numerical absence across symbolic and non-symbolic formats. In contrast, we show that these representations of numerical absence are distinct to those evoked by perceptual absences. This result held even after controlling for stimulus-level confounds which generate surface-level similarities between perceptual absences and non-symbolic empty sets. Our results extend a boundary between perception and cognition to the domain of absence and provide insight into the different mechanisms employed by the human brain to both perceive and conceive of absences.

articles_hidden.title: Joint (versus individual) task representations are activated spontaneously and preferentially: evidence from switch cost asymmetry
articles_hidden.authors: Shaheed Azaad; Kassandra Friebe; Günther Knoblich; Natalie Sebanz
articles_hidden.abstract: We routinely face the decision to act either alone or with another person. Research has found that humans exhibit a joint action preference, choosing to coordinate even when it is unnecessary and inefficient. Here, we tested one mechanism that might contribute to this preference: that joint task representations are activated spontaneously and preferentially to individual task representations. To this end, we conducted a secondary (meta)analysis of seven experiments (total N = 288) in which dyads completed a stimulus-response task requiring switching between individual and joint responses. Switch-cost asymmetry between the two trial types revealed that joint task representations were represented preferentially to individual task representations. This held even though participants did not coordinate intentionally, responding together only incidentally when a stimulus cued responses from both. In other words, the task was represented jointly and preferentially activated, spontaneously. Our results add to a body of joint action research indicating that a suite of spontaneous perceptual and cognitive processes automatically prepare us to coordinate with others.

articles_hidden.title: From what they hear to what they say: The distribution of word classes in the output of young English-speaking children and their caregivers
articles_hidden.authors: Antje Endesfelder Quick; Karsten Schmidtke-Bode
articles_hidden.abstract: Usage-based approaches propose that children assimilate the statistical regularities of their input. While prior studies have documented such input–output correlations for specific constructions, more systemic properties like word-class distributions have received less attention. The present study examines twelve English-speaking children aged two to three from the Manchester Corpus, comparing their part-of-speech (POS) distributions with their mothers' at three time points. Maternal distributions remain highly stable; children's speech is initially noun-heavy but approaches maternal patterns by age 2;9. These findings suggest that, even at more abstract levels of grammatical organization, children's developing grammars reflect the distributional properties of their input.

articles_hidden.title: Diffusion MRI Metrics as Markers of Neuroinflammation in Mental Illness
articles_hidden.authors: Lena K L Oestreich
articles_hidden.abstract: Neuroinflammatory mechanisms are increasingly implicated in mental illness, but their characterization in the living human brain remains challenging. Diffusion magnetic resonance imaging (dMRI) is sensitive to tissue microstructure and offers a scalable approach for studying immune-related brain changes, yet it does not measure inflammation directly. Inflammatory processes alter the cellular and extracellular geometry that constrains water diffusion, and glial activation, edema, demyelination, and axonal injury may produce overlapping or opposing diffusion signatures. This review evaluates the extent to which commonly used and emerging dMRI metrics can support an inflammatory interpretation. It distinguishes signal representations, including diffusion tensor and kurtosis imaging, from biophysical models such as free-water imaging, neurite orientation dispersion and density imaging, diffusion basis spectrum imaging, and newer compartment models, and examines their mechanistic sensitivity and limitations. A review of studies combining dMRI with immune-related measures in psychiatric populations identified a heterogeneous literature dominated by small samples, peripheral biomarkers, and within-group associations. Free-water measures showed the most consistent associations with inflammatory markers, whereas tensor-derived findings were variable and large population studies indicated very small effect sizes. Evidence from compartment models, molecular imaging, and intervention studies remains sparse. Validation studies in experimental, histological, ex vivo, and cellular systems demonstrate that diffusion signals can reflect immune-related microstructural change but are not specific to inflammation. Future work should prioritize multimodal validation, mechanistically informed acquisition and modeling, and explicit testing of competing explanations. Once validated, dMRI could provide a scalable means of mapping immune-related microstructural change across the brain in mental illness.

articles_hidden.title: TO MONETIZE OR NOT: INFLUENCE OF INDIVIDUAL DIFFERENCES AND GENDER IN MONETARY VALUATION OF MEANINGFUL EXPERIENCES
articles_hidden.authors: Jude A. Beale; Anne Z. Murphy
articles_hidden.abstract: Money is a universal measure of value that influences most decisions. For centuries, humans have used it to exchange goods and experiences. Research in psychology and behavioral economics, however, shows that there may be limits to what individuals are willing to exchange for money. This study examined the monetary values people assign to personal experiences, and whether willingness to engage in monetary valuation differs between males and females. Five hundred and twenty-nine participants completed an online survey in which they provided the minimum amount of monetary compensation it would require to complete ten separate hypothetical scenarios, with the option to refuse any task. The hypothetical tasks ranged from temporary restrictions and social isolation to public disclosure, loss of memories and permanent identity changes. Based on the results from previous economic decision-making studies, we hypothesized that females would refuse to price tasks more than males and that males would request higher compensation for priced tasks. We also hypothesized that permanent or identity-altering tasks would result in higher refusal rates than temporary ones in both genders. Whether resistance to monetary valuation is a consistent individual tendency was also examined. Our results showed that participants who refused to price one hypothetical task were more likely to refuse other tasks. While no gender differences were observed for any task regarding the monetary value requested, females refused significantly more tasks than males (4.43 vs. 3.17, p < .001). Refusal rates were highest for permanent or identity-altering tasks and lowest for temporary tasks. Lastly, refusal rates for loss of digital pictures/videos were nearly identical to losing contact with friends and family. Together, these findings suggest that monetary valuation involves two separate decisions: whether or not to assign a monetary value and, if so, how much to request. Individuals differ consistently in their willingness to engage in monetary valuation, and gender influences the decision to engage rather than with the amount requested.

articles_hidden.title: Multivariate Resting-State EEG Organization in Autism: Shared Age-Related Structure and Diagnostic Context Dependent IQ Associations
articles_hidden.authors: Yang WANG; Yingying Wang; Sandra Chan
articles_hidden.abstract:
Resting-state electroencephalography (EEG) studies of autism have often sought categorical
differentiation between autistic and typical neurodevelopmental groups, with limited stability
across features or classifiers. A neurodiversity-informed perspective views autism as part of
human neurodevelopmental variation, while recognizing associated disability and support needs.
In this view, overlap between autistic and non-autistic EEG distributions is not merely
classification noise, but may reflect shared dimensions of neural organization. A complementary
question arise is whether position along these dimensions has different functional meaning across
diagnostic contexts. We conducted an exploratory secondary analysis of 726 eyes-open resting-
state EEG features previously extracted in a published multi-site autism EEG study, with a final
analytic sample of 767 children and adolescents: 344 controls (CON), 347 participants classified
by the Autism Diagnostic Observation Schedule as Autistic Disorder (ADOS-A), and 76
classified as Autism Spectrum (ADOS-S). Principal component analysis was applied once to the
pooled sample without including age, sex, IQ, or diagnostic group. The dominant component
(PC1) was interpreted post hoc by examining its EEG feature loading pattern, its association with
chronological age, the consistency of this age association across diagnostic groups, and the
concentration of age-related variance across components. We then tested whether age-adjusted
position on this component was differentially associated with general cognitive performance
(i.e., IQ) across groups. PC1 explained 15.94% of feature variance and was characterized by the
strongest positive loadings on delta-band power and the strongest negative loadings on sample
entropy. PC1 showed a significant negative association with chronological age (𝑟 = −0.846,
𝑝 < .001), indicating that older age was associated with relatively lower delta power and higher
sample entropy along this component, consistent with previously reported developmental EEG
changes. Age-related EEG variance was concentrated primarily on PC1 rather than on
subsequent components, supporting its interpretation as a shared age-related EEG dimension.
After removing PC1’s linear association with age, residual PC1 scores (PC1r) were negatively
associated with IQ within the ADOS-A group (𝑏 = −0.612, 𝑝 < .001), but not within the
control or ADOS-S groups. Pairwise slope contrasts indicated that this association was
significantly more negative in ADOS-A than in CON, whereas ADOS-A vs. ADOS-S and
ADOS-S vs. CON contrasts were not significant. These findings shift emphasis from categorical
EEG abnormality toward individual variation within a broadly shared age-related EEG
organization, in which brain–cognition coupling depends on diagnostic context.

articles_hidden.title: Estimating the Hyperlocal Patterning of Environmental Quality and Health and Wellbeing
articles_hidden.authors: Arianna M Gard; Mengyu Liao; Deena Ahmad Shariq; Joelle Fuchs; Sriparna Sen; Taylor Leigh Wilds; Hyung Cho Kim; Brian Kim; Taylor M. Oshan
articles_hidden.abstract: Despite a robust literature linking environmental conditions to health and wellbeing, much of our understanding of the spatial patterning of human behavior is at coarse geographies and without attention to the psychological components of wellbeing (e.g., identity resolution, coping).This investigation queries the hyperlocal spatial patterning of psychological constructs related to environmental quality and health and wellbeing, in a sample of 367 adult residents (63% female, 43% Black or African American) in Washington, DC. Residents were recruited via address-based population-based sampling. Administrative measures of environmental quality were more strongly spatially organized than perception-based measures, but measures of health and wellbeing did not show any hyperlocal spatial patterning in this dataset. Findings elevate the relevance of Geographical Psychology, and the need for interdisciplinary research to better operationalize resident’s space and time allocation as a precondition for understanding environmental effects on health and wellbeing.

articles_hidden.title: Neuroscience-Informed Psychoeducation for Psychotherapy: Understanding How Therapy Supports Brain-Based Change
articles_hidden.authors: Marc L. Copersino; Jamie Berry
articles_hidden.abstract: Psychotherapy can be conceptualized as a structured, experience-dependent process of learning supported by neuroplasticity. Although psychotherapies differ in theory, technique, and therapeutic entry points, they may engage overlapping functional domains of therapeutic learning and change. This chapter presents a transdiagnostic, domain-based framework in which neuroplasticity provides the biological capacity for change and learning serves as the overarching therapeutic process. Five interacting domains organize the framework: emotion regulation and threat learning; cognitive control and belief updating; memory updating and integration; motivation, reinforcement, and habit learning; and social and relational learning and co-regulation. These domains are conceptual organizers rather than discrete mechanisms common to all psychotherapies. Repeated and emotionally meaningful experiences may support changes in expectations, emotional responses, memories, behavior, self-understanding, and interpersonal functioning. The framework also provides a practical structure for neuroscience-informed psychoeducation (NIPE).
