A critical step is translating the transparency ethos into a comprehensive set of ethical principles and benchmarks that can guide eventual open science practices. Drawing on Emanuel’s biomedical research ethics framework, this article maps open science practices onto eight established ethical principles. Examples are offered on how these principles and related benchmarks motivate specific, contextually appropriate practices. The systematic ethics framework offers researchers a principled basis for building local capacity to engage with open science practices.

articles_hidden.title: An Analysis of Flavor Distribution and Consumer Perception On Color In Life Savers Neon Gummies
articles_hidden.authors: Shriyans Tiwari; Aarush Jain
articles_hidden.abstract: This study examines the influence of artificial coloring, flavor naming, and  package design on consumer preference of the gummy. Although previous research has examined a product's packaging or a product's color, our study combines marketing and psychological factors to understand what appeals to the consumers. In this experiment, a survey was conducted with over one-hundred participants, asking them their preferred gummy color, flavor name, and whether or not they liked the packaging. In addition to this, the frequency and distribution of the colors was measured from eight packages of Life Savers gummies. Results revealed that Cherry Lime Splash was the most appealing flavor name, suggesting that combinations of exotic flavors appeal most to the consumers. Red emerged as the most appealing flavor color to consumers, while blue appeared most frequently in the package. These findings emphasize that both visual appeal and flavor naming significantly influence consumer decisions. Additionally, blue appearing the most was surprising, as this didn’t correlate with consumer preference. Ultimately, it is recommended that companies replace the artificial dies used to make the colors appealing, with natural alternatives such as beet juice, turmeric, and spirulina. These colors will help the gummies maintain strong visual appeal, while avoiding the usage of artificial dyes. Future research should examine whether natural colors would match or surpass artificial colors in terms of consumer preference.

articles_hidden.title: From Psychological States to Self-Reports: A New Perspective on Response Bias
articles_hidden.authors: Jess Grimmond; Scott Brown; Quentin Frederik Gronau; Guy Hawkins
articles_hidden.abstract:
Self-report measures are a cornerstone of psychological science, yet little attention has been
devoted to the processes through which internal experiences become observable responses. We
propose a theoretical account of self-report in which responses reflect two concurrent sources of
information: the latent states individuals seek to communicate and the response processes
governing how those states are expressed. We formalise this framework for Likert-type data using
the Latent State and Response Style (LASARS) model, an ordinal-threshold approach that
separates latent state expression from response style processes. Across applications to novel and
previously published data, we show that response styles are stable across time and survey
instruments, while individuals retain the capacity to modify their response style without changing
the latent states they wish to express. We further demonstrate a novel prediction of the
framework: that response style information obtained in one context can be used to reduce
response style confounding in another. Together, these findings support a view of self-report as a
communicative decision process rather than a direct reflection of latent states. More broadly, they
suggest that understanding psychological measurement requires explaining not only what people
experience, but also how they choose to express those experiences

articles_hidden.title: A systemic approach to self-harm in schools in Poland – a policy brief
articles_hidden.authors: Lea Satala; Daria Biechowska
articles_hidden.abstract: Self-harm among young people is a significant public health concern in Poland, while schools remain an underused setting for its early identification and prevention. Despite existing mental health initiatives and regulations, the Polish education system lacks uniform, systemic procedures for responding to self-harm, resulting in fragmented and unequal support across schools. This policy brief examines the scale and consequences of self-harm among young people, the current regulatory and institutional framework and evidence from school-based interventions in Poland and internationally. It argues that schools are particularly important for early intervention because most young people who self-harm remain in regular contact with school staff. The brief recommends a scalable, systemic intervention consisting of three complementary elements: (1) a short universal online training course for all school staff, (2) a uniform procedure for responding to self-harm and (3) a clearly defined pathway for referral to specialist support. The proposed training would strengthen staff competencies in recognising warning signs, conducting supportive conversations and directing students to appropriate services. Rather than introducing extensive new regulatory obligations, the proposal uses existing institutional mechanisms and recommends integration with the National Health Programme, professional development and staff onboarding. By establishing a common minimum standard of response, while accounting for institutional and resource constraints, the proposed approach offers a feasible first step towards a broader whole-school model of mental health support and self-harm prevention in Poland.

articles_hidden.title: A short-form decision-making task preserving value-based choices and their relationship to apathy in older adults
articles_hidden.authors: Dorothée Morand-Grondin; Madeleine Sharp
articles_hidden.abstract: Apathy, or diminished motivation, is increasingly understood as reflecting biases in value-based decision-making. The Everyday Choice Task offers an ecologically grounded setting for investigating this relationship. In this task, older adults rate everyday activities on 19 different value attributes, and then make choices between pairs of activities. Prior analyses of these value attributes recover three main value dimensions (effort, reward, and obligation) that significantly predict choice behavior, while overweighting of effort during choice is selectively associated with apathy. In this study, we tested whether a brief version of the task, inquiring about these three dimensions directly rather than using the full set of attributes, would preserve relationships between value, choice, and apathy observed using the original instrument. Older adults (n = 110) completed both the original and brief versions of the task in a randomized order, along with the Apathy Motivation Index. Ratings of effort, reward, and obligation derived from the original and brief versions of the task were strongly correlated. In both versions of the task, ratings of effort, reward, and obligation significantly predicted choice, and greater apathy severity was associated with a selective overweighting of effort. These findings support the use of the brief Everyday Choice Task as an efficient measure of value-based decision-making in future research.

articles_hidden.title: Validity, Diagnostic Accuracy, and Feasibility of Trail Making Test in Virtual Reality for Mild Cognitive Impairment
articles_hidden.authors: Panagiotis Kourtesis; Antonia Ioakeimidou; Myrto Dimakopoulou; Christina Anastasopoulou; Maria Roussou; Petros Roussos; Chrysanthi Nega; Ion Beratis
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Immersive virtual reality (VR) adaptations of neuropsychological tests change how participants respond and must be validated in each clinical population. We evaluated the Trail Making Test in Virtual Reality (TMT-VR), a head-gaze version of the paper-and-pencil Trail Making Test (hereafter, TMT) that records completion times and wrong-target selections automatically, in older adults with and without mild cognitive impairment (MCI).
Methods: In this case–control evaluation, 84 adults aged 60–89 years (42 with clinically diagnosed MCI, 42 healthy comparison participants) completed the TMT-VR, the TMT and the Mini-Addenbrooke’s Cognitive Examination (M-ACE), with pre- and post-exposure cybersickness ratings. Planned analyses examined feasibility, convergence, group differences and diagnostic accuracy for all 26 TMT-VR scores against their TMT counterparts and the M-ACE, with demographic adjustment, multiplicity correction, bootstrap validation and education-matched sensitivity analysis.
Results: All participants completed both TMT-VR parts, and cybersickness ratings decreased over the session. Part B completion times correlated positively across formats within both groups. Participants with MCI were slower and made more wrong-target selections on TMT-VR Part B but not Part A. Score for score, the TMT-VR matched the TMT on Part B completion time and discriminated MCI more effectively on the Part B, total and B−A error scores and every Part B-specific derived score; these effects persisted after demographic adjustment and widened in the education-matched subsample. The TMT's advantage lay in Part A completion time, and its error scores carried little discriminatory information. With education equalised, the TMT-VR B−A scores gave balanced operating characteristics and approached the M-ACE, which every TMT score remained below. The M-ACE discriminated more accurately than any single trail-making score of either format.
Conclusions: The TMT-VR is a feasible, well-tolerated adaptation with convergent validity against the TMT and known-groups validity for MCI. Because it discriminated MCI more effectively on the Part B-specific and error-based scores that carry the test's executive demand, it emerges as the preferable Trail Making Test format within neuropsychological batteries for MCI; whether it adds diagnostic information beyond global screens such as the M-ACE must be established in consecutive clinical referrals, together with age- and education-stratified normative cut-offs.

articles_hidden.title: Beyond Lineups: An ROC-Expected Utility Framework for Eyewitness Identification
articles_hidden.authors: Yueran Yang; Justice Healy; Janice Burke; Max Guyll
articles_hidden.abstract: How should the legal system and scholars evaluate lineup performance? To answer this important question, this paper introduces a receiver operating characteristic-expected utility (ROC-EU) framework, which bridges two prominent evaluation methods in eyewitness research. The framework emphasizes investigators as the primary decision-makers who use eyewitness evidence for classifying suspects’ guilt. This perspective shift not only helps clarify confusions in interpreting lineup ROC analysis but also expands the scope of lineup evaluation. Specifically,  the expected utility component of the framework enables a holistic assessment across distinct investigative stages: the prior probability of guilt captures independent incriminating evidence collected before a lineup; likelihoods of investigator classification outcomes capture factors that shape witness responses during a lineup; and utilities of investigator classification outcomes capture the real-world legal and societal consequences that follow investigator classification decisions after a lineup. By positioning lineup evaluation within the broader investigative context, the ROC-EU framework provides a more comprehensive approach to understanding and

articles_hidden.title: From Population–Case Mismatch to Cumulative Homogenisation in AI-Assisted Cognition
articles_hidden.authors: Fangxing Bai
articles_hidden.abstract: A growing literature reports homogenisation under generative AI assistance and offers diverse explanations, yet a unified account grounded in AI’s statistical foundations remains underdeveloped. Through a parallel thought experiment, this Perspective derives how population–case mismatch creates differences between model-based and independent human trajectories, and how AI intervention can turn these differences into cumulative homogenisation. The degree and rate of homogenisation vary with the stage of intervention. The same mechanism also explains why AI can support scientific research under conditions that limit mismatch and support independent judgement.

articles_hidden.title: Self-Referential Social Processing in Schizophrenia and Bipolar Disorder: Advancing Theoretical Precision and Clinical Insights with Model-Based Neuroscience
articles_hidden.authors: Carly A Lasagna; Jacob Kraft; Michael D. Nunez; Takakuni Suzuki; Tyler Grove; Stephan F Taylor; Ivy Fei Tso; Timothy Joseph Pleskac
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background. Individuals with schizophrenia (SZ) and bipolar disorder (BD) often misjudge whether social cues, like eye contact, are meant for them, which can fuel symptoms and functional impairment. These difficulties appear to stem from disruptions in how social information is dynamically processed (“evidence accumulation”). We used neurocognitive joint modeling to investigate which neural signals shape evidence accumulation during gaze perception and whether these brain-behavior links help explain disrupted self-referential social processing.

Methods. Leveraging EEG data from N=99 SZ, BD, and healthy controls (HC) during a self-referential gaze perception task, we built joint drift-diffusion models characterizing how different trial-level EEG features translated to evidence accumulation and behavior. Joint models were compared against each other (and models using task-averaged EEG or behavior only) for their ability to predict task behavior and relevant clinical dimensions, including paranoia, functioning, and cognition. We examined whether the best-performing model differentiated patients and HC.

Results. The best-performing joint model explained evidence accumulation through trial-level fluctuations—not task averages—in two neural signals: CPP and frontal midline theta, implicated in subjective deliberation/certainty and top-down modulation, respectively. Less reliable translation of trial-level CPP signals to evidence accumulation impaired gaze perception in SZ and BD. Mapping how trial-level theta dynamics translated to evidence accumulation captured paranoia and functioning better than behavior or task-averaged neural metrics alone.

Conclusions. Model-based approaches that embrace the within-person variability of neural signals may reveal more nuanced, clinically relevant perspectives on the pathophysiology of SZ and BD than those using task-averaged brain activity or behavior alone.

articles_hidden.title: Structural Equation Modeling with Causal Discipline: A Practical Tutorial from Regression and Mediation to Latent Variables and Growth Models in R and Mplus
articles_hidden.authors: Subir Hait
articles_hidden.abstract: Structural equation modeling (SEM) makes it easy to draw paths, estimate latent-variable models, and decompose associations, but those conveniences can blur three distinct questions: what statistical parameter is being estimated, what construct is being measured, and what additional assumptions would justify a causal interpretation. This tutorial organizes SEM around that three-layer distinction. Using one synthetic educational dataset, it moves from regression and path analysis through mediation, confirmatory factor analysis, latent-variable SEM, measurement invariance, longitudinal measurement models, and latent growth curves. Parallel examples in R using lavaan and Mplus show how the same model is represented across software. The mediation section makes the statistical-versus-causal distinction concrete: it derives the linear product-of-coefficients decomposition, shows when it can identify a natural indirect effect under stronger assumptions, and uses a residual-correlation sensitivity analysis with a known-truth simulation. Measurement-error attenuation, partial invariance, longitudinal latent means, and conditional growth models show why better statistical fit or richer latent-variable structure does not by itself create causal identification. A frozen reproducibility bundle supplies the data-generating process, truth files, software syntax, benchmark estimates, and independent numerical checks. The intended audience is graduate students and applied researchers who know regression and want a practical route into SEM without treating an arrow in a fitted model as evidence of causation.

articles_hidden.title: Working Memory and the Effectiveness of Written Corrective Feedback on Production Accuracy of the English Definite Article
articles_hidden.authors: Mohammad Nowbakht; Thierry Olive
articles_hidden.abstract: This study investigated the role of working memory (WM) in the effectiveness of direct, indirect, and metalinguistic written corrective feedback (WCF) on the production accuracy of the English definite article among pre-intermediate EFL learners. One hundred and thirty-five learners (72 female, 63 male) performed four picture-composition tasks and one argumentative essay transfer task, received WCF on their definite article errors, and rewrote their compositions accordingly. WM was measured using a first-language Operation Span Task (OSPAN). Results showed that WM predicted the effectiveness of metalinguistic and direct WCF at both immediate and delayed post-tests but did not predict the effectiveness of indirect WCF. Metalinguistic WCF produced the highest accuracy gains, which were maintained at the delayed and transfer assessments; direct WCF also outperformed indirect WCF. The findings are discussed in relation to cognitive load theory (Sweller, 1988; Sweller et al., 1998)—which accounts for how WM constraints shape learners' differential responses to instructional feedback of varying explicitness—and Schmidt's (1990) Noticing Hypothesis and cognitive models of writing (Hayes, 1996; Kellogg, 1996; Olive, 2004).

articles_hidden.title: Low family income and behavior problems in early childhood: Is family stress the causal mechanism?
articles_hidden.authors: Gülbin Şengül-İnal; Nicolai T. Borgen; Eric Dearing; Henrik Daae Zachrisson
articles_hidden.abstract: The Family Stress Model (FSM) provides a causal theory for how a family’s economic situation influences children’s behavioral outcomes through increasing income-related stress on parents, existing research on FSM is overwhelmingly correlational. We compared between-family FSM associations—the analytical approach typically used in cross-sectional and longitudinal FSM studies—with within-family FSM associations. The latter provides a more stringent causal test by eliminating bias from time-invariant confounders and unobserved between-person heterogeneity. We used longitudinal data (N=80,349) on maternal distress, relationship satisfaction, and child externalizing and internalizing behavior problems, assessed when the children were 18, 36, and 54 months from the Norwegian Mother, Father and Child Cohort Study (MoBa). For household income, we used registry data. In both between- and within-family models, lower income was associated with more behavior problems, with total effect sizes being approximately two to three times larger in the former models. The proportion of indirect effect explained by family stress mediators was sizable in the between-effects model. In contrast, the within-effect model showed no indirect effect of family stress mediators. These results are consistent with the concern that between-family estimates of the FSM are confounded by unobserved factors that vary across families.

articles_hidden.title: Large Language Models for Test-Enhanced Learning: A Tutorial and Proof of Concept
articles_hidden.authors: Ariana Modirrousta-Galian; Daryl Yu Heng Lee; Frederic Dick; Eva Lash; David Shanks
articles_hidden.abstract: Practice tests improve retention of studied information and enhance learning and retrieval of new information (test-enhanced learning; TEL). In five preregistered studies (total N = 623)—four online randomized experiments and one correlational classroom study with final-year psychology undergraduates—we examined whether large language models (LLMs; Gemini and ChatGPT) can generate practice tests that promote TEL and whether this use of LLMs can be feasibly incorporated into a classroom setting. LLM-generated multiple-choice tests with fixed feedback did not improve 2-day recall of a TED Talk relative to a control (Studies 1 and 2). In contrast, LLM-generated short-answer tests with personalized feedback significantly improved 7-day recall of an educational video relative to rewatching it (Studies 3 and 4), regardless of whether final test format matched that of the practice test. In the classroom study, participation in fortnightly LLM-generated short-answer tests (with personalized feedback) on lecture content was positively associated with graded assessment performance, and students’ attitudes towards this use of LLMs were generally favorable. Overall, we demonstrate that LLMs can substantially reduce the practical burden of implementing TEL, while maintaining sufficiently good question quality and enabling automated personalized feedback, and that this approach can be feasibly deployed in an undergraduate psychology class.

articles_hidden.title: Causal Inference in Mediation Studies When Using Psychological States as Mediators
articles_hidden.authors: Guangyu Zhu; Yiyun Shou; Michael Smithson
articles_hidden.abstract:
The growing interest in the underlying causal mechanisms of phenomena has led to the widespread application of mediation models in social science research. Researchers usually employ regression-based approaches (such as Baron and Kenny’s criteria, Sobel test and SEM) to explore causal relationships. However, the effectiveness of regression-based approaches in establishing causal relationships relies on two key assumptions: temporal order between variables and the elimination of confounders.
Previous literature has cautioned researchers about these restrictions, but misuses of regression-based approaches persist when the assumptions are not satisfied or not testable. In addition, researchers may encounter various challenges in assessing the causal relationship between variables, especially when using psychological states as mediators. These challenges include but are not limited to: (1) Psychological states are latent variables; (2) Discrepancy between measurement lag and causal lag; (3) Potential unknown or uncontrolled confounders; and (4) Bad control problem.
This article discusses the limitations of regression-based approaches and the challenges in assessing causal mediation relationships when using psychological states as mediators. It then elaborates several advanced approaches to address these challenges.

articles_hidden.title: No evidence that positive outcomes elicit a stronger sense of agency once correcting for publication bias: a commentary on, and re-analysis of, Mariano et al. (2025)
articles_hidden.authors: Robrecht van der Wel; Shaheed Azaad; Pernille Hemmer; John Michael
articles_hidden.abstract: In a recent meta-analysis, Mariano et al. (2025) conclude that people experience a stronger sense of agency over positive than negative outcomes, indexed by temporal compression. In this commentary, we evaluate that claim and identify several concerns about its validity. First, we argue that temporal compression effects should be standardized before being combined, because values in milliseconds are not necessarily comparable across different paradigms. When we analyzed standardized effects, evidence for a valence effect was absent once adjusting for publication bias. Second, we identified data integrity issues, identifying several studies that were included but either (1) did not manipulate outcome valence at all, or (2) contained only a positive or negative condition compared to a neutral condition. Excluding these studies meant that even unstandardized effects did not support Mariano et al.’s headline finding.

articles_hidden.title: Intentional Forgetting of Autobiographical Memories: Current Neuroimaging Evidence and Moving Towards an Integrationist EEG-fMRI Approach
articles_hidden.authors: Dhruv Aggarwal; Palmer Smith
articles_hidden.abstract:
Intentional Forgetting (INF) is one of many human memory processes which has gathered academic intrigue in emergent literature. Understood as a conscious and voluntary cognitive effort to suppress the recall of, or remove certain memories, INF has been extensively studied in associative paradigms. However, its application to autobiographical memory (AM) remains under-investigated, especially within neuroimaging studies. First, we summarize existing neuroimaging literature on intentional forgetting of autobiographical memories (INF-AM). Upon reviewing, we found evidence to be fragmented, providing no clear consensus around the neural bases of INF-AM. We argue this fragmentation is, in part, a result of a reliance on single-modality applications of electroencephalograph (EEG) and functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) methodology. 
EEG and fMRI, however, are complementary in their respective temporal and spatial superiority. Subsequently, we propose the application of an EEG-fMRI integrationist approach to INF-AM. We discuss how its application may help address conceptual, paradigm-level, and methodological concerns. Since human AM and the process of forgetting are inherently longitudinal, we contrast the popular cross-sectional design with a longitudinal alternative. We then present the application of the integrationist approach to longitudinal INF-AM designs. Though cognizant of the limitations that may accompany such an approach, we present the integrationist approach as a much needed and promising way forward in decoding the neuroscience of INF-AM.

Keywords: intentional forgetting, autobiographical memory, neuroimaging, EEG-fMRI, integrationist

articles_hidden.title: Neural representations and adaptive states in human action control
articles_hidden.authors: Christian Beste
articles_hidden.abstract: Adaptive behaviour requires goals to remain effective while actions are revised when circumstances change. This chapter integrates a collaborative research programme with wider theories and findings on cognitive control, episodic memory, neural dynamics, and clinical variation. It develops a selective narrative synthesis centred on the content, stability, retrieval, and reconfiguration of perception–action representations. Established accounts of goal maintenance, conflict monitoring, proactive and reactive control, and the expected value of control provide complementary explanations of how control is recruited. Event coding and binding–retrieval frameworks specify the representations on which these adjustments operate. EEG decomposition and multivariate analyses help distinguish representational contents and their temporal organisation, while oscillatory and connectivity findings identify candidate processes for coordinating their use. Aperiodic activity offers a further perspective on task-dependent processing biases, but pharmacological and biophysical evidence limits its interpretation as a unique measure of excitation–inhibition balance or metacontrol. Intervention studies connect neural dynamics with neurochemical modulation, while demonstrating dependence on baseline state, experience, and the operation targeted. Developmental and clinical evidence reveals both shared constraints and dissociable routes to similar behavioural outcomes. The proposed integration links representational operations, neural coordination, and control policy through testable predictions. It retains distinctions between descriptive markers, computational explanations, causal influences, and clinical benefit. Progress depends on separating competing accounts experimentally, establishing measurement reliability, and testing generalisation across tasks, samples, and settings.

articles_hidden.title: THE EVOLUTION OF DYSLEXIA AS A MEDICAL, EDUCATIONAL, AND SOCIAL CONCEPT: A CONCEPTUAL ANALYSIS OF DYSLEXIA
articles_hidden.authors: Tyler Ogata
articles_hidden.abstract: Phenomena relating to reading difficulties assume many names but none more controversial than dyslexia. Previous historical accounts of the so-called “dyslexia debates” (Elliott & Grigorenko, 2024b; Kirby, 2020) focus on definitions of dyslexia that incorporate the assumption that dyslexia results from some specific, albeit not completely understood, neurobiological etiology of specific reading challenges. Similar disagreements appear presently in the form of competing conceptualizations of dyslexia (Elliott, 2020; Odegard et al., 2024) and their influence on the International Dyslexia Association’s 2025 definition of dyslexia. The ensuing conceptual analysis examines dyslexia according to its past, present, and possible future conceptualizations by highlighting the varied contexts in which dyslexia evolved, namely the fields of medicine, education, and disability. The analysis reveals that the concept of dyslexia has become entangled in paradigmatic differences between these contexts. It is suspected that these differences will continue to subject dyslexia to the same old debates and limit the translation of developing thought on dyslexia into meaningful service delivery systems. A sketch of an integrative framework is proposed to guide dyslexia’s future.

articles_hidden.title: Facilitation and Attenuation of Learning to Novel and Familiar Stimuli Through Contextual  Mismatch: Experimental Evidence and a Computational Model
articles_hidden.authors: Jialin Shi; Mark Haselgrove
articles_hidden.abstract: Learning about the relationship between a stimulus and an outcome typically progresses more successfully when the stimulus is novel, compared to when it is familiar. This phenomenon, referred to as latent inhibition, is widespread across the animal kingdom and continues to motivate the development of theories of learning. Recently, Haselgrove et al. (2025) reported a series of experiments that revealed conditions under which this influential phenomenon could be reversed. They demonstrated, using pseudoword stimuli, that successful associative learning about a novel or a familiar stimulus was a function of the mismatch between the novelty of the stimulus and the context in which is trained. Thus, in a context that sustains novelty, learning about a stimulus-outcome relation progressed more successfully to a familiar stimulus than a novel stimulus (reversed latent inhibition). Here we report three experiments that reproduce and extend the generality of these findings. We show that the effect can be obtained with images as stimuli, and when participants are equated for the effects of cognitive load during familiarization. To explain these results, we propose that novelty and familiarity are stimulus elements that can compete for associative strength alongside the elements of a stimulus that are activated by its physical characteristics (e.g. its colour, saturation, etc.). We then describe a simple computational model that serves as proof of this concept, and which reveals that latent inhibition, and its reversal, can be simulated without appeals being made to learned variations in attention or memory/response interference.

articles_hidden.title: When does cortical coherence carry shared content? Compatibility and self-reconstruction as testable conditions
articles_hidden.authors: Sebastian Bobadilla-Suarez
articles_hidden.abstract: Synchrony accounts treat collective phase order as the mechanism that integrates distributed cortical activity. We show formally that shared content and a self-model each need a condition beyond phase order, and state it. Three conditions are separated: coherence (collective phase order), compatibility (agreement of independently decoded local descriptions where regions overlap) and self-reconstruction (accurate recovery of the global state from an internal encoding). Compatible local descriptions determine a unique global state. Coherence bounds disagreement between overlapping descriptions only through shared encoders of bounded sensitivity, and the bound grows as the square root of the population read: on one simulated cortical sheet it constrains at most 10 sites, chaining through overlapping patches extends it to 0.312 mm, and across distant regions the link from coherence to content is an assumption. A contracting self-map fixes one state but reconstructs accurately only states within a diameter set by its error and contraction factor. Lean 4 verifies these implications; one model satisfies all connecting hypotheses at once, showing consistency, not cortical realization. The conditions yield a disconfirmable comparison: at matched phase coherence and single-region decoding accuracy, decoders fitted independently on two regions should agree more, beyond their separate accuracies, on perceived than on unperceived stimuli classified by a no-report marker. Choosing the overlapping regions by what each decodes makes the unity correlate operational relative to a pre-registered decoder and criterion. An exploratory EEG analysis is a measurement check only. Unity and a minimal self remain interpretations that need an independent experiential endpoint.

articles_hidden.title: Children’s Behavior to Response-Independent Stimuli: A Replica of Wagner and Morris’ (1987) Superstition Experiment
articles_hidden.authors: Karen Henao; Erika Garcia; Alvaro Arturo Clavijo-Alvarez; Mónica Arias-Higuera; Camilo Hurtado-Parrado
articles_hidden.abstract: Skinner (1948) dubbed the idiosyncratic responses of pigeons exposed to noncontingent accidental or adventitious reinforcement “superstitious”. According to Skinner’s interpretation, the rate of these responses is expected to be higher under richer, non-contingent schedules (e.g., FT15s) than under leaner schedules (e.g., FT30s). However, children’s response rate in replications of Skinner’s superstition experiment did not show a clear difference between FT15s and FT30s schedules. This study evaluated whether the response rate was higher during an FT15s or an FT45s schedule by replicating Wagner and Morris’ (1987) methodology. Five-year-old children played with a tablet application in which they received virtual balls independently of their behavior. We expected that the response rate of idiosyncratic responses displayed during the game should have been higher under the FT15s schedule than under the FT45s, as accidental reinforcement frequency is higher. Our findings did not conform to Skinner’s interpretation. An approach based on stimulus control and behavioral systems better accounts for our results.

articles_hidden.title: Varying Dimensions of Language Input Predict Language and Executive Function Development Across Socioeconomically Diverse Families
articles_hidden.authors: Rachel R Romeo; Alexus Guadalupe Ramirez; Klaudia I. Kulawska; Amy E. Carolus; Katie A McLaughlin; Meredith Rowe; Liliana Lengua
articles_hidden.abstract: Children’s early language experiences are linked to their language and executive functioning (EF) development, and vary by socioeconomic status (SES). However, unique features may support different cognitive domains because input is multifaceted. The present study characterizes the dimensional structure of maternal language input and examines how these dimensions vary by SES and predict language and EF development across the preschool years. Thirteen metrics of maternal speech were extracted and/or manually coded from semi-structured play with 275 mother-child dyads when children were 3 years (137 male, 138 female; 65% White, 4% Black, 2% Latino, 2% Asian, 28% multiracial). Children’s language and EF were assessed four times between ages 3 and 5 years (data collected 2008–2012). Exploratory factor analysis revealed four input dimensions: linguistic quantity, linguistic complexity, interactiveness, and conceptual input. These differentially predicted children’s baseline language and EF performance, but not growth. Specifically, interactive and conceptual input predicted language skills, while complexity predicted EF skills. The four dimensions jointly mediated the relationship between SES and baseline language (β=0.053), and a serial pathway linked SES through input and language to EF (β=0.052). These findings reveal distinct pathways through which specific features of early input support children’s language and EF.

articles_hidden.title: The Impact of Effectiveness of Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction (MBSR) on Mindfulness and Perceived Stress in Healthy Adults
articles_hidden.authors: Ampere A. Tseng
articles_hidden.abstract: This paper reviews and examines the effectiveness of Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction (MBSR) interventions in enhancing mindfulness and mitigating stress-related symptoms. Drawing on trial data from 13 selected studies involving 574 generally healthy adults, this research seeks to establish a robust correlation between heightened mindfulness and reduced perceived stress. We assessed mindfulness using the Mindful Attention Awareness Scale (MAAS) and measured stress reductions through self-reported questionnaires. Normalized effectiveness scores, calculated as percentages from pre-intervention baselines, enabled linear regression analyses. To ensure the integrity of our findings, we rigorously controlled for external influences by isolating MBSR as the exclusive intervention and MAAS as the sole mindfulness measurement. Aggregate data confirm positive outcomes: mindfulness improvements ranged from 3.77% to 26.80%, and stress reductions varied from 8.41% to 49.05%. Linear regression trendlines reveal a strong positive correlation between increased mindfulness and decreased perceived stress. This highlights the profound benefits of MBSR interventions in enhancing mental well-being and suggests their potential for widespread integration into mental health initiatives. Ultimately, this article not only underscores MBSR's role in promoting mental well-being but also offers a quantitative framework for predicting health outcomes based on mindfulness levels.

articles_hidden.title: Approach-avoidance contingencies shape expression memory and valence evaluation
articles_hidden.authors: Arijit De; Kinkini; Jeeviga Yasokaran; Ashvit Varaganti; William A. Cunningham; Adrian Nestor
articles_hidden.abstract: Facial expressions guide approach and avoidance, but actions toward a person may also change how that person is later represented. We tested whether learned action-category relations shape the accuracy of later expression-memory reports and affective evaluation. Across three online experiments, participants (N = 629 in primary analyses) learned either a congruent mapping (approach Happy, avoid Disgust) or the reversed mapping. Experiment 1 implemented approach and avoidance as looming and receding faces; Experiments 2-3 used stationary faces and response-contingent monetary progress, and Experiment 3 changed both identities and target-expression intensity. After training, participants reported previously encountered expressions using an identity-cued continuous-report wheel built from neural-network-generated expression continua and rated faces for valence and arousal. Reversing the mapping produced a crossover interaction: each expression category was reported more accurately when assigned to approach than to avoidance. This crossover persisted after exact chance adjustment and controls for face-recognition ability and final rule sensitivity. Further, each category was rated more positively when approached; this evaluative effect extended to once-exposed identities in Experiments 1–2 and never-trained identities in Experiment 3. No corresponding arousal interaction was detected. These findings identify learned action-category relations as a source of structure in subsequent expression-memory accuracy and evaluation, linking action learning to the reporting of remembered emotional content and the evaluation of new category members.

articles_hidden.title: Predicting the Sustainability of Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction (MBSR) Effects: The Influence of Baseline Mindfulness on Longitudinal Outcomes
articles_hidden.authors: Ampere A. Tseng
articles_hidden.abstract: This article examines the influence of baseline mindfulness on the effectiveness of Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction (MBSR) interventions. Data from twelve MBSR studies (568 participants) were analyzed to assess changes in mindfulness and stress over an eight-week intervention and a subsequent two-month follow-up. The findings show that MBSR significantly enhances mindfulness and reduces stress (17–28%), with individuals exhibiting lower baseline mindfulness experiencing the greatest gains in both outcomes. However, evidence for sustained mindfulness enhancement beyond the intervention period is weak, suggesting that while baseline mindfulness may represent a stable trait, mindfulness cultivated during MBSR functions more as a transient state. Concluding remarks summarize the main findings and outline directions for future research on the durability of mindfulness-based intervention effects during follow-up periods.

articles_hidden.title: Nonconscious Threat Extinction Using Mid-Level Visual Features
articles_hidden.authors: Jamie Greer; Annika Inampudi; Patrick Mair; Joseph E. Dunsmoor; Talia Konkle; Elizabeth A. Phelps
articles_hidden.abstract: Exposure therapy is an effective treatment for emotional memory-related disorders, but it can be aversive because it requires repeated confrontation with feared stimuli. We explored an alternative using “texforms,” unrecognizable stimuli derived from images of animals and objects that preserve mid-level visual features and evoke similar ventral visual stream brain activation patterns. Participants underwent threat Acquisition using recognizable images of animals and objects, with exemplars from one category intermittently paired with shock (CS+) and exemplars from the other never paired with shock (CS-). During Extinction, participants viewed new images of animals and objects (conventional extinction), texform versions of those images (texform extinction), or a neutral video (no extinction), all without shock. At Test, participants viewed novel recognizable images of animals and objects. Only the no extinction group exhibited higher skin conductance responses to CS+ than CS- exemplars beyond the first few Test trials. These findings suggest that exposure to the mid-level visual features of learned aversive stimuli can attenuate learned threat responses through nonconscious extinction.

articles_hidden.title: Unjust World Theory: A Tripartite Model of Justice Worldviews and the Moralization of Inequality
articles_hidden.authors: Gabrielle Ibasco; Azim Shariff
articles_hidden.abstract: The just world belief (JWB)—the heuristic that people get what they deserve—has long explained why people may legitimize social inequality. However, far less has been theorized about the other side of the coin: believing in an unjust world. Rather than the unjust world belief merely reflecting the absence of the JWB, we explicate a typology of three distinct justice worldviews, or psychological lenses for interpreting and responding to an unequal status quo. In addition to the JWB, we introduce the non-just world belief (non-JWB; outcomes are randomly determined, uncorrelated with deservingness) and the anti-just world belief (anti-JWB; people get what they least deserve). Across 8 studies leveraging 12 unique samples (N = 20,777), we used correlational, longitudinal and experimental designs to evidence the functions and consequences of each worldview. In Studies 1-3 (Construct), we establish that the two unjust world beliefs are distinct from each other and from the JWB, and are relatively stable dispositions that meaningfully track differences in status. In Studies 4–5 (Profile), we show that the non-JWB captures a morally unstructured worldview associated with epistemic uncertainty and diminished meaning in life, whereas the anti-JWB captures an existentially coherent yet critical orientation toward power. Consequently, in Studies 6–8 (Implications), the anti-JWB, over and above the JWB, predicts opposition to social inequality in both attitudes and voting behaviors, particularly when such opposition involves disempowering the socioeconomic elite. Together, these findings contribute to an understanding of distinct routes through which people appraise and respond to inequality.

articles_hidden.title: Faculty Evaluations of DEI Statements for Academic Hiring
articles_hidden.authors: Nathan Honeycutt
articles_hidden.abstract: Diversity, equity, and inclusion (“DEI”) statements have become a popular additional evaluative criterion for academic hiring and promotion, but little to no empirical research has been conducted to assess how university faculty evaluate these statements. The present set of experiments sought to fill this void. Across seven studies (ntotal=4,953), tenured/tenure-track university faculty rated DEI statements that did not discuss race/ethnicity and gender diversity actions or efforts (i.e., statements that lacked equalitarian content) significantly lower than those that did. Specifically, faculty perceived these “alternative” statements to be weaker DEI statements, and perceived the applicants who submitted these statements to be less competent, less hireable, and less likable. Furthermore, faculty were less likely to recommend–often by a large margin–that the applicants behind these “alternative” statements pass an initial screening and be advanced for further review. Evaluative penalties were most severe toward DEI statements focusing only on viewpoint diversity actions and efforts (Studies 1-4), but also manifested for statements focusing only on rural diversity (Study 6), or only on socioeconomic diversity (Study 7). Findings for disability diversity (Study 5) were mixed. These studies provide novel insight on how DEI statements are perceived and evaluated by university faculty.

articles_hidden.title: The Neurophysiology of Binding and Retrieval in Action Control and Its Alterations in Tourette Syndrome
articles_hidden.authors: Christian Beste; Christian Frings; Alexander Munchau
articles_hidden.abstract: Goal-directed behavior requires that perception and action are bound together and coordinated so that what we perceive can be translated into appropriate actions. The Binding and Retrieval in Action Control (BRAC) framework describes this process as a dynamic interplay between two complementary operations: binding and retrieval. Understanding the neurophysiology of these processes has become a central aspect of cognitive neuroscience. Recent evidence links them to the rhythmic synchronization of neural activity - oscillations in the theta, alpha, and beta frequency ranges - that coordinate distributed cortical and subcortical networks. These oscillations provide a temporal code that allows the brain to integrate information across space and time while flexibly reconfiguring internal representations. The second part of this chapter applies the BRAC framework to Gilles de la Tourette Syndrome (GTS). Traditionally viewed as a motor-inhibition disorder, GTS is increasingly recognized as a condition of altered perception-action integration. Empirical findings reveal that event-file bindings in GTS are excessively strong or unstable and that the oscillatory coordination underlying their regulation is disturbed. By tracing the links between rhythmic neural dynamics and behavioral control, BRAC offers a mechanistic bridge between basic neurophysiology and the clinical phenomenology of tics.

articles_hidden.title: Recommendations & Caveats for Recruiting Stratified Samples Across Race/Ethnicity, Gender, and Socioeconomic Status Using the Prolific Online Platform
articles_hidden.authors: Julia Machina; Kimberly A. Muellers; Xiqiao Chen; E. Samuel Winer
articles_hidden.abstract: Though online sampling methods have progressed, psychology literature continues to include primarily white, educated, upper-class samples. This work will outline the methodology of a stratified community study examining demographic differences in fear of happiness and depression among U.S. adults. Drawing on prior research suggesting variation in emotional processes across social identities, we implemented a fully crossed stratified sampling design to ensure equal representation across race/ethnicity (Black, Asian, Latine, White), gender (cisgender male, cisgender female), and socioeconomic status (SES). Eligible participants were 18-65 years old and residing in the U.S. SES categories were defined as ≤ $50,000 (low), $50,000 - $100,000 (middle), and ≥ $100,000 (high). A priori power analysis (G*Power) indicated a target of 42 participants per cell (N=1,008) to detect medium effects. Following the exclusion of 75 uncategorizable cases, the per-cell target was adjusted to 38, maintaining adequate power for medium-to-large effects. Participants were recruited in SES-based blocks via Prolific. Procedures to preserve stratification, confidentiality, and analytic rigor will be discussed, highlighting methodological considerations for equity-focused psychological research. These methods can ensure adequate power and representation when examining relationships between intersectional identities and psychological phenomena in online samples.

articles_hidden.title: Computational and neuropsychiatric dimensions of motivation differentially predict everyday physical activity
articles_hidden.authors: Sara Z. Mehrhof; Camilla Nord
articles_hidden.abstract: Physical activity benefits physical and mental health, yet population-level engagement in physical activity is low and variable, particularly among individuals with mental health problems. We investigated how neuropsychiatric and computational variables of motivation relate to physical activity in a large, general-population sample (N = 1,105). Both neuropsychiatric (apathy and anhedonia) and computational (effort sensitivity during effort-based decision-making) measures predicted total physical activity. Decomposing physical activity into activity stage and intensity revealed clear dissociable and independent effects: Apathy and anhedonia, but not effort sensitivity, primarily predicted whether individuals participated in activity at all, as well as amount of sedentary time. Computational effort sensitivity, on the other hand, predicted the amount of activity individuals engage in, with effects scaling with intensity. Our findings suggest neuropsychiatric and computational dimensions of motivation govern distinct components of real-world physical activity, with implications for the development of targeted physical activity interventions.

articles_hidden.title: Flexibility in Abstract Thought: Context-Dependent Representations of Integer Magnitude
articles_hidden.authors: Nicholas Allan Vest; Martha W. Alibali
articles_hidden.abstract: Negative numbers are challenging because they lack direct perceptual referents and require reasoning about magnitude in a relational, bidirectional space. This review examines how people represent and use integer magnitude on the mental number line, a cognitive tool that learners initially use for positive numbers, focusing on the flexibility with which this tool is deployed across contexts. Synthesizing evidence from cognitive psychology, developmental science, and mathematics education, we evaluate three broad representational accounts: componential accounts, which treat sign and magnitude as separable symbolic elements; extension accounts, which posit a continuous magnitude representation extending across zero; and reflection accounts, which propose a symmetry-based organization of magnitude around zero. Across experimental paradigms, task formats, and age groups, findings reveal substantial variability in behavioral signatures of integer processing. We argue that this variability reflects context-dependent recruitment of multiple coexisting representations rather than a single, fixed structure or a stage-like developmental progression. On this view, the mental number line functions as a dynamic cognitive tool that can be reparametrized in the moment to support rule-based, analog, or relational reasoning. Understanding how integer magnitude is flexibly represented and used provides insight into the mechanisms of abstract thought, coordination of representations, and conceptual change.

articles_hidden.title: Delayed Feedback Improves Learning in Individuals with Parkinson’s Disease
articles_hidden.authors: Kai Sucich; Christopher J. Cagna; Erica Weber; Ekaterina Dobryakova
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Learning and memory deficits are common in Parkinson’s Disease (PD). Effectively processing performance-related feedback is integral to learning but is often impaired in PD. Delaying feedback presentation by 6 seconds has been shown to circumvent these deficits during incremental learning tasks. The potential learning benefits of longer feedback delays, however, are unknown. The current study examined the effects of a 6-second delay and a 25-minute delay on learning during a declarative memory task in individuals with PD. 

Methods: Thirty participants with PD completed a verbal paired-associates task, during which they learned word pairs via trial-by-trial accuracy feedback presented immediately after making responses (No Delay; ND), after a 6-second delay (Short Delay; SD), and after a 25-minute delay (Long Delay; LD). Mixed effects models examined the influence of feedback timing condition on both final test performance and on improvement in performance between the learning and test phases. Exploratory hierarchical mixed models with neuropsychological tests examined potential individual difference predictors of delayed feedback learning.

Results: Both SD feedback and LD feedback predicted significantly greater improvement in performance, compared to ND feedback. Better working memory performance on the Digit Span Backwards Test predicted significantly greater improvement from LD feedback.

Conclusion: Longer feedback delays improve learning during a paired associates word learning task in individuals with PD. Shorter delays previously demonstrated to benefit incremental learning may also benefit other forms of learning. Working memory capacity may be an important predictor of these learning benefits.

articles_hidden.title: Reinforcement learning as a foundation for psychodynamics
articles_hidden.authors: Zack Dulberg; Jonathan D. Cohen
articles_hidden.abstract: In this article we consider the use of reinforcement learning (RL) as a formal framework for understanding traditional psychodynamic phenomena. We show how RL can be used to provide new insights as well as normative explanations for key psychodynamic constructs, grounding them in principles of reward maximization and adaptation. We illustrate this by reviewing two recent studies in which simulations of adaptive agents offer new explanations for psychodynamic processes, discuss how RL could account for both similarities as well as individual differences in human psychological profiles, and outline possible future directions for this approach. We conclude that, by providing a computational foundation for psychodynamic concepts, RL may contribute to the development of a more rigorous science of psychological dynamics and their disruption in clinical conditions.

articles_hidden.title: The contribution of geometrical regularities in the Ames room illusion
articles_hidden.authors: Maria Dvoeglazova; Elena Gorbunova; Tadamasa Sawada
articles_hidden.abstract: In the Ames room illusion, a regularly-shaped room is perceived when an irregularly-shaped room is seen from a specific viewpoint and this misperception of the shape induces a misperception of the sizes and the positions of objects in the room. It has been considered that the illusion was caused by geometrical regularities that are satisfied by the illusory, regular shape but that are violated by the actual, irregular shape. These regularities are rectangularity of a trihedral corner, perpendicularity between contours and between planar faces, and parallelism between contours. In this study, we conducted three psychophysical experiments to test how the geometrical regularities contribute the Ames room illusion. The visual stimuli used in the experiments were systematically controlled using computer graphics and virtual reality technologies. Experiment 1 tested the effect of the configurations of the room. Experiments 2 and 3 tested the effect of the shapes and configurations of the room. The results of the experiments showed that rectangularity and perpendicularity contribute positively to the illusion, but that parallelism may have a negative effect.

articles_hidden.title: Reading and writing anxiety in Finnish school children aged 9-15: Associations with gender, grade level, and reading competence
articles_hidden.authors: Rosa Salmela; Santeri Holopainen; Tomi Rautaoja; Emilia Nordenswan; Katarina Alanko; Pekka Räsänen
articles_hidden.abstract:
Purpose: This study examined the level of reading and writing anxiety in a cross-sectional sample of Finnish school children and the moderating roles of gender, grade level, and reading competence. 

Method: We used a reading and writing anxiety questionnaire (RWAQ) that consists of three factors: workload-related reading and writing anxiety, evaluation-related reading and writing anxiety, and social reading and writing anxiety. Linear regression modeling was used to analyze how gender, grade level, and reading competence moderate different dimensions of reading and writing anxiety. Participants were 9,723 Finnish-speaking children in grades 3–9, including 4,832 girls and 4,891 boys.

Results: Finnish school-age children showed relatively low reading and writing anxiety overall, but it increased with age (lowest in grades 3–5, highest in grades 7–9). This was especially evident in girls’ social and evaluation-related anxiety, while boys reported higher workload-related anxiety across grades. Lower reading competence was linked to higher reading and writing anxiety, but this effect varied by gender. Math anxiety and general anxiety were controlled in the models, and both anxiety types predicted reading and writing anxiety strongly.

Conclusion: Together the results suggest that workload-related reading and writing anxiety, evaluation-related reading and writing anxiety, and social reading and writing anxiety are distinct dimensions of reading and writing anxiety, and that future research could benefit from accounting that grade level, gender, and reading competence may influence these dimensions differently.

articles_hidden.title: Goals in Focus: A single-blind multi-method randomized‑controlled pilot feasibility trial of a targeted CBT approach for motivational negative symptoms of schizophrenia
articles_hidden.authors: Matthias Pillny; Alisa Schormann; Tania Marie Lincoln
articles_hidden.abstract: Motivational negative symptoms of schizophrenia are closely associated with diminished goal-directed behaviour. Goals in Focus (GiF) is a novel cognitive–behavioural intervention targeting a comprehensive set of mechanisms implicated in motivational negative symptoms and reduced goal-directed behaviour. This single-blind, randomised controlled pilot trial examined the feasibility, safety, and acceptability of GiF. Thirty Participants with schizophrenia-spectrum disorders and at least moderate motivational negative symptoms were randomised to receive either up to 24 GiF sessions over six months or a waitlist control condition. Blinded assessments were conducted at baseline and six months post-randomisation (T1). Feasibility was evaluated against prespecified criteria for recruitment, eligibility, consent, retention, data completeness, attrition, and treatment exposure. Safety and acceptability were assessed through adverse event monitoring and satisfaction ratings alongside qualitative feedback, respectively. Preliminary efficacy was examined using with the motivational negative symptoms subscale of the Brief Negative Symptom Scale as the primary outcome and ecological momentary assessment (EMA) of goal pursuit mechanisms. All feasibility criteria were met except for treatment exposure. GiF was safe and well accepted. The baseline-adjusted effect on motivational negative symptoms at T1 was small and imprecise (b = 0.94, 95% CI [−3.17, 5.05]), compatible with both improvement and deterioration. EMA outcomes showed more promising signals of improvement. Overall, GiF appears to be feasible safe and well accepted although refinements to treatment exposure are warranted before progressing to a definitive efficacy trial.

articles_hidden.title: Daily loneliness and alcohol use in Alcohol Use Disorder: an 8-week EMA study of within-person associations
articles_hidden.authors: Anja Kräplin; Fabian Arntz; Gianna Spitta; Jan Luca Wiedenhöft; Noemi Keng; Yoonha Park; Katharina Hoffmann; Shuyan Liu; Louisa Diallo; Michael N. Smolka
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background and Aims: Loneliness has been suggested as a risk factor for alcohol consumption (AC), potentially contributing to a cycle whereby loneliness increases drinking, which in turn exacerbates loneliness through alcohol-related consequences. However, longitudinal evidence is inconsistent, and little is known about short-term, within-person associations in individuals with alcohol use disorder (AUD). We examined concurrent and lagged bidirectional associations between loneliness and AC in daily life and whether these associations varied according to social contact, mood, age, and gender.
Design: Ecological momentary assessment (EMA) study with daily assessments over 8 weeks. Within-person associations were examined using fixed-effects panel regression models; multilevel models examined moderation by age and gender.
Setting: A real-life context with data collection between December 2025 and June 2026 in Germany.
Participants: The final analytic sample comprised 58 adults meeting at least two DSM-5 criteria for AUD (74% men; mean age = 48.8 years, SD = 8.3).
Intervention: Observational study without interventions.
Measurements: Daily alcohol use (yes/no) and quantity (grams), loneliness, social contact, perceived social support, and mood valence and calmness were assessed using smartphone-based EMA. Concurrent and prospective associations across consecutive days were examined, accounting for autoregressive stability.
Findings: EMA compliance was high (96.7%). Greater-than-usual loneliness was associated with lower probability of alcohol use during the same retrospective assessment interval (b = −0.092, 95% CI [−0.151, −0.033], pFDR = .006) and lower alcohol quantity (b = −15.89 g, 95% CI [−24.16, −7.61], pFDR = .003). Prospective associations in either direction were small, with confidence intervals constraining their plausible magnitude. The concurrent association between loneliness and alcohol quantity was stronger on days with social contact, higher positive mood valence and calmness, and among men. Mood also moderated the prospective association between loneliness and subsequent alcohol use, although simple slopes were not significant.
Conclusions: In adults with AUD, loneliness was associated with lower AC concurrently whereas prospective associations in either direction were small. The concurrent association varied by social and mood context and gender, suggesting that loneliness alone may provide limited information about imminent drinking risk.

articles_hidden.title: Exploring the Renin–Angiotensin System as a Potential Approach for Managing Perimenopausal Depression
articles_hidden.authors: Helena Jelenska; Andrea Reinecke
articles_hidden.abstract:
Perimenopause is characterised by debilitating psychological symptoms, including
a two- to four-fold increased risk of depressive symptoms during this sensitive time. Current first-line treatment strategies, such as antidepressants and hormonal therapy, are proven to be only moderately effective and linked to severe adverse effects. With the population of perimenopausal women rapidly growing due to rising life expectancy, novel strategies to prevent or mitigate perimenopausal symptoms of depression are of increasing importance.
Perimenopause is marked by pronounced sex-hormone changes, primarily declining oestrogen. Both have been linked to increased depression risk. On the other hand, the renin–angiotensin system (RAS), an endocrine system involved in blood pressure regulation, has been linked to depression, with RAS-based pharmacological manipulations having antidepressant effects. Perimenopausal hormonal changes closely interact with the RAS by upregulating the depressogenic Ang II–ACE–AT₁R pathway and downregulating the protective Ang-(1–7)–ACE2–MasR/AT₂R pathway. This narrative review summarises research highlighting the RAS as a potential novel treatment target for depression in perimenopausal women and proposes a hypothesis-generating framework to guide future research.

articles_hidden.title: Tuning in: how interoception shapes body image across early adolescence
articles_hidden.authors: Mariana Von Mohr; Rosie Donaghy; Vivien Ainley; Abigail Agyemang; Manos Tsakiris
articles_hidden.abstract: Early adolescence is a critical time marked by dynamic changes in physiology, appearance and social environment. These changes are also reflected in how adolescents perceive themselves, in-cluding their bodies. The transition from pre-pubertal through pubertal stages allows us to con-sider the development of the self from the perspective of how body perception, both from within and from the outside, changes. While research in adults and post-puberty adolescents suggests that lower interoceptive accuracy is associated with greater body image concerns, how these fac-tors interact during puberty remains unknown. We tested a sample of 181 girls (aged 10-14 years), spanning from pre-puberty to post-puberty, on measures of interoceptive accuracy and behavioural and self-report measures of body image. Lower interoceptive accuracy predicted greater body image dissatisfaction. Moreover, this relationship was moderated by puberty stage, showing that the protective effect of higher interoceptive accuracy against body image dissatis-faction was stronger during more advanced stages of puberty. Our findings show that interocep-tive influences extend from the basic multisensory integration to conscious attitudes about our body during a critical developmental period, highlighting the positive role that better interocep-tion can play in mental health.

articles_hidden.title: Associations between adverse childhood experiences, parent-child and peer attachment relationships, and daily-life self-harm in adolescents
articles_hidden.authors: Julie Janssens; Ginette Lafit; Eva De Corte; Robin Achterhof; Karlijn Susanna Francisca Maria Hermans; Anu Pauliina Hiekkaranta; Inez Myin-Germeys; Olivia J Kirtley
articles_hidden.abstract:
Objective: Adverse childhood experiences (ACEs) are associated with self-harm, but it remains unclear whether they are differentially associated with self-harm thoughts and behaviours and which factors may attenuate these associations. We investigated associations between ACEs and lifetime and daily-life self-harm thoughts and behaviours in adolescents, and whether paternal, maternal, or peer attachment relationship quality moderated these associations. Additionally, we explored associations with specific types of ACEs.
Method: N = 1014 adolescents (mean age = 14.05 years, SD = 1.91; 66.66% female) were recruited from the general population through schools across Flanders, Belgium. Retrospective questionnaires assessed ACEs, lifetime self-harm thoughts and behaviours, and paternal, maternal, and peer attachment relationship quality. Experience Sampling Methodology (ESM) assessed daily-life self-harm thoughts and behaviours ten times per day for six days.
Results: Greater exposure to ACEs was associated with lifetime self-harm and with greater odds of reporting self-harm thoughts and behaviours in daily life, but not with the intensity of daily-life self-harm thoughts when present. Maternal attachment relationship quality attenuated the associations between ACEs and lifetime self-harm and between ACEs and daily-life thought intensity, but did not moderate the occurrence of daily-life self-harm thoughts or behaviours. Paternal and peer attachment relationship quality did not moderate these associations. Exploratory analyses indicated variation across ACE types, with sexual victimization showing the most consistent associations across lifetime and daily-life self-harm outcomes.
Conclusions: Findings are consistent with conceptualizing ACEs as background vulnerability factors within the pre-motivational phase of the IMV model and suggest that maternal attachment relationship quality may attenuate some associations between ACEs and adolescent self-harm. Distinguishing between the occurrence and intensity of self-harm thoughts in daily life may help clarify how childhood adversity relates to self-harm.

articles_hidden.title: Causal Strength Under Structure Uncertainty
articles_hidden.authors: Björn Meder; Magda Osman; Simon Stephan; Michael R. Waldmann
articles_hidden.abstract: How should a learner estimate the strength of a causal influence when it is uncertain whether the causal relation exists? We address this question using the framework of Bayesian causal induction. Existing accounts have primarily focused either on inference about causal structure or on estimation of causal strength under an assumed structure. We propose structure-averaged causal strength as a method for estimating causal strength under structure uncertainty. By averaging causal strength across alternative structures according to their posterior probabilities, the account provides a strength estimate that reflects uncertainty about both whether a causal relation exists and how strong it is. Normatively, our analyses clarify how causal strength should be estimated when the existence of the causal relation itself remains uncertain. Empirically, structure-averaged strength provides accurate predictions of human judgments of causal influence across a broad set of published studies, suggesting that human causal judgments reflect uncertainty about both causal strength and causal structure. Together, our analyses show how inferences about causal structure shape judgments of causal strength under uncertainty.

articles_hidden.title: The ‘stickiness’ of disgust: Testing the hypothesis of disgust intractability in the context of instrumental reversal learning.
articles_hidden.authors: Emily Bagley; Camilla Nord
articles_hidden.abstract: Discrete emotion theories conceptualise fear and disgust as distinct emotions. This notion is supported by the finding that Pavlovian disgust conditioning is more resistant to extinction than fear conditioning—disgust may be ‘stickier’ than fear. Dimensional emotion theories challenge this, suggesting that categorical differences between emotions reflect variations along shared dimensions of valence and arousal. Reinforcement learning assumes a dimensional framework: assuming that learning from negative events depends on an outcome’s valence and arousal. Here, using a novel online reversal learning task and modelling framework (n = 340), we show that instrumental punishment learning is not ‘outcome agnostic’. Emotion-learning differs from points-based learning, and disgust-learning is uniquely ‘sticky’, altering perseverative error-rate, lose-shift probability, and a model-based ‘stickiness’ parameter, relative to other types of learning. This suggests that whilst some features of learning are shared between emotions, disgust has a distinct behavioural profile, with implications for emotion science and computational psychiatry.

articles_hidden.title: From Prediction Accuracy to Prediction Use: A Monitoring-Centered Framework for Interactive Sport Expertise
articles_hidden.authors: Yingzhi Lu; Mengkai Luan; Xiaoran Gao; Wenzi Wang; Chen Yiheng; Chenglin Zhou
articles_hidden.abstract: Action anticipation is widely recognized as a cornerstone of expert performance in interactive sport. Decades of research have shown that skilled performers predict upcoming actions more accurately than less-skilled performers by extracting kinematic cues and integrating them with contextual information. This literature has provided a powerful account of how anticipatory predictions are formed. Yet, interactive sport rarely ends when a prediction is generated, because opponents continue to move, sensory evidence changes, contextual priors may mislead, and performers must determine whether an initial prediction remains useful for action. In this narrative review, we argue that the field should move beyond anticipation accuracy toward the adaptive use of anticipation during unfolding interaction. Drawing on sport expertise research, predictive-processing accounts, performance-monitoring theory, observed-action error studies, and sport-specific neurophysiological evidence, we propose a monitoring-centered framework for interactive sport expertise. In this framework, anticipation generates probabilistic reference states, monitoring evaluates whether these states remain aligned with unfolding input, and functional discrepancy processing determines whether mismatch matters for action goals, affordances, and motor plans. We further argue that discrepancy processing is graded and functionally meaningful rather than binary. From this perspective, expert performers may not only predict better; they may also detect diagnostic mismatch more selectively, tolerate irrelevant variability, and couple action-relevant discrepancy information with sport-specific motor preparation and adjustment. The framework yields testable predictions for assessment, training, and future research on expert performance in sport.

articles_hidden.title: When Vision Disagrees with Language: Private and Population-Level Color Knowledge  in Red–Green Dichromacy
articles_hidden.authors: Jiahui Lu; Ziyi Xiong; Peijun Yuan; Xiaoying Wang; Yanchao Bi
articles_hidden.abstract: Human concepts are shaped by two distinct information sources: private sensorimotor experience and socially transmitted knowledge mainly conveyed through language in an abstract symbolic form. Because information geometry in these sources is largely aligned, their relative contributions to conceptual representation are difficult to disentangle. We exploit a group-level dissociation, in which the alignment between sensory color geometry and population-level language structure diverges systematically (red–green dichromacy vs. trichromacy), and a model-level dissociation (object-color geometry derived from large language models vs. from image-based sensory models), to disentangle vision and language contributions to object knowledge. Sensory color geometry differed behaviorally and neurally between dichromats and trichromats, yet behavioral object-color representations converged across groups and corresponded robustly with language-derived geometry. LadATL consistently expressed language-derived geometry across tasks and groups, whereas LpFG showed a group-dependent representational profile in the chromatic-object task: trichromats showed relatively greater correspondence with sensory-derived geometry, whereas dichromats retained correspondence with both geometries. Dichromats also showed stronger intrinsic connectivity of LadATL with LpFG and EVC. These findings reveal how the brain flexibly draws on sensory evidence and socially transmitted knowledge to maintain population-aligned conceptual representations across heterogeneous sensory experiences.

articles_hidden.title: Impossibility and Logical Contradictions Can Enhance the Perceived Value of Fictional Theological Propositions
articles_hidden.authors: Takuetsu Yajima; Eisuke Niida; Yo Nakawake
articles_hidden.abstract: Supernatural concepts are often thought to gain cultural attraction by violating intuitive expectations in limited ways, but many theological doctrines also involve logical contradictions or impossibilities. It remains unclear how such formal violations influence people’s evaluations of religious propositions. In the present study, 96 Japanese adults rated 20 fictional theological propositions on dimensions related to perceived value, including importance, profundity, interestingness, sacredness, and shareability. Those propositions were rated for impossibility and logical contradiction. A composite positive-evaluation score was derived from items rating perceived value and analyzed using linear mixed-effects models. The result shows higher impossibility and higher logical contradiction predict higher positive evaluations of the propositions. These findings suggest that impossible and contradictory theological content can be positively evaluated.

articles_hidden.title: Correspondence Is Not Mechanism: A Construct-Validity Audit of Implicit Egotism
articles_hidden.authors: Simon Bibby
articles_hidden.abstract: People like the letters of their own names a little more than other letters, and the digits of their own birthdays a little more than other digits. From those small laboratory preferences, a research programme has inferred that people are disproportionately drawn to places, partners, occupations, and purchases carrying their own letters, names, or numbers, and that unconscious self-association is what draws them. This article develops a seven-question diagnostic standard for evaluating whether evidence linking a laboratory effect to real-world outcomes identifies the proposed mechanism or only a correspondence. The standard is applied in a paper-by-paper audit of implicit egotism. Both preferences have laboratory support, although the name-letter effect is more extensively replicated. The extension claims audited here lack comparable evidence that specifically identifies the proposed mechanism. Across the archival, field, and corpus literature audited here, the designs cannot separate implicit egotism from marriage within ethnic groups, cohort effects, and family lineage, and where randomisation removes those confounds, awareness of the cue, ordinary similarity, attention and social distance remain. Where reanalysis has applied corrected baselines, many of the original effects have reduced or disappeared, and where correspondence survives, unconscious self-association has not been identified as its source. The strongest residual archival finding, examined as a limiting case, does not isolate the mechanism either. The audit therefore offers a revised evidential assessment of one programme and a diagnostic standard applicable to other laboratory-to-real-world mechanism claims. In the laboratory the phenomenon is robust. Outside it, the evidence does not yet show that it shapes the choices people make.

articles_hidden.title: Unique and shared effects of single-session intervention proximal outcomes on 3-month depression symptoms in adolescents: A commonality analysis
articles_hidden.authors: Laura Jans; Arielle C. Smith; Isaac Lev Ahuvia; Jessica L. Schleider; Jeremy William Eberle
