CBG produced a significant dose X task interaction: divided attention was enhanced at 0.3 and 3.0 mg/kg, while sustained attention was mildly impaired, an effect limited to the shortest (100 ms) stimulus duration. Guanfacine did not affect sustained attention but impaired divided attention starting at 0.2 mg/kg. Neither CBG nor guanfacine produced sedation.
Conclusions: Low-dose CBG selectively enhances divided attention while mildly impairing sustained attention, a dissociation not explained by sedation or overt motor effects, and distinct from the alpha-2 agonists tested. These findings support continued investigation of CBG's therapeutic potential for attention deficit.

articles_hidden.title: Adolescent Mental Healthcare as a Public Utility: A Multi-Sectoral Economic Case for Proactive Investment
articles_hidden.authors: Mackenzie Swirbul; Emily Peake; Anne Bischops; Marie-Laure Charpignon; Maimuna S. Majumder; Aarthi Padmanabhan
articles_hidden.abstract:
Adolescence is a critical developmental period marked by substantial neuroplasticity and the onset of most psychiatric disorders. Despite this epidemiologic reality, the current US mental healthcare landscape remains largely reactive rather than proactive, leaving nearly half of symptomatic youth untreated and generating a considerable economic burden through lost productivity and increased healthcare expenditures. While clinical outcomes are well-documented, the multi-sectoral fiscal consequences and potential returns on investment of such proactive youth mental healthcare remain poorly integrated into US policy frameworks. 

This narrative review synthesizes evidence from econometric analyses and longitudinal studies across four key sectors: education, legal and correctional, labor market (caregiver productivity), and healthcare. We describe how untreated mental health conditions contribute to high-cost, crisis-driven care, chronic school absenteeism, and increased involvement with the juvenile correctional system, while also quantifying their effects on caregiver workforce participation and productivity. Furthermore, we highlight emerging public financing models that conceptualize mental healthcare as an essential public good. 

Current evidence suggests that proactive investment in accessible adolescent mental healthcare yields meaningful socioeconomic returns. Strategic investment in youth mental healthcare should therefore be regarded as both a public health imperative and a fiscal priority.

articles_hidden.title: Detecting Abrupt Changes in Developmental Trajectories with Continuous-Time State-Space Models
articles_hidden.authors: Marcos Romero-Suárez; Sy-Miin Chow; Pablo Fernández Cáncer; Eduardo Estrada
articles_hidden.abstract:
Developmental trajectories are typically characterized by gradual, monotonic change. But what happens when a trajectory shows an abrupt shift? A child's reading ability may suddenly drop following the onset of anxiety or peer victimization, or accelerate after a sustained reading habit takes hold. When such shifts go undetected, they are absorbed into background noise, obscuring who is affected, when the disruption occurred, and why.
This article addresses that gap, focusing on identifying which individuals experience abrupt changes and when. We extend an existing outlier detection framework to continuous-time state-space models and propose a combined detection criterion (ρ² & SOI) that improves the balance between sensitivity and false-positive control relative to existing alternatives. A Monte Carlo simulation (3 × 3 × 3 × 2 = 54 conditions, 1,000 replications each) compared two model specifications and two existing statistics against the proposed criterion. Detection is sharpest under a deterministic model with process noise fixed to zero, which outperforms the correctly specified alternative and prevents abrupt changes from being absorbed into background variability. Once shocks are identified, a corrected re-estimation with them explicitly incorporated improves recovery of the process noise variance, which is otherwise systematically overestimated.
Knowing which individuals experienced abrupt changes, and when, transforms outlier detection into a practical scientific tool, linking disruptions to their causes and informing targeted prevention and intervention. To support adoption, we provide a step-by-step tutorial, annotated R functions ready to be sourced, and an example dataset that reproduces the full pipeline, applicable to any developmental domain.

articles_hidden.title: A Standardized Protocol for Fear Extinction Enhancement Research
articles_hidden.authors: Xandra Kredlow; Meghan Whalen; Patrick Laing; Lingwei Ouyang; August C. Morgan; Samuel Emerson Cooper; Bram Vervliet; Joseph E. Dunsmoor
articles_hidden.abstract: For over a century, fear conditioning and extinction have served as a foundational model and laboratory protocol for studying how fear is learned and regulated in health and disorder. Several recent innovations in exposure treatments for anxiety-related psychopathology follow advances in fear extinction research. However, the field lacks a standardized protocol—critical given the many consequential parameters in conditioning protocols—that provides a benchmark standard for systematic research on how to improve exposure via enhanced extinction. Here, we present a standardized differential fear conditioning protocol based on international expert input via survey and initial multi-site validation data (n=196; 65% female). The protocol demonstrates expected patterns of fear acquisition and sufficient extinction and return of fear response needed for tests of enhanced extinction. The protocol is simple to implement and amenable to modification, providing an accessible tool for both field-domain experts and allied fields with interest in fear and anxiety.

articles_hidden.title: When Effort Stops Meaning Something: A Cognitive Systems Model of Persistence, Disuse, and Re-entry
articles_hidden.authors: Arya Jadhav; Lawrence R. Burns
articles_hidden.abstract: Learning depends not only on task performance, but on whether effort remains coupled to interpretable signals of progress, competence, and continued agency. External cognitive systems can disrupt this coupling when they absorb cognitive work that would otherwise sustain internal learning dynamics. We introduce the Cognitive Cost Comparator (CCC), a mechanistic agent-based model of engagement-gated learning under external offloading. In the model, heterogeneous agents allocate effort between internal cognition and an external aid across 300 discrete time steps. Although the present simulations instantiate the external system as AI assistance, the architecture is intended to generalize to cognitive tools that alter the perceived cost of task completion. The model couples three feedback processes: a confidence-engagement loop that gates learning opportunity, an offloading-disuse loop that erodes internal confidence and raises engagement thresholds, and a scaffolding-interpretability mechanism that determines whether effort produces meaningful progress signals. Learning states are modeled as dynamic attractors rather than fixed outcomes. Across simulations with 4,500 agents, engagement reliability was the strongest predictor of terminal confidence (Spearman r = 0.72). Scaffolding primarily prevented entry into disengaged failure states, but did not reliably restore agents once disengagement had stabilized; recovery increased meaningfully only when scaffolding was paired with explicit re-entry mechanisms. These findings suggest that cognitive systems involving human learners and external aids must be evaluated not only by performance support, but by whether they preserve the conditions for effortful re-engagement after failure.

articles_hidden.title: Lines We Cross: Identity Complexity at the Boundary Between Activism and Radicalism
articles_hidden.authors: Michelle Blaya-Burgo
articles_hidden.abstract: Violent radicalization and politically motivated violence pose significant threats to global peace, security, and social cohesion. These problems are costly, and reactive approaches have not effectively reduced their incidence. Because conflict is inevitable, prevention efforts should take precedence. This paper examines social identity complexity as a potential buffer against violent radicalization, proposing that complex identity structures – perceptions of having multiple, distinct ingroup memberships – may reduce susceptibility by preventing individuals from fixating on a single identity and pushing it to extremes. Two studies tested this idea. Study 1 (N = 226) used a 2×2 design manipulating identity complexity (simple vs. complex) and self-uncertainty (low vs. high). Results showed that simple identity structures increased radicalism intentions, resulting in a greater relative preference for activism among those with complex identities. Study 2 (N = 240) examined political identity and natural levels of identity-uncertainty. Results showed that higher uncertainty predicted more radicalism. Further, when political identity was highly salient, uncertainty increased intentions to engage in radicalism. Across studies, most participants favored activism over radicalism; however, the findings suggest that uncertainty can push intentions toward more extreme forms of action, while access to multiple identities may help protect against fixation on a single identity.

articles_hidden.title: Unpacking cognitive variability: Dynamic systems modeling to understand daily cognitive change in healthy aging and mild cognitive impairment
articles_hidden.authors: Andrew J. Aschenbrenner; Joshua James Jackson
articles_hidden.abstract: It is increasingly accepted that single scores are insufficient to fully capture the complexities of cognition as it relates to daily life. Many studies now employ repeated cognitive assessments to measure variability in scores across the testing sessions. Exploration of additional characteristics of participant’s time series may provide more explanatory power in understanding cognitive health in aging and early neurodegenerative disease. We administered a standard attention test daily for 3 weeks to healthy younger adults, healthy older adults and participants diagnosed with cognitive impairment. Participants self-rated the frequency of their cognitive failures in daily life. We used an established cognitive model to decompose participant scores into two latent parameters, mean inputs and “dissipation” which reflects the speed with which one returns to baseline performance after a deviation in scores. More traditional summary statistics, including mean performance and variability, were also calculated. Linear regression was used to compare group differences on each outcome and their association with real-world cognitive failures. Results indicate that variability in scores followed a U-shaped pattern across groups. Variability changes in cognitive impairment were due exclusively to changes in the dissipation parameter and this parameter was uniquely related to self-rated cognitive failures. Our findings indicate dissipation may reflect high levels of cognitive reserve, which protects against the manifestation of functional symptoms in daily life. More generally, our results underscore the importance of using repeated cognitive assessments in studies of healthy and pathological aging, as traditional measures of performance did not evince relationships with cognitive failures.

articles_hidden.title: Neuroscience-Informed Psychoeducation for Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
articles_hidden.authors: Robin Aupperle; Dalia El-Shafie; Claire A. Lavalley
articles_hidden.abstract: Over the past several decades, substantial progress has been made in elucidating the neurobiological mechanisms underlying trauma exposure and posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD), including alterations in large-scale brain networks involved in threat detection, emotional regulation, and cognitive control. Neuroscience-informed psychoeducation (NIPE) represents a compelling approach for translating neuroscientific research to impact real-world clinical care. In this Chapter, we first summarize current neurobiological models of PTSD and the growing literature supporting how evidence-based treatments for PTSD, such as prolonged exposure, cognitive processing therapy, or medication-based approaches, at least partially target these neurobiological mechanisms thought to be maintaining symptoms. Next, we review the variable use of NIPE within evidence-based psychotherapies, including first-line treatments such as prolonged exposure (PE) and cognitive processing therapy (CPT) as well as second-line and emerging treatments. We also discuss the availability and limitations of stand-alone NIPE materials relevant to PTSD for clinicians, patients, and the public. Finally, we emphasize considerations and future directions for the field. This includes the need for (a) development of standardized, evidence-based NIPE materials that are grounded in sound neuroscientific evidence, emphasize neuroplasticity, are available in accessible and engaging formats, and are adaptable to diverse populations and contexts and (b) randomized controlled trials comparing NIPE materials to standard psychoeducation approaches. NIPE holds considerable potential to enhance treatment outcomes and reshape public understanding of trauma-related disorders, with its continued evolution requiring further research and development to fully realize these benefits.

articles_hidden.title: Remote Digital Cognitive Assessment in a Trial-Ready Alzheimer’s Cohort: A Scalable Approach for Early Intervention Studies
articles_hidden.authors: Andrew J. Aschenbrenner; Hannah Wilks; Matthew Welhaf; Samhita Govindan Katteri; Sarah H. Stout; Martin Sliwinski; Tammie Benzinger; Brian A Gordon; Yan Li; Richard J. Perrin
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Early detection of cognitive decline in Alzheimer’s disease (AD), particularly in preclinical stages, is critical for evaluating therapeutic interventions. Traditional cognitive assessments often lack reliability and require lengthy in-person visits, limiting scalability for younger, trial-ready populations.
Objectives: To evaluate the feasibility, reliability, and validity of high-frequency remote digital cognitive assessments in individuals with autosomal dominant Alzheimer’s disease (ADAD).
Participants: 162 mutation carriers and non-carriers from DIAN-TU from 20 international sites (Ages 19-69 years).
Measurements: Participants completed remote assessments via personal smartphones, prompted four times daily for seven days (approximately 3 minutes per session), and conventional in-clinic cognitive testing at baseline. Adherence, test–retest reliability (intraclass correlation coefficients [ICCs]), construct validity (confirmatory factor analysis), and sensitivity to clinical impairment were evaluated.
Results: Average adherence was 41%. Despite this, remote measures demonstrated excellent reliability (ICCs > 0.90 after 10 sessions) and strong construct validity, with tasks loading onto memory, attention, and executive function domains. Model fit was poorer in symptomatic individuals (CDR > 0), consistent with cognitive dedifferentiation during disease progression. Both remote and traditional composites were sensitive to clinical impairment, with similar effect sizes and increasing group differences near expected symptom onset.
Conclusions: High-frequency remote cognitive assessment is feasible, reliable, and valid in a relatively young international ADAD cohort. This approach offers substantial advantages for clinical trials, including reduced participant burden, improved accessibility, and enhanced reliability, supporting its integration into early-intervention studies.

articles_hidden.title: Cultivating Flourishing through Yoga Nidra Practice in Students: A Longitudinal Randomised Waitlist-Controlled Study
articles_hidden.authors: Vicky Kachera; Neha Shekhawat; Saurabh Mishra; Alka Mishra; James Gomes; Rahul Garg
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: University students globally face an escalating mental health crisis (Paiva et
al., 2025), yet interventions often overlook the active cultivation of complete well-being
(flourishing). Objective: This randomized, waitlist-controlled study evaluated the impact of a
14-week Yoga Nidra Practice (YNP) module on mental distress and complete well-being at a
premier technical institute in India. Methods: One hundred and forty students (N=140) were
randomized 1:1 to either a structured YNP intervention or a waitlist control (WC) group.
Primary outcomes included depression, anxiety, perceived stress, sleep quality, flourishing, life
satisfaction, mood and peace of mind. Secondary outcomes assessed cognitive flexibility,
visual scanning, processing speed and academic performance. Results: The YNP group
demonstrated significantly greater improvements than the WC group across six primary
outcomes: depression (p < .001, r = -0.35), anxiety (p < .001, r = -0.34), life satisfaction (p <
.001, r = 0.34), perceived stress (p = .003, r = -0.29), flourishing (p = .004, r = 0.28), and peace
of mind (p = .001, r = 0.32). Furthermore, while sleep quality significantly deteriorated in the
WC group compared to baseline (p = .003), it remained same in the YNP group (p = .817)
resulting in a significant between-group difference (p = .010, r = -0.25). YNP group also
achieved significantly greater gains in cognitive flexibility compared to the WC group (TMTB: p = .001, r = -0.32). Reflexive thematic analysis revealed that effective coping practices
facilitated a foundational shift from reactivity to response, cultivating an inner calm that drove
holistic restoration. This central mechanism resulted in significant physical restoration,
cognitive enhancement, and the integration of mindful living into students' daily academic
routines. Conclusion: This YNP module is a potent, scalable intervention that reduces
psychological distress, and educators may consider including it in their curriculum to support
students' holistic well-being, particularly those in high-stress environments.
Keywords: Yoga Nidra, Psychological Distress, Sleep Quality, Cognitive Flexibility, Mental
Well-being, Students.

articles_hidden.title: The development and psychometric evaluation  of the brief Compulsive Pornography Use Scale  (CPUS-4)
articles_hidden.authors: Terezie Babilonová; Halley M. Pontes; Helena Pipova; Táňa Reháková; Štěpán Komrska; Jaroslava Suchá
articles_hidden.abstract: Online pornography use has increased worldwide in recent decades, with problematic use being associated with negative mental health outcomes. However, no brief instrument is currently available to specifically assess Problematic Pornography Use (PPU) by operationalizing the behavioral manifestations of Compulsive Sexual Behavior Disorder (CSBD) as defined in the 11th International Statistical Classification of Diseases (ICD-11). This study aimed to develop the Compulsive Pornography Use Scale (CPUS-4). The sample consisted of 1,023 Czech adults that completed an online survey assessing pornography use behaviors, Pornography Addiction Screening Tool (PAST), Depression, Anxiety, Stress Scales-21 (DASS-21), and Three-Item Loneliness Scale (UCLA-3). Exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses indicated a single-factor structure of the CPUS-4, supporting its factorial validity. The scale demonstrated high internal consistency and significant associations with theoretically related constructs, supporting both convergent and concurrent validity. Overall, the CPUS-4 appears to be a valid and reliable brief instrument for assessing pornography-related behavioral manifestations within the ICD-11 framework for CSBD.

articles_hidden.title: Predicting Across Classifier Systems: Homographic Interference in Mandarin Learners of Japanese
articles_hidden.authors: Chuyu Huang; Yuki Hirose; Takeshi Kishiyama; Itsuki Minemi; Saki Tsumura; Xilai Zang; Theres Grüter
articles_hidden.abstract: Numeral classifiers in languages such as Japanese and Mandarin Chinese provide semantic information that can constrain upcoming nouns. Although listeners have been shown to use classifier information predictively, little is known about how speakers of one classifier language process classifiers in another, particularly when formally corresponding classifiers differ in their semantic mappings. We investigated this question using a visual-world eye-tracking paradigm with 37 L1-Mandarin learners of Japanese and 40 L1-Japanese listeners. Participants heard sentences in which a classifier preceded the target noun and selected a referent from a three-picture display. We manipulated whether the Japanese classifier uniquely identified the target and whether a competitor was compatible with the semantic category associated with the homographic Mandarin classifier. Cluster-based permutation and divergence-point analyses of target-to-competitor fixation ratios showed that both groups used classifier information predictively, with earlier target preference when the classifier uniquely constrained the referent. Crucially, only the L1-Mandarin group showed slower target convergence when the competitor matched the Mandarin classifier category. These findings indicate that advanced L2 learners can use classifiers predictively while remaining susceptible to cross-linguistic competition from the L1 classifier system, consistent with models in which lexical-semantic representations are interconnected across languages.

articles_hidden.title: Amotivated Solitude: Naming the Space Between Vairagya and Escapism
articles_hidden.authors: Pooja Tyagi; Baljeet Kaur
articles_hidden.abstract: Recent global data indicate that roughly one in six people worldwide experience loneliness, prompting the World Health Organization to name social disconnection a public health priority. Yet not everyone who prefers solitude over social engagement is lonely, distressed, or withdrawing from life. A growing body of solitude research documents this distinction, but the specific combination addressed here, a preference for solitude that is neither reactively avoidant nor autonomously growth-seeking, remains unnamed. This preference is neither the growth-oriented non-attachment described by the Indian philosophical concept of Vairagya, nor the reactive, affect-driven retreat captured by passive escapism, nor the impairment associated with loneliness or clinical depression, nor the positively-valenced enjoyment described by affinity for aloneness. This paper proposes Amotivated Solitude (Preference) to name this gap: a dispositional or situational preference for solitude that is low in both autonomous, growth-seeking motivation and reactive, anxiety-driven avoidance. Drawing on self-determination theory's amotivation continuum, the solitude-motivation literature, and the developmental construct of unsociability, this paper differentiates the proposed construct from eight neighbouring constructs, addresses the risk of construct proliferation (the jingle-jangle problem) directly, and presents a conceptual map locating the construct along a volition-outcome spectrum. It outlines a research program for construct validation, including qualitative grounding, item development, and psychometric testing against existing non-attachment measures, and closes with limitations and open questions for discussion regarding naming, boundary conditions, and trait versus state framing.

articles_hidden.title: New Ecological Paradigm Scale Revised (NEPS- R): Evidence for a Two-Factor Structure and Measurement Invariance
articles_hidden.authors: Marília Montenegro; Filipa Nunes; Ana Rodrigues de Lemos; Joana Cadima; Paula Mena Matos; Tiago Ferreira
articles_hidden.abstract: The New Ecological Paradigm Scale-Revised (NEPS-R) is among the most widely used measures of ecological worldview, yet there’s a lack of consensus on its factorial structure, and evidence on its measurement invariance across gender, particularly within parental dyads, is scarce. This study examined the psychometric properties of the NEPS-R in a sample of 255 mothers and 219 fathers of preschool-aged children in Portugal. Confirmatory factor analysis compared the original unidimensional structure, the theoretical five-factor model, and a two-factor Ecocentrism-Anthropocentrism structure. A refined 10-item two-factor solution provided the best fit for both mothers and fathers, outperforming the unidimensional and five-factor alternatives. This model demonstrated full configural, metric, scalar, and strict invariance across parental gender, indicating that mothers and fathers interpret and respond to the NEPS-R items equivalently. These findings support a bidimensional conceptualization of ecological worldviews and provide novel evidence of measurement invariance for the NEPS-R using dyadic parental data. This study provides a psychometrically robust and gender-invariant instrument capable of comparing mothers' and fathers' ecological worldviews within the same family, with implications for research on intergenerational transmission of pro-environmental values and for family-based environmental interventions.

articles_hidden.title: An Experience-Sampling Study of Daily Affect and Global Life Satisfaction in the United States and Japan
articles_hidden.authors: Hiroki Hirano
articles_hidden.abstract: Evidence for cultural differences in affect–life satisfaction associations has largely come from retrospective measures, and whether these variations also emerge when emotional experiences are captured in daily life remains less clear. Therefore, the present study analyzed experience-sampling data collected over a two-week period to examine associations of momentary positive and negative affect with global life satisfaction among U.S. and Japanese adults. In both groups, higher positive affect and lower negative affect were each uniquely associated with greater life satisfaction. The primary analysis also indicated a stronger relationship between positive affect and life satisfaction among Japanese than U.S. participants, although this cultural contrast was not consistently statistically significant across sensitivity analyses. Meanwhile, the strength of the link between negative affect and life satisfaction did not differ significantly between the two groups. Considered alongside prior research using retrospective reports, the current findings highlight the importance of both cultural context and assessment methods in understanding the emotional correlates of life satisfaction.

articles_hidden.title: Grounding meaning in social and emotional experience: Challenges and opportunities
articles_hidden.authors: Pablo Solana
articles_hidden.abstract: Within the broader debate on how the mind and brain represent meaning, multiple representation theories have positioned social and emotional experience, along with their underlying neural systems, as key sources for concept grounding. In this article, I review the current evidence for this proposal and discuss several conceptual and methodological challenges, including the limited capacity of behavioral evidence to support this view, the difficulties associated with interpreting neuroimaging findings, the need for stronger causal evidence, and the importance of adopting open science practices. I argue that these limitations converge on a common concern: in their current form, many findings taken to support multiple representation theories of socio-affective grounding do not provide sufficiently diagnostic evidence to empirically adjudicate between them and competing accounts of semantic representation. In response, I outline a set of methodological recommendations and underexplored ideas that may help refine the theoretical framework, generate more decisive tests, and guide future research.

articles_hidden.title: Revisiting Cross-Modal Matching in the Light of Luce’s Global Psychophysical Theory
articles_hidden.authors: Katharina Naumann; Jürgen Heller
articles_hidden.abstract: This study presents a replication of the classical cross-modal matching experiment by J. C. Stevens and Marks (1965, Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the USA, 54, 407-411), which examined loudness-to-brightness and brightness-to-loudness mappings.  We extend prior work by complementing traditional group-level analysis with an individual-level examination and by applying the theory of global psychophysics with internal references. This mathematical framework formalizes the underlying mechanisms of cross-modal matching behavior. In matching tasks, the well-documented phenomenon termed the regression effect emerges, wherein the adjusted stimuli gravitate toward mid-level intensities. To model this effect, we implement a novel Bayesian estimation of the global psychophysical model for cross-modal matching. In a sample of seven subjects, including many repetitions at the subject level, the regression effect is observed at both the aggregated and individual levels. The model effectively captures the prevalent nonlinearity in individual matching curves. We discuss the theoretical and methodological implications of these findings and outline directions for future research.

articles_hidden.title: Brain–Environment Rhythmic Coupling: An Interdisciplinary Review of Rhythm Synchronization between the brain and the environment
articles_hidden.authors: Farzaneh Behzadi; Amir Kalantarifard; Dylan Chau Huynh; Lars Brorson Fich; Aja Khalid Hussein; Zakaria Djebbara
articles_hidden.abstract: Rhythm is a fundamental aspect of both architectural design and brain–body dynamics, yet research across these domains remains fragmented and largely descriptive. The absence of a shared conceptual framework limits systematic investigation of how architectural rhythms interact with human brain–body dynamics and may influence cognition and behavior. Drawing on enactivism and the concept of natural attunement, we propose that movement through patterned spaces may convert spatial organization, such as repeated forms, geometric intervals, and variations in light, into temporally structured sensory input. Neuroscience studies have shown that sub-second, strictly periodic sensory stimulation can produce phase-consistent neural responses under restricted laboratory conditions. However, it remains unknown whether repeated, aperiodic, or movement-dependent architectural structures generate comparable temporal organization in neural activity during active navigation. We therefore hypothesize that temporally structured environmental input may align with ongoing neural and bodily activity, a process we refer to as brain–environment rhythmic coupling. To better understand this hypothesis, we first propose a structured vocabulary that classifies architectural rhythms according to their structural complexity, spatiotemporal arrangement, and constituent visual elements, with particular emphasis on visuomotor rhythms. We then consider candidate mechanisms that may support this coupling, including magnocellular processing, stimulus-locked responses, phase resetting, and, under restricted conditions, neural entrainment. By integrating insights from architecture, neuroscience, and cognitive science, this paper proposes a conceptual framework that positions rhythm as a bridge between built environments and brain–body dynamics, while providing a basis for future empirical research on design, action, cognition, and well-being.

articles_hidden.title: Adaptive search promotes asymmetrical learning
articles_hidden.authors: Samuel David Jones; Paul Rauwolf
articles_hidden.abstract: Recent theoretical work has argued that learning trajectories are shaped by adaptive search and satisficing. The central idea of this work is that the value of an information source (i.e., its utility or valence) modulates engagement, sampling density, and encoding fidelity, providing a behavioural pathway to variation in learning outcomes. The current manuscript reports the first explicit empirical test of this idea in adults using a modified version of a multi-step decision-making paradigm known as 'Mouselab'. Across two experiments and six sub-tasks, N=101 participants searched a decision tree at a cost until settling on and executing a high-value policy. While Experiment 1 involved a non-symbolic decision space, Experiment 2 incorporated symbolic cues that allowed us to determine the extent to which associative learning is sensitive to underlying value structure. We found that value-sensitive adaptive search promoted rank-dependent learning asymmetries at test – estimates for the value of the best symbol were near veridical, while those for low-value symbols were at chance. In addition, we found that (i) informative symbolic cues shifted search from balanced exploration (breadth ≈ depth) towards depth-first exploitation; (ii) cue-guided search developed rapidly, with high-value symbol exploitation emerging within a handful of trials; (iii) search evidenced a win-stay tendency and was sensitive to cue valence, with individuals quickly pruning negatively valued branches; (iv) raising cost constrained search volume but preserved its depth-first, cue-sensitive character; and (v) observed individual differences in search behaviour were not predicted by common measures of cognitive function. These results provide new insight into how adaptive search and satisficing shape learning, supporting an emerging theory of the behavioural origins of individual differences in human development.

articles_hidden.title: Investigating which type of maltreatment has the largest impact on health:  The challenge of measurement error
articles_hidden.authors: Milan Zarchev; Henning Tiemeier
articles_hidden.abstract: To answer the question of which type of maltreatment has the largest impact on health outcomes, researchers often simultaneously enter multiple maltreatment predictors in a single regression model. However, this approach of mutual adjustment is problematic, as some maltreatment types (e.g. physical neglect) are often measured with more error than others (e.g. physical abuse). Greater measurement error attenuates effect sizes and reduces statistical power to detect associations, implicitly creating the appearance that better measured maltreatment types are more impactful. The attenuation is particularly severe in mutually adjusted models, as maltreatment types tend to correlate with each other. Researchers comparing maltreatment types should routinely report on reliability estimates such as McDonald’s omega and present separately-estimated associations next to the mutually adjusted model.

articles_hidden.title: Effects of task-switch proportion and strategy instructions on cognitive stability and flexibility
articles_hidden.authors: Lara Sophie Knaup; Marcus Möschl; John Dylan Haynes; Marie Therese Bartossek; Thomas Goschke
articles_hidden.abstract: To meet the challenges of daily life, we must continuously adapt to optimize the balance between cognitive stability and flexibility depending on the current task demands. The control dilemma theory posits that cognitive stability and flexibility are polar opposites on the same dimension incurring opposing costs and benefits, resulting in a trade-off. Accordingly, a shift towards flexibility (i.e., reducing costs of task-switching) incurs costs in stability (i.e., increasing interference costs), and vice versa. Here, we manipulated the list-wide proportion of task-switches between a flexibility (75% task-repeats) and a stability (25% task-switches) condition. We interspersed coveted trial sequences with balanced task transitions between strongly biased sequences while retaining the list-wide 75:25 ratios. Additionally, we asked participants to adapt to the prevalent transition type by behaving more flexible or stable. We hypothesized that switch costs would be reduced within the flexibility condition, that simultaneously reduced interference in the stability condition would be indicative of a trade-off, and that both control adaptations would persist within the balanced trial sequences. In a within-subjects design, participants (N = 96) completed two online sessions of a classic cued task-switching paradigm. While we did not observe the hypothesized trade-off in either of the two sequence types, the level of flexibility was adapted within the biased sequences, but this effect decayed within the balanced sequences. Taken together, these results highlight that individuals are able to adapt cognitive control modes supporting cognitive flexibility remarkably fast in response to dynamic changes in the likelihood of local trial transitions.

articles_hidden.title: Rates and covariates of suicidal behaviour and mental ill-health in young Australians: findings from wave one of the Right Here, Right Now national survey
articles_hidden.authors: Jo Robinson; Bridget Kenny; Elise Carrotte; Shu Mei Teo; Caroline X. Gao; Eleanor Bailey; India Bellairs-Walsh; Gowri Rajaram; Deanna DeCicco; Alex Dalton
articles_hidden.abstract:
Objective: To examine the rates of suicidal ideation, self-harm, and symptoms of depression and anxiety among Australians aged 12 to 25 years, and covariates.
Design: A multi-wave national cross-sectional survey.
Setting and participants: Participants were recruited online from research panels, boosted through convenience sampling. Data were weighted by age, gender, and location.
Main outcomes: Rates of suicidal ideation, self-harm, depressive and anxiety symptoms. Population-weighted descriptive statistics were used to examine prevalence; logistic and linear regressions identified demographic, clinical and social covariates.
Results: N=2,863 participants were included in analysis. Mean age was 18.6; 50.7% (1439/2840) were cisgender men/boys; 4.5% (127/2840) were trans and/or gender diverse. One in three (32.1%, 859/2680) reported lifetime suicidal ideation, 26.8% (748/2787) lifetime self-harm and 8.0% (210/2631) lifetime suicide attempt. Twelve-month prevalence rates were 14.6% (387/2655) for suicidal ideation and 12.5% (347/2779) for self-harm. 38.9% (1107/2847) reported at least moderate depression symptoms, and 34.6% (988/2857) reported at least moderate anxiety symptoms. Rates of suicide-related behaviour, depression and anxiety were highest in trans and/or gender diverse young people followed by cisgender women/girls. Covariates for suicidal ideation and self-harm included loneliness, younger age, depressive symptoms, >2 adverse childhood experiences, and suicide bereavement. Covariates associated with depression and anxiety outcomes also included social exclusion/withdrawal, sleep problems, and alcohol or other drug problems.
Conclusions: Suicidal ideation, self-harm and mental ill-health in young Australians appear higher than previous estimates, and are particularly high among young women/girls and trans and/or gender diverse youth. Findings highlight the need for urgent responses that extend beyond individual-level intervention to address the broader social conditions shaping young people’s mental health. The study also points to the need for timely and robust data that can inform practice and policy and help evaluate new initiatives. Future waves of this survey will help these efforts.

articles_hidden.title: The relation between math anxiety and math self-concept to math performance varies across study math load
articles_hidden.authors: Krzysztof Cipora; Maristella Lunardon; Ida von Lehsten; Gabriella Daroczy; Klaus Willmes; Hans-Christoph Nuerk; Christina Artemenko
articles_hidden.abstract: Arithmetic skills are important to navigate everyday tasks and to successfully engage in the fields of science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM). Among the factors supporting these skills, lower math anxiety and higher math self-concept show consistent associations with better performance. However, the effect size of these associations is heterogeneous, and the factors that contribute to this variability are still not fully understood. Most of the studies on adults were conducted among psychology students, who may not be representative of the whole population and do not consider the different importance that mathematics plays for individuals’ careers. Therefore, the present study investigated whether the relation of arithmetic performance to math anxiety and math self-concept varies between university programs with different levels of math load. 836 German university students were included in the present online study. They completed self-report questionnaires to assess math anxiety and math self-concept and a timed arithmetic task. We found that arithmetic performance is negatively associated with math anxiety and positively with math self-concept overall, but the size of this association is different across math loads of the individuals’ study programs. Specifically, these associations were considerably stronger among students in university programs with low math load compared to students in programs with high math load. We conclude that the math load of the university program is a factor to take into account, as results from students of a particular subject (e.g., psychology) are not representative of the relationship of math anxiety and math self-concept with math performance and should not be overgeneralized. Specifically, those individuals whose negative attitudes do not translate to lower performance are the ones likely to be enrolled in math intense programs.

articles_hidden.title: Exploring links between type- and timing-specific characteristics of childhood maltreatment and epigenetic aging in formerly out-of-home placed young adults
articles_hidden.authors: Maria Meier; Eva Unternaehrer; Danielle Otten; Inga Schalinski; Laura Gurri; Marc Schmid; David Bürgin; Vera Clemens
articles_hidden.abstract:
Childhood maltreatment (CM) is a key risk factor for psychopathology, physical morbidity and premature mortality, potentially mediated by epigenetic processes like DNA methylation. While differential links between type and timing of CM and psychopathology are increasingly acknowledged, it remains unclear how type- and timing-specific characteristics of CM are associated with epigenetic measures of biological aging, including age acceleration, mortality risk, and the pace of aging. We thus aimed to explore these links in an at-risk sample of formerly out-of-home placed adults who often report significant exposure to CM and high rates of adverse health outcomes. 
One-hundred-sixteen young adults previously placed in youth residential care (33% women, age M = 26.3 years, SD = 3.6) completed the Maltreatment and Abuse Chronology of Exposure (MACE-X) and provided blood samples to estimate DNA methylation using the Illumina Infinium MethylationEPIC BeadChip Microarray. In preregistered analyses, conditional random forest regressions were used to estimate the importance of CM types (abuse, neglect, peer victimization, sexual abuse), timing (ages 3-18), and global measures (severity, multiplicity, duration) for the prediction of markers of epigenetic aging (Hannum’s and Pheno’s age acceleration and DunedinPACE). 
Abuse from age 9 until late adolescence predicted Hannum’s age acceleration more strongly than global CM measures and was consistently and negatively associated with it. BMI was positively linked to Hannum’s age acceleration. We found no association between CM and newer epigenetic clocks (i.e., Pheno’s age acceleration and DunedinPACE). 
In an at-risk sample of formerly out-of-home-placed young adults with high rates of CM, we provide first evidence that parental abuse from mid childhood until late adolescence – a potential sensitive period – was linked to decelerated epigenetic aging. CM should therefore be assessed dimensionally, rather than as a single, undifferentiated cumulative exposure.

articles_hidden.title: Daring to leave the laboratory: Why operational neuroscience requires a different research strategy
articles_hidden.authors: Jerome I. Rotgans
articles_hidden.abstract: In this opinion paper, we highlight why taking neuroscience into complex operational environments requires a different analytical logic from that used in controlled experiments. Laboratory paradigms are powerful because they isolate cognitive processes, repeat conditions and compare averaged responses. Operational work removes much of that control. A critical event may occur only once, several cognitive processes may unfold together, and the meaning of a neural response depends on what the individual or team was doing at that moment. We describe a pragmatic approach developed through our neuroergonomics work. We transform continuous haemodynamic signals into discrete ROI-specific activation events, producing an event-by-ROI activation matrix (Spearfish code). These events are then linked to synchronized video and operational data and compared with expert or desired-performance benchmarks. This approach does not recreate laboratory causality in the field. It provides a structured way to identify when and where potentially meaningful activation occurs and to interpret it against performance and context. We discuss its use for training, cognitive-load mapping, human-centred automation and team workload allocation, while making explicit the limits of the resulting inference.

articles_hidden.title: Empirically derived phenotypes can reduce diagnostic heterogeneity
articles_hidden.authors: Miriam K. Forbes; John F. Buss; Daniel P. Moriarity; Eiko I Fried; Holly Frances Levin-Aspenson; Lorenzo Lorenzo-Luaces; Kasey Stanton; Ashley L. Watts; Gregory W. Forbes
articles_hidden.abstract: Diagnostic heterogeneity is a longstanding challenge for the classification of mental illness because people who receive the same diagnosis can differ markedly in their symptom presentations as well as in the mechanisms underlying those symptoms. High heterogeneity undermines both the clinical utility of diagnostic labels and the scientific accuracy of research that treats disorders as coherent constructs. In this study, we examined heterogeneity across six internalizing disorders (specific phobia, social anxiety disorder, agoraphobia, generalized anxiety disorder [GAD], major depressive disorder [MDD], and posttraumatic stress disorder [PTSD]) using three complementary approaches to quantifying heterogeneity: 1) descriptive heterogeneity (how many symptom profiles can theoretically satisfy the diagnostic criteria, and how many are observed in practice), 2) person-focused heterogeneity (whether diagnostic labels capture people with similar symptom presentations), and 3) construct-focused heterogeneity (whether diagnostic labels group symptoms with similar patterns of association with external validators). Analyses drew on subsamples from a large convenience sample with elevated psychopathology, predominantly from Australia and the USA (n = 14,762, mean [SD] age = 38.0 [18.0]; 55% women). Results showed that specific phobia was consistently the least heterogeneous; social anxiety disorder, agoraphobia, and GAD had mixed results; and MDD and PTSD were highly heterogeneous across all metrics. Notably, empirically derived phenotypes nested within each disorder substantively reduced heterogeneity relative to the DSM diagnoses. The study provides both a systematic multi-method approach to characterising different types of diagnostic heterogeneity, and a practical path toward more precise and informative constructs that can be implemented by rescoring existing data.

articles_hidden.title: Increasing Youth Engagement with Community Arts through a Youth-led, AI-supported pathway
articles_hidden.authors: Nikki Rickard; Simone Minett; Simon D'Alfonso; Kejian Cui; Thomas Whitford
articles_hidden.abstract: Young adults experience high rates of loneliness, yet existing interventions are often poorly suited to this population. Social prescribing offers a promising, non-clinical alternative, but uptake among young people is low, and pathways remain largely designed for older adults. The aim in this two part study was to co design a youth friendly digital tool that supports engagement with community-based arts activities, and to pilot the acceptance of this tool for diverse young adults.  A participatory co-design approach was employed (Study 1), comprising exploratory youth workshops (n = 24) and interviews with community leaders (n = 6), complemented by a larger scale youth survey (n=269), to understand the needs, barriers and enablers to participation in community-based arts activities for young adults (18-30 years). In Study 2, we used a strengths-based, positive youth development approach to translate the co-design and survey outcomes from Study 1 into an AI-powered conversational platform l, consulting three youth co researchers throughout. The platform prototype (‘Connie’) was pilot evaluated for usability by a sample of diverse young adults (n=22). Survey respondents showed strong interest in a digital discovery tool (84%), with preferences for personalisation and ease of use. Five themes were identified across youth and community leaders’ qualitative data: trust and authenticity, reducing uncertainty, belonging and social confidence, inclusive participation, and lowering barriers to engagement. Connie was rated highly by trial users across all usability domains, with an average of 80% satisfaction. The findings provide support for the viability of a digital tool to support youth social prescribing. Findings suggest that personalised activity discovery can help reduce the uncertainty that prevents many young people from engaging with community-based activities. Effectiveness was also supported by transparency about how AI was used, sensitivity to different levels of user social readiness, and inclusion of diverse stakeholders in the tool’s design.

articles.title: Captured by the Ballot: Non-Partisan Judicial Elections and Democratic Erosion in Mexico
articles.authors: Brett Ryan Bessen
articles.abstract: Public tolerance for democratic erosion is often attributed to voter partisanship. Voters are thought to overlook undemocratic maneuvers to support the partisan in-group. Yet, backsliders  often disavow traditional parties and frame their reforms as non-partisan. I examine the role of voter partisanship in non-partisan elections, showing how elite manipulation of the information environment can generate partisan outcomes that facilitate backsliding—even when citizens prefer non-partisan outcomes on average. I examine Mexico’s 2025 judicial elections, pairing a conjoint experiment with an analysis of the electoral results. While the conjoint indicates that voters preferred independent judges, the electoral results indicate that government-aligned candidates on illicitly circulated voter guides (acordeones) received the most support, contributing to the partisan capture of the Supreme Court. Elite manipulation of the information environment and electoral incentives—rather than partisan preferences among the eligible electorate—were primary contributors to the court’s partisan capture.

articles.title: Empirical Reasoning About FOI Request Delays in the European Union
articles.authors: Jukka Ruohonen
articles.abstract: Freedom of information (FOI) is a human right and an important concept for the transparency and accountability of governments and public administrations. It is also essential for democracy. Despite a long research lineage on FOI laws and their use by citizens, existing empirical knowledge is still limited regarding the inner workings of FOI requests. This limitation applies particularly to the European Union (EU) and the documents possessed by its various institutions. To help at addressing this limitation, the paper presents a few empirical observations about FOI requests in the EU context. By using a dataset containing 500 requests made between 2022 and early 2023, the insight presented cover the EU institutions targeted, the requesters making FOI requests, and particularly the bureaucratic delays in handling of FOI requests. According to results based on a regression analysis, the bureaucratic delays vary according to both the EU institutions and the individual requesters.

articles.title: Responsibility to Prepare: From Individual Security to Collective Resilience
articles.authors: Paulus Damgaard; Jonas Toubøl; Lærke Høgenhaven
articles.abstract: In the context of heightened geopolitical tensions, European societies increasingly frame private crisis preparedness as integral to societal resilience. Once viewed as antisocial survivalists, preppers now offer insight into civil society’s role in prepar-edness. Drawing on a netnographic study of one of Denmark’s largest Facebook prepper groups (2015-2024), this article examines how the group members per-ceive responsibility for crisis preparedness across four periods: before COVID-19, during the pandemic, after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, and following the Danish government’s 2024 appeal for household preparedness. Findings reveal a dominant individualistic framing in stable times, but a shift towards collective understandings of responsibility following official communication during crises. The article con-tributes to sociological research on crisis preparedness by demonstrating how per-ceptions of crisis contexts and state communication shape preppers’ responsibility frames, challenging static portrayals of preppers as antisocial and highlighting how individualised practices of preparedness can evolve into collective orientations that complement state capacity.

articles.title: Resistance to Backsliding: The Role of Democratic Conceptions
articles.authors: Noam Gidron; Yotam Margalit; Lior Sheffer; Itamar Yakir
articles.abstract: We examine who mobilizes against democratic backsliding, focusing on mass protests against the judicial overhaul advanced by the Israeli government in 2023. As contemporary subversion of democracy is often driven by governments that won an electoral majority, we posit that protesting against the government's actions requires people to have a thick conception of democracy that goes beyond majority rule. Drawing on panel data collected before and after the overhaul's announcement, we show that citizens vary substantially in their conception of democracy, and that a thick conception not only predicts protesting against backsliding but also moderates the role of other key factors in mobilizing against democratic erosion. The findings highlight the role of small-d democrats in safeguarding democracy.

articles.title: Social Networks and Unequal Income Returns to Education: Gender Differences and Cross-National Context
articles.authors: INVEST Flagship; Emmi Mäkeläinen; Aki Koivula
articles.abstract: This study examines how social networks are associated with unequal income returns to education and whether these associations vary by gender and across national contexts. Using data from the International Social Survey Programme (ISSP) 2017 from representative samples in 15 countries, the study analyses the interrelations between educational attainment, social ties, and personal income. The analyses distinguish both the status of social contacts and the type of ties to the upper middle class, while also examining variation by gender and country-level income inequality. The results show that access to upper-middle-class contacts is associated with wider educational differences in income, and that close ties, especially family members, relatives, and close friends, are more strongly associated with income than weaker ties. These patterns also vary by gender, with educated men’s income more strongly associated with upper-middle-class ties than educated women’s. In addition, educational differences in the association between social networks and income are more pronounced in countries with higher levels of income inequality. The study contributes to research on social stratification by showing that income returns to education are socially embedded and also vary by gender and national context.

articles.title: An Atlas of Economic Activities in the UK: a fine-grained typology of economic activities from open, large-scale web archive data
articles.authors: Leonardo Castro Gonzalez; Emmanouil Tranos; Levi John Wolf; Rui Zhu; Emerald Dilworth
articles.abstract: We present the Atlas of Economic Activities in the UK, a granular and dynamic typology of economic activities. Built using large-scale web data from Common Crawl, the Atlas captures how UK businesses describe their economic activities, creates an activity typology and geolocates them at the postcode level. The Atlas provides a complementary source to established industrial classifications, which are static and insensitive to the evolution of economic activities. It is designed to support research and policy analysis requiring fine-grained information about economic activities over space and time. The Atlas is developed transparently using open tools and web archive data, so that it can be replicated and adapted to different research and policy contexts.

articles.title: Organising the Social Layer: How Organisational Paradoxes Shape Engagement in Cryptocurrency Communities
articles.authors: Annika Aebli; Fabienne Silberstein-Bamford; Joshua Silberstein Bamford
articles.abstract: Cryptocurrencies (crypto) and their underlying blockchain technologies are designed around the promise of collective organising without reliance on centralised authority, intermediaries, and hierarchical coordination. Yet sustaining collective participation in decentralised networks without conventional forms of coordination remains an organisational challenge. This study demonstrates that keeping participants engaged in crypto communities depends on continuous work within crypto’s social layer. Drawing on the organisational paradox lens and 26 semi-structured interviews with developers, team members, and regular users across four crypto communities, we show that sustained engagement depends on balancing organisational paradoxes rooted in communication, decision-making, and community development: technical discourse versus social-media-style interaction, decentralised participation versus centralised guidance, and scaling versus a sense of authentic community. Our findings suggest that continually balancing, rather than resolving these tensions is essential for engagement and community cohesion. This research contributes to the theoretical understanding of decentralised organising by showing how collective participation can be maintained in organisational arrangements that seek to reduce reliance on conventional centralised structures. More broadly, we show that decentralisation does not eliminate the need for organising but relocates much of this work to the social layer of interaction, coordination, and community building, where contradictory demands must be continually negotiated to keep participation workable and sustainable.

articles.title: The Electoral Costs of Exclusion: Women’s Candidate Placement and Party Performance
articles.authors: Iris E. Acquarone; Alba Huidobro
articles.abstract: Political elites continue to behave as if including women in electable positions is electorally risky, despite growing evidence of voter support for gender-inclusive representation. This paper advances a theory of the electoral costs of exclusion, arguing that continued exclusion can become electorally costly when parties fail to adapt to changing electoral responses to women's representation. Using data from Spanish local elections (2003-2019) and a difference-in-differences design, we show that parties increasing women's representation in electable list positions gain votes and seats relative to parties that do not; this divergence coincides with gains among parties increasing women's representation and losses among those maintaining or reducing it. These consequences grow over time and are strongest where inclusion is voluntary rather than quota-mandated. Our findings challenge the idea that underrepresentation persists because inclusion fails electorally, pointing instead to a changing electoral constraint some elites may fail to recognize: exclusion has become costly.

articles.title: Health system and hospital utilization in Chile, 1952–2020: trends, reforms, and inflection points
articles.authors: Mauricio Matus-Lopez
articles.abstract: Objective. To collect and analyze longitudinal data on hospital discharges in Chile between 1952 and 2020, both at the national level and within the public subsystem. Patterns of change were identified in relation to the following key institutional milestones: the Curative Medicine Act of 1968, the creation of the National Health Services System in 1979, and the implementation of the Universal and Guaranteed Access Reform in 2005. Methods. A first-of-its-kind time series was constructed using official sources from the Ministry of Health and institutional documents. Indicators were calculated for the total number of discharges, discharge rates per thousand population, and comparisons with the United States. The analysis included exploratory graphics and construction of segmented regression models. Results. Hospital discharges rose steadily, with two periods mirroring robust expansion of the private sector: between 1982 and 1987 and between 2006 and 2019. Public provision of hospital services slowed or decreased with the 1979 reform and with the 2005 reform, although not with the 1968 reform. Conclusion. This study provides empirical evidence on the long-term trajectory of Chilean hospital services and confirms a structural contrast between the country's major health system models and the differences in their reforms. It also underscores the need for long-term information to analyze the impact of health reforms.

articles.title: Rethinking methods for studying online information and health decision-making: a participant-centred approach
articles.authors: NIHR Policy Research Unit in Reproductive Health; Elena Proffitt; Nicola Merrett; Lois Harvey-Pescott; Jennifer Hall; Abigail McNiven; Abimbola Ayorinde; Kamilla Abdullayev; Rebecca French; Kelly Dickson
articles.abstract:
Online information, accessed through social media, websites, apps and artificial intelligence, is frequently described as shaping health attitudes and decision-making.  Many methodological approaches to understanding how online information influences decisions provide important insights into online content, information exposure, or user perspectives, but often struggle to capture the personalised and algorithmically curated digital environments people encounter, how they engage with information as it appears in their everyday lives, and how such encounters intersect with wider social, cultural and personal contexts to shape decision making. New methodological approaches are needed that can generate meaningful evidence about the varied realities of navigating online health information and the role it plays in decision-making.  

Drawing on reproductive justice and feminist principles that privilege participant expertise and lived experience and informed by literature and collaboration with lived and learnt experts, we co-designed a participant-centred longitudinal content-oriented study exploring the influence of online information on contraceptive decision-making. Inspired by Photovoice approaches, participants documented in real time the online information they encountered over a one-month period, capturing content presented through their own tailored digital environments. Interviews conducted before and after the collection period explored contraceptive experiences, attitudes, decision-making and reflections on the role of online information. By combining real-time documentation with in-depth interviews, this approach enabled interpretations of participants lived encounters with online information, including algorithmic changes, emerging trends, current events, and the types of content that resonated with them. Collaborators with lived experience were involved throughout the methodological development and interpretation and analysis of findings.  

This participant-selected content-oriented longitudinal design demonstrates the value of methodologies that capture and generate evidence on lived digital and offline realities as they unfold in real time. Understanding how online information shapes health decision-making requires moving beyond approaches that treat the internet as an isolated and static influence on behaviours. Online information is not a singular, stable object of inquiry but dynamic, personalised, algorithmically mediated and embedded within broader social, cultural, and political contexts. Methodologies that recognise this complexity are essential for generating evidence capable of informing empathetic and meaningful health care and support and care for people prioritising their needs and navigating complex health decisions.

articles.title: Detecting Inequality in Noisy Communication: Promises and Pitfalls of Large Language Models
articles.authors: Susanne Reinhardt; Jonathan J.B. Mijs; David Schieferdecker; Michael Vaughan
articles.abstract: How inequality is communicated shapes how it is explained, understood, and legitimated or contested. Yet studying these communicative processes at scale is challenging because inequality is multidimensional, often expressed implicitly and relationally, and context dependent. We argue that large language models (LLMs) shift, but do not eliminate, these methodological challenges. We trace the development from manual content analysis to rule-based computational approaches and machine learning to LLMs and assess how these methods combine conceptual alignment, semantic sensitivity, contextual sensitivity, and scalability. LLMs help relax some longstanding trade-offs between semantic sensitivity to meaning and scalability, thus promising more comprehensive analyses of established research questions and opening possibilities for comparative research across contexts. Yet untapping their full potential for research on inequality communication depends on addressing problems concerning conceptual validity, representation, comparative measurement, and substantive inference. We conclude by outlining a research agenda for rigorous LLM-based inequality communication research.

articles.title: What influences the time to reach a tenured university professorship? Insights from machine-learning
articles.authors: Jasmin M. Kizilirmak; Frauke Peter
articles.abstract: The race to professorship is influenced by many factors, ranging from individual achievements to systemic structures. Prior research has underscored the significance of aspects such as academic productivity, institutional affiliations, and personal choices in shaping academic careers, but comprehensive analyses in specific contexts remain limited. The last two decades have seen strategic shifts within the German academic system, most notably with the introduction of junior and tenure-track professorships intended to offer a more secure career path. Yet, uncertainties persist regarding the determinants of career trajectories to tenured university professorship. Addressing this gap, this paper uses unique and novel longitudinal data of German professors to elucidate the various pathways to professorship. Based on a sample of individuals who successfully secured full university professorship, we estimate comprehensive models using machine learning to determine relevant factors that predict the time needed to reach this position. Key correlates are obtaining a habilitation, having held positions with leadership responsibilities, and disciplinary fields.

articles.title: A New Era of Political Socialization? The Interplay Between Political Social Media Exposure, Conspiracy Thinking, and Political Distrust Among Dutch Younger vs. Older Generations
articles.authors: Tamar Montagne; Anouk Smeekes
articles.abstract: In recent years, populist radical-right parties (PRRP) have gained substantial electoral support in European countries, especially among younger voters. However, few studies have focused on the generational divide in PRRP voting behavior and the factors that explain why current younger generations are more likely to vote for PRRP. The current study addresses this research gap by examining whether generational differences in PRRP voting can be explained by variations in political social media exposure (PSME) and its indirect pathways through conspiracy thinking and political distrust, while accounting for the moderating role of anti-immigrant attitudes. Drawing on insights from developmental psychology, political psychology, and political science, we developed an interdisciplinary framework. We tested our expectations in the context of the Netherlands using data from the Dutch Parliamentary Election Study 2023, drawing on a sample of Dutch eligible voters. Results showed that current younger generations (Generations Y and Z) were more likely to vote for PRRP compared to older generations, partly explained by their higher PSME and subsequently, stronger conspiracy thinking and political distrust. Results further showed that the effect of conspiracy thinking on PRRP voting was particularly pronounced for respondents with low levels of anti-immigrant attitudes.

articles.title: What is edtech for? A cross-national popularity index of educational apps
articles.authors: Lulu Shi; Basak Bozkurt
articles.abstract: Digitalisation in education is so far described through broad indicators such as market growth, venture capital investment, infrastructure provision, or device availability in schools and homes. While useful, these measures reveal little about for what purposes digital technologies are used in education, and how these purposes vary across national contexts and time. This article addresses these gaps by developing an education app popularity index based on daily top-200 education app rankings across twelve countries between 2017 and 2023: Belgium, Denmark, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, Norway, Poland, Spain, Switzerland, the United Kingdom, and the United States. Drawing on app metadata, education apps are categorised according to the services and functions they offer to understand for what purpose they serve. The ranking is then aggregated to analyse category prominence over time and across countries to understand popularity of education apps by category. The study makes three contributions. First, it provides a granular account of what educational apps offer, showing that the educational app landscape is not dominated by a single type of service but consists of a heterogeneous mixture of tutoring tools, management platforms, parent-facing communication apps and a range of apps supporting infomal learning. Second, it shows the popularity of different types of digital education services and how and their popularity shift over time. Third, it shows that these patterns vary across country contexts. Differences across countries point to that edtech usage is not only driven by individual preferences but by distinct institutional arrangements and cultures. Lastly, this study also advances a methodological approach for understanding the realities of edtech deployment by using Google Play Store data, the world’s largest app market in terms of content volume.

articles.title: Autonomy, Adolescents, and Artificial Intelligence
articles.authors: Michael J. S. Beauvais
articles.abstract:
In this essay, I explore the potential implications of adolescent use of AI assistants on the development of adolescents’ capacities for autonomy. Thinking through these issues from the perspective of first principles is, I believe, needed in order to sharpen our understanding of some of the issues AI assistants pose for young people. A clear analysis will suggest which legal or policy prescriptions should follow. 

I first give an overview of adolescent use of AI assistants, noting their popularity and the variety of use contexts. Drawing upon the work of Catriona Mackenzie, I then outline a relational conception of autonomy that conceives of autonomy as having three distinct dimensions: self-determination, self-governance, and self-authorization. The precision of Mackenzie’s conception allows us to more carefully consider how different uses and contexts of technological use can affect individuals’ capacities for autonomy. Using this three-dimensional conception of autonomy, I propose three potential interventions for law and policy: thinking beyond harms, substantive privacy protections, and autonomy impact assessments.

articles.title: The Vanishing Mutual Citation
articles.authors: Maayan Matsliah
articles.abstract: Mutual citation – a pair of publications that cite each other – provides a simple measure of reciprocation linkage within scientific literature. Such pairs arise because papers are not published in strict sequence: authors often cite each other's preprints and working papers, add citations during revision, and sometimes publish related papers together. Using OpenAlex citation data from 1975 to 2023, we ask two questions: how has the rate at which papers reciprocate citations changed over five decades, and are interdisciplinary papers reciprocated less often than non-interdisciplinary papers? Contrary to both expectations, reciprocation declined sharply rather than rising with improved discoverability of scholarly work, and interdisciplinary papers did not reciprocate less than non-interdisciplinary papers. Mean mutual citations per paper fell by ~88% and the pooled mutual-citation rate fell by ~95% between 1975 and 2023. Papers citing three or more fields (interdisciplinary) exceeded the reciprocation rates of papers citing one or two fields (non-interdisciplinary) across a central band of six reference-count deciles (10-46 references, accounting for approximately 58% of the corpus), reciprocating up to 17% more. The two groups converged at 47-64 references (a 0.6% gap, non-interdisciplinary papers slightly ahead), and non-interdisciplinary papers reciprocated up to 28% more at the shortest and longest reference lists (3-9 and 65-5,000 references).

articles.title: Press freedom shapes the link between mainstream and social media use for news and climate change understanding: evidence from 30 countries
articles.authors: Laurent Cordonier; Didier Witkowski; Florian Cafiero
articles.abstract: A recent meta-analysis examining the relationship between individuals’ information behaviour and their views about climate change found that, on average, using social media and other user-generated online sources was more strongly associated with science-consistent climate beliefs than using mainstream media. The present study, however, investigates whether these associations vary across countries depending on the level of press freedom, as mainstream journalism is better able to foreground scientific expertise and challenge misleading climate claims when operating freely, whereas social media may provide a partial alternative to constrained domestic mainstream coverage. Accordingly, mainstream media use was hypothesised to be more positively associated with science-consistent climate beliefs and knowledge in countries with greater press freedom than in those with lower press freedom, while the opposite pattern was expected for social media use for news. The analysis draws on a survey of 23,500 respondents in 30 countries. Within each country, survey-weighted models estimated associations between mainstream and social media use for news and four outcomes: belief in the existence of climate change, belief in its anthropogenic nature, belief in its negative consequences, and climate change knowledge, adjusting for sociodemographic characteristics. Overall, mainstream media use was more often positively associated with science-consistent beliefs and knowledge than social media use. Cross-national analyses then tested whether these country-specific associations varied with press freedom, controlling for socioeconomic development. For each outcome, the association with mainstream media use was more positive in countries with greater press freedom than in those with lower press freedom, whereas the association with social media use for news showed the opposite cross-national pattern. These findings suggest that mainstream media generally contribute more to public understanding of climate change than social media, especially where press freedom is greater, while social media may play a partial compensatory role where domestic journalism is constrained.

articles.title: Researcher well-being as a leading indicator in research-funding governance: A system dynamics exploration of top-down versus bottom-up allocation
articles.authors: Tomoko Sakai; Satoshi Sano
articles.abstract: Governments face a recurring dilemma in dividing public research funding between top-down, competitive, mission-oriented programmes and bottom-up, investigator-led institutional grants. This research note presents an exploratory system dynamics model that endogenizes researcher motivation, conceived following self-determination theory as a slow-moving stock of psychological capital, within the feedback structure linking funding allocation, research outputs, and societal returns. Simulation experiments across three policy scenarios reveal a consistent time-asymmetric pattern. First, accelerating the shift toward competitive funding produces an earlier but lower peak in societal returns, followed by sustained decline. Second, shifting toward bottom-up funding restores motivation but opens a transition valley in returns whose depth grows with transition speed. Third, delayed corrective reallocation exhibits hysteresis: once motivation is depleted, even aggressive reallocation requires roughly two decades before returns recover. One-at-a-time sensitivity analysis indicates that these qualitative patterns persist across the tested parameter ranges, while the level of long-run returns proves highly sensitive to the weight placed on discretionary research time, around which the baseline system undergoes a regime shift. The model implies that researcher well-being functions as a leading indicator of research-system health, preceding declines in publication-based lagging indicators. We derive three testable propositions and outline an agenda for empirical calibration, beginning with a national baseline survey of researchers being launched in Japan. For funding governance, the results imply that monitoring leading indicators and pacing allocation transitions matter as much as choosing the allocation ratio itself.

articles.title: Provisioning for human needs at low resource use: institutional lessons from Cuba, Costa Rica and Ecuador
articles.authors: Chirag Dhara; Gustav Cederlöf; Viviana Cordero; Carolina Mauri; Tannya Pico; Soumyajit Bhar
articles.abstract: In the pursuit of sustainable development, Global South countries face the challenge of advancing wellbeing without breaching environmental limits. A central question for development policy is what institutional and policy configurations can deliver high levels of human need satisfaction at low ecological cost.
