articles_hidden.title: No King, and Other Matters—America’s Perspectives in Mid-2026 on Democracy, Authoritarianism, and Election-Related Violence:  Findings from a Nationally Representative Survey
articles_hidden.authors: Garen J. Wintemute; Bradley Velasquez; Sonia Robinson; Krista Neumann; Shaina Sta Cruz; Aaron Shev; Daniel Joseph Tancredi; Elizabeth A. Tomsich; Mona A. Wright; Veronica Pear
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Political violence and the rise of authoritarianism are emerging threats to the nation’s health, stability, and future as a representative democracy. To inform and facilitate prevention efforts, we present new and updated findings on the public’s views on authoritarianism and its support for and willingness to engage in election-related and pro- or anti-government violence. 

Methods: Findings are from Wave 5, conducted May 15-June 15, 2026, of a nationally representative annual longitudinal survey of adult members of the Ipsos KnowledgePanel that was initiated in 2022. Findings are for the cohort as a whole and for subgroups defined by political party/Make America Great Again (MAGA) movement affiliation. Year-to-year change for items included in 2025 and 2026 is estimated using mean change scores. Cross-sectional findings for 2026 are presented as weighted prevalences and item scores.

Results: The completion rate was 90.7%; there were 7,552 respondents. Nearly 90% of respondents continued to consider it very or extremely important that the US remain a democracy (change 0.01, 95% CI -0.00, 0.03). Agreement with expressions of authoritarianism was much less common; it decreased for the statement, “having a strong leader for America is more important than having a democracy” (change -0.04, 95% CI -0.07, -0.02) and others. In 2026, 2.1% (95% CI 1.6%, 2.7%) of respondents agreed strongly or very strongly that President Trump should be made king, but nearly half (47.7%, 95% CI 46.2%, 49.2%) agreed strongly or very strongly that he should be impeached and removed from office. 

There was little agreement with 5 actions the federal government might take in 2026 that employed violence to enforce its policies or suppress its critics in the US; the prevalence of strong or very strong agreement ranged between 4.4% and 9.6%. Across 12 items, there was very little agreement with actions—including violence—the federal government might take to subvert elections; strong or very strong agreement ranged between 2% and 4%. Willingness to commit violence was rare. For example, only 1.6% (95% CI 1.2%, 2.1%) were very or completely willing to use violence “to make sure that President Trump remains in office after his term ends.” Decreases from 2025 to 2026 in support for expressions of authoritarianism and for government-initiated violence were common across the spectrum of party/MAGA movement affiliations.

Conclusions: With national elections a few months away, Americans remained strongly supportive of democracy, did not endorse authoritarianism, and rejected the use of force by the current federal government to enforce its policies or subvert elections. They were deeply unwilling to engage in violence. These hopeful findings can inform and guide efforts to preserve democracy and prevent political violence.

articles_hidden.title: What the Balkan Barometer Can and Cannot Rank: A Measurement Audit of the Western Balkans' Flagship Survey
articles_hidden.authors: Milos Kankaras
articles_hidden.abstract: The Balkan Barometer, annual since 2015 with roughly 1,000 face-to-face interviews in each of six Western Balkan economies, is cited across the region as what its citizens think. We evaluate it as a measuring instrument from the Regional Cooperation Council's own released microdata for 2023 to 2025, within a total survey error frame. The published percentages reproduce from the microdata (440 of 444 cells within one point). Of the fifteen pairwise economy differences on each of thirty 2025 headline items, 71 percent are resolvable at a design effect of 2.0, but only 40 percent of adjacent-rank pairs are: six points is the least difference at which two economies of 1,000 can be told apart. The WB6 figure is an unweighted mean of six economies whose populations differ tenfold; under population weights it moves by 6 to 12 points on the most-quoted items, including EU membership (64 versus 58 percent in 2025). Of twenty-three headline series present in all three editions, four are comparable throughout; between 2024 and 2025 the changed series moved by 14 points on average against 6 for the stable ones. The 2025 institutional battery is scalar invariant once two cells are freed, police in Kosovo* and courts in North Macedonia; with them freed, Kosovo*'s raw-score lead disappears and the top three economies cannot be separated. The two published editions score 16 of 32 on a documentation checklist built from what the ESS, the Eurobarometer and the AAPOR Transparency Initiative publish routinely; precision, comparability and limitations score zero. We report two database errors and a file anomaly for correction, and close with the four things a technical report would need to contain.

articles_hidden.title: Your AI Knows Your Story. Should It Die With You?
articles_hidden.authors: Alexander Seifert
articles_hidden.abstract: Personal conversations with AI assistants increasingly contain memories, reflections, and records of changing judgment that may outlive their users. This commentary argues that selected exchanges could form a digital legacy: not a posthumous replica, but a personal testimony curated while the person is still able to correct it. Such legacies may be especially meaningful for people who wish to pass on their experience beyond their immediate family. Their creation, however, requires explicit consent, designated recipients, durable access, and a clear separation between the user's own words, the system's contributions, and any interpretations generated later. Whether such archives transmit wisdom or support bereavement remains an open question.

articles_hidden.title: Still Secularizing: Cohort Replacement, Rebound, Overreporting, and Gender Convergence in a Pooled Analysis of Eight National Surveys
articles_hidden.authors: David Eagle; Joshua Gaghan
articles_hidden.abstract: Recent reports claim young men in the United States are becoming more religious. This would signal an end to the longstanding pattern of cohort-driven declines in religiosity. Pooling young-adult trends within eight national surveys measuring affiliation, attendance, salience, prayer, and biblical literalism, we find no measure shows a credible increase among young men, and the youngest cohort is no more religious than its predecessor was at the same age. The gender gap is narrowing because women are secularizing faster, not because men are returning, which likely reflects gender-based ideological realignment. Religiosity has rebounded from its pandemic trough, but not credibly past pre-pandemic levels, and the gap between self-reported attendance and time-use diaries has widened. Intense religious identity is also declining across cohorts. Variability between surveys, a post-pandemic rebound, and growing measurement drift are all confounding patterns of religious change. Cutting through the noise, cohort replacement continues to organize American religion.

articles_hidden.title: Daily Dynamics of Urban Racial Segregation in the United States
articles_hidden.authors: Cody Arlie Reed
articles_hidden.abstract: This study examines racial segregation changes across the day and week to assess three perspectives in urban sociology: social isolation, compelled mobility, and cosmopolitanism. I link mobile phone tracking data collected on 18 days in January 2020 to 2020 Census data on the racial composition of estimated home tracts. Using the Theil multigroup segregation index, I estimate hourly racial segregation in 18 large U.S. commuting zones. Racial segregation is highest overnight, declines during weekday work hours, and is generally higher on weekends than weekdays. These patterns are most consistent with the compelled mobility perspective, under which lower racial segregation is expected when residents travel beyond their neighborhoods to access employment and other resources. Relatively high weekend racial segregation offers only weak support for social isolation. Friday and Saturday nights and the following early mornings have lower racial segregation than Wednesday at the same hours, offering clearer partial support for cosmopolitanism. Although the data do not identify why people travel, they show that the clearest declines in racial segregation coincide with the workday. Measuring racial segregation across hours and days thus helps distinguish theoretical accounts of how racial segregation persists or diminishes beyond residential neighborhoods.

articles_hidden.title: Mind the Gap: Elite Preferences for Redistribution and How they Differ from the Mass Public
articles_hidden.authors: Mogens K. Justesen; Marko Klašnja; Sara B. Hobolt; Robert Klemmensen
articles_hidden.abstract:
Increasing inequality has raised concerns over the disproportionate influence of the rich on public policies. Central to such concerns is the assumption that elite policy preferences are unified and differ significantly from the general public. We theorize economic elites as fiscal constituencies, highlighting intra-elite differences in policy preferences based on elite sources of affluence and therefore fiscal claims they face from the state. 
Employing high-quality administrative and survey data, including conjoint experiments, from Denmark, we compare tax and spending preferences in the general population with the largest samples to date of the top 1% by income and wealth. While elites are more economically conservative, they are not uniformly anti-redistribution; the asset-rich are less conservative than the income-rich; and their preferences often differ over tax policy. These findings highlight elite group differences based on their relation to the fiscal structure of the state and offer new insights into the micro-foundations of unequal representation in advanced democracies.

articles_hidden.title: Ranking Data in Political Science
articles_hidden.authors: Yuki Atsusaka; Shubhangi Singh
articles_hidden.abstract: Across scientific disciplines, researchers have used ranking data to study people's comparative judgments, preferences, and decision-making over a range of items. While existing data-sharing infrastructures in statistics and machine learning, such as PrefLib, offer a rich collection of ranking datasets, including those related to politics, they are not necessarily designed specifically to support cumulative research in social science. In this work, we introduce the first large-scale database of political rankings based on various studies from leading political science journals. Our first release covers 52 datasets from 27 original studies published between 2005 and 2025. Our database demonstrates notable variation in substantive topics and forms of ranking data that go well beyond canonical examples of candidate evaluations and value orientations, enabling researchers to perform comparative analyses, replication, reanalysis, methodological evaluation, and new substantive research with real-world political rankings. Along with validating our database, we illustrate it by replicating key findings in four selected studies, including those of multiple identities in American politics, the representation of Muslims in India, factional leaning in the Syrian civil war, and legislative accountability for affordable health care.

articles_hidden.title: Causal Inference in the CLS Cohort Studies
articles_hidden.authors: Liam Wright; Georgia D Tomova; Martin Nejedly; George Ploubidis; Richard J. Silverwood
articles_hidden.abstract: Correlations between variables in cohort and other observational studies do not necessarily indicate causal effects and may instead reflect bias due to confounding, sample selection processes, or measurement issues. Thankfully, multiple statistical methods, frameworks, and research designs have been developed that – when used judiciously – can aid making causal inferences with observational data. This is especially the case with CLS’s cohorts, which have several properties (e.g., longitudinal assessment and rich and varied data collection) that that can make the assumptions of these methods more plausible or provide ample opportunities for each method’s use. In this guide, we provide an overview of the possibilities for causal inference in CLS’s cohorts. Specifically, we: (1) provide background on the problem of causal inference in observational data, (2) detail the attributes of CLS’s cohorts that can support causal inference, and (3) outline an extensive set of methods and research designs that – assumptions permitting – can be used to estimate causal effects in CLS’s cohort data, illustrating each with existing applications and highlighting opportunities for further work.

articles_hidden.title: An Atlas of Economic Activities in the UK: a fine-grained typology of economic activities from open, large-scale web archive data
articles_hidden.authors: Leonardo Castro Gonzalez; Emmanouil Tranos; Levi John Wolf; Rui Zhu; Emerald Dilworth
articles_hidden.abstract: We present the Atlas of Economic Activities in the UK, a granular and dynamic typology of economic activities. Built using large-scale web data from Common Crawl, the Atlas captures how UK businesses describe their economic activities, creates an activity typology and geolocates them at the postcode level. The Atlas provides a complementary source to established industrial classifications, which are static and insensitive to the evolution of economic activities. It is designed to support research and policy analysis requiring fine-grained information about economic activities over space and time. The Atlas is developed transparently using open tools and web archive data, so that it can be replicated and adapted to different research and policy contexts.

articles_hidden.title: Analysis of the Social System in Post-Capitalist Society
articles_hidden.authors: 周勇
articles_hidden.abstract: The ability to enhance productivity is pivotal in determining the success of a social system. Beyond scientific and technological advancements, productivity primarily hinges on workers' production enthusiasm and labor quality, the scale of production within each unit, and the pattern of resource allocation. Under given productive forces, the scale of production per unit is determined by the rate of exploitation imposed by owners upon laborers. As productive forces advance, new production models emerge. To boost productivity, the rate of exploitation diminishes, elevating the political and social standing of the populace, thereby giving rise to new social formations. Undifferentiated human labor constitutes the origin of goods value, while interest and capital gains represent the outcome of value distribution. Goods prices in the market are primarily determined by supply, with the labor value of goods serving as the equilibrium point of supply—thus constituting the market's equilibrium price. The labor theory of value can explain the Equity Risk Premium Puzzle. The higher the automation level of enterprises, the lower the value of goods, and in the long run, the lower the profits of enterprises. After the highly developed productive forces in capitalist society, the vast majority of industries will become low-profit public infrastructure services, making it difficult for private entities to continue operating. Public ownership will replace private ownership. The future social structure will be a “communist society” characterized by public ownership and distribution according to need as the mainstay, supplemented by private ownership and distribution according to work under a free-market economy. In the historical development toward communist society, there exists no so-called transitional stage of socialist society. In this communist society the state will persist, giving rise to a united human government where selfless dedication becomes the socially advocated moral standard. Under current productive forces, public ownership impedes both productive and economic development. Marxism is mistaken about the reasons and timing for the inevitable collapse of the capitalist system. Contemporary society faces issues such as welfare systems, nationalization, unified currencies, and China's economic and political structures.

articles_hidden.title: Assessing and identifying special protection needs among refugees in the EU: Overview and Synthesis of Evidence and Policy Recommendations
articles_hidden.authors: Niklas Nutsch; Maren Hintermeier; Andreas W. Gold; Clara Perplies; Nils Robson; Veronika Wiemker; Till Bärnighausen; Sven Rohleder; Kayvan Bozorgmehr
articles_hidden.abstract: The EU’s Reception Conditions Directive requests member states to identify special protection needs among asylum seekers and refugees, but assessment practices remain inconsistently implemented across Europe. We systemically searched scientific and grey literature and synthesised evidence of 81 eligible documents to identify recommendations for assessing special protection needs and their implications for policy and practice. The evidence indicates that vulnerability, which may necessitate special protection, is multidimensional, intersectional, and dynamic. This requires early, continuous, and multimethod assessment rather than one-off screening. Effective assessment systems combine standardised procedures with individualised assessment, referral pathways, and multidisciplinary collaboration. We identified 51 screening tools, however, no single tool was universally accepted and used, highlighting that implementation depends less on individual tools than on coordinated, person-centred systems supported by rights-based documentation, informed consent, and secure information sharing. These findings provide evidence-informed directions for strengthening assessment of special protection needs systems across the EU.

articles_hidden.title: Living Arrangements, Going Outdoors, and Well-Being Among Older Persons: Examining Their Associations in a Swedish Population
articles_hidden.authors: Jeanette Melin; Marie-Louise Möllerberg; Marit Preuter; Kristofer Årestedt
articles_hidden.abstract:
Aim: This study examined associations between living arrangement, frequency of going outdoors, and well-being among older persons in Sweden, with particular attention to their interaction.
Methods: Community-dwelling older persons (n = 1,727) across nine Swedish municipalities participated in a cross-sectional survey. Well-being was assessed using the Older Persons’ Well-being Scale (OPWELLS). Linear regression models examined associations and interactions.
Results: Living alone was associated with lower well-being compared to cohabiting, whereas going outdoors more frequently was associated with higher well-being. The association between living arrangement and well-being differed by outdoor frequency.
Conclusions: Frequency of going outdoors was strongly associated with well-being irrespective of living arrangement. However, the association between living alone and well-being varied with outdoor frequency. Thus, living alone should not be considered an isolated indicator of lower well-being in older age and highlights the importance of considering living arrangements within the broader context of older persons’ everyday lives.

articles_hidden.title: An Assessment of the Vanderbilt-Washington University Report on Sociology
articles_hidden.authors: Julian Go
articles_hidden.abstract: The Sociology portion of the Vanderbilt-Washington University Report (VWUR) claims to have studied the discipline of sociology and asserts that sociology’s search for truth has been compromised by what the author calls “politicization.” I find that the VWUR’s claims are unsubstantiated and based upon fundamental errors. The problem is not lack of data but rather that the author, Dr. Ashley Rubin, misunderstands and misrepresents the data she does have while failing to check her own biases. She mistakenly reads politicization into everything she sees, reaffirming a thesis she had already held before her supposedly impartial study without taking the appropriate steps to suspend her bias. The VWUR violates the very social scientific standards that it purports to defend while distracting us from other problems facing social science.

articles_hidden.title: ‘Intersectionality in the Mind’: Applying an Intersectional Lens to the Study of Lay Perceptions of Inequality
articles_hidden.authors: Margherita Cusmano
articles_hidden.abstract: Research on lay perceptions of inequality has typically examined economic, gender, and racial inequalities separately and treated social positions additively. Using migrants as a case study, this study employs an intersectional lens to investigate perceptions of inequality. Drawing on interviews and group discussions with 47 participants, the analysis shows, first, that individuals framed different inequalities as interdependent, showcasing what I term ‘intersectionality in the mind’. Second, their intersectional social positions informed how they understood broader patterns of inequality. These findings demonstrate the value of intersectional approaches in analysing the complexity of lay perceptions of inequality. This study points toward methodological and conceptual developments that can better capture both how people cognitively link inequalities and how intersecting social positions inform these perceptions.

articles_hidden.title: What the World Studies, Invents and Reports About Urban Heat
articles_hidden.authors: Narendra Kumar
articles_hidden.abstract: We assemble 20,422 scholarly papers on urban heat islands (1990–2025), read the 17,101 that carry an abstract sentence by sentence, and join them to 96,726 news articles (2021–2025), 4,123 patent families, 14,576 recorded heat incidents, registers of companies, funding rounds and government funding events, and the annual accounts of Indian companies. Eight results stand out. (1) The field grew about 9 times faster than the scholarly literature as a whole, and in 2015–2019 titles naming "extreme heat" overtook those naming "heat island". (2) Of 2,409 papers that attribute urban heat to a cause, 48% name urbanisation and land-use change; attribution to anthropogenic heat fell from 18.4% to 7.7%. (3) Research and news describe different problems: at equal text length, 28% of research openings raise mitigation against 1.6% of news leads, while 22% of news leads are forecasts or warnings against 1.4% of research. (4) They also describe different places: China accounts for 31% of the research and 2.3% of English-language coverage, and Delhi receives 7.4 times the coverage its research share would predict. (5) Invention has outrun science: patent families for cool and permeable pavements grew 12-fold in a decade against 2.4-fold for the research on them. (6) Across 194 studies the median reported cooling from urban trees is 2.0 °C (air temperature 2.0 °C, surface temperature 2.9 °C). (7) Between 2021–22 and 2024–25 news coverage moved from the hazard to the people exposed: workers, schools, the elderly and hospital patients each rose 1.4- to 2.4-fold as a share of heat articles while wildfire and drought fell by about half and climate change — raised in about one article in ten — fell by a quarter. (8) The market record is thin: 140 of 5.05 million companies state a heat or cooling purpose, and recorded capital is $2.7 billion of cooling-infrastructure finance against $48 million of venture funding; larger Indian cooling companies grew revenue 25% a year over three years against 16% for Indian companies generally. Every cause category extracted from the research was tested against an independent second reader; three failed, and no result reported here rests on them.

articles_hidden.title: A POLÍTICA DE EXPANSÃO ECONÔMICA SIMBIÓTICA PULSANTE DOS ESTADOS UNIDOS: MECANISMOS DE INFLUÊNCIA GLOBAL E EXPLORAÇÃO DE RECURSOS ESTRANGEIROS
articles_hidden.authors: Juliano Paniago de Alcântara
articles_hidden.abstract: O estudo propõe o modelo da “Política de Expansão Econômica Simbiótica Pulsante” para descrever a projeção de poder dos Estados Unidos como sequência recorrente de coerção, reestruturação e extração, e o submete a séries temporais, a um painel país×ano e a quatro estudos de caso (Iraque, América Latina, Ucrânia e Golfo Pérsico). Na série 2000–2024, a associação entre gastos militares e renda de investimento direto no exterior é, no longo prazo, absorvida pelo ciclo de renda mundial; em primeira diferença, a precedência dos gastos militares tem o sinal previsto e significância marginal. Em painel país×ano com cerca de oito mil observações, a presença militar americana associa-se a maior comércio e a maior participação americana nas importações do hospedeiro, sem precedência estabelecida. No Golfo, o acesso americano ao mercado iraniano colapsa após a ruptura de 1979 e as sanções subsequentes. Formaliza-se a “pulsação” como construto temporal falseável, distinto do smart power.

articles_hidden.title: Does Carbon Pricing Outperform Command-and-Control Regulation? Firm-Level Evidence from Korea’s Dual Regulatory Framework
articles_hidden.authors: Pyung Kim
articles_hidden.abstract: This study exploits South Korea’s unique dual-policy, in which an emissions trading scheme (ETS) and a command-and-control program (Target Management System, TMS) operate in parallel, to compare carbon pricing with prescriptive regulation at the firm level. Using a difference-in-differences design on firm-level panel data from 2011 to 2022, I find that ETS-regulated firms reduced energy use by 5.8% to 8.8% and carbon emissions by 7.3% to 8.5% relative to TMS firms, while effects on carbon intensity were not robust. These reductions were strongest in the more market-oriented phases of the ETS, which featured allowance auctioning and benchmark-based allocation, pointing to the importance of incentive-based policy design.

articles_hidden.title: Financial Sector Stability and Credit Growth in Nepal:  A Case Study
articles_hidden.authors: Nirmal Gurung
articles_hidden.abstract: Nepal’s financial system has undergone waves of credit booms, especially in the pre- and post-COVID-19 pandemic periods, which raises questions about the health of the banking sector. This paper examines the association between credit growth and banking sector health using secondary data from Nepal Rastra Bank and the International Monetary Fund. The World Bank for fiscal years 2016/17-2023/24. It is found that private sector credit grew at nearly 29 percent in 2016/17 and more than 27 percent in 2020/21, which far exceeded the overall economy’s growth rates. Credit boomed due to large remittance inflows, low real interest rates, and rapid expansion of bank outlets and digital products. Heavy lending to real estate, housing, construction, and import sectors. Consequently, the quality of banks’ assets declined as credit growth slowed down sharply in 2021/22. The non-performing loan ratio, which averaged between 1.2 and 1.8 percent during the boom years, rose to about 2.6 percent in 2022/23 and 3.7 percent in 2023/24. The capital adequacy ratio of banks dipped from 14.5 percent in 2016/17 to 12.8 percent in 2023/24. The study concludes that rapid credit growth, albeit beneficial for a short time, may pose significant financial stability risks if the lending environment worsens and credit becomes concentrated in a few sectors. The paper recommends enhanced risk-based supervision, countercyclical capital buffers, diversification of credit to productive sectors, improved governance, and enhanced capital markets to complement bank lending

articles_hidden.title: Social Ecology and Diagnostic Visibility: A Cross-National Analysis of Autism Spectrum Disorder Prevalence in 55 Countries
articles_hidden.authors: Isha Sarah Snow
articles_hidden.abstract: Cross-national variation in autism spectrum disorder (ASD) prevalence is commonly attributed to differences in diagnostic infrastructure and case ascertainment. We tested whether cultural individualism predicts this variation independently of detection capacity, and whether the result is robust to known limitations of Hofstede's widely used but methodologically dated Individualism Index (IDV). Using 55 countries (GBD 2019 ASD prevalence, World Bank GDP, an author-constructed diagnostic infrastructure index, Hofstede's IDV, and a recently validated individualism-collectivism index built from nationally representative survey data; Akaliyski et al., 2025), we found the raw individualism-ASD correlation is robust to measurement choice (Hofstede: r = 0.702; validated index: r = 0.624; both p < .001, n = 47 non-screening countries with both measures available). However, its apparent independence from detection capacity is not robust: partial correlations controlling for GDP and diagnostic infrastructure remain significant with Hofstede's IDV (partial r = 0.30-0.39) but collapse to non-significance with the validated index (partial r = -0.14 to 0.09, ns), because the validated index correlates far more strongly with diagnostic infrastructure (r = 0.919) than Hofstede's IDV does (r = 0.818). The four mandatory-screening countries (Japan, South Korea, Singapore, Taiwan) exceed their IDV-predicted prevalence under both measures, though less dramatically using the validated index (1.57x vs. 2.84x), indicating measurement error in Hofstede's scores inflated the original screening-policy estimate. These findings show the bivariate cultural-prevalence association is genuine, but caution against treating it as evidence independent of detection capacity without testing robustness to cultural measurement choice.

articles_hidden.title: Theravada Buddhism in Contemporary China and Its Followers
articles_hidden.authors: Ampere A. Tseng
articles_hidden.abstract:
This paper studies the influence of Theravada Buddhism in contemporary China, with a 
focus on the seven ethnic minorities that share a considerable presence of Theravada Buddhism. 
It also considers the populations of Theravada Buddhists among the seven ethnic minorities, as 
well as from another 49 official-recognized ethnicities. It discovers that the Theravada Buddhist 
population increases from 1.3868 million in 2010 to 1.4519 million in 2018 and is expected to 
grow to 1.4786 million by 2027. The present study finds that the Dai ethnicity is not only 
essential for spreading Theravada Buddhism to other ethnicities but it also has the largest 
Theravada Buddhist ethnicity in China, which represents more than 72% of the total Theravada 
Buddhist population. Finally, it discloses that the seven ethnicities each have their own forms of 
folk religions with their faith showing a mix of folk religion with Theravada Buddhism.

articles_hidden.title: The Dai People and Their Relationship with Theravada Buddhists in Yunnan: A Profile and Population Analysis
articles_hidden.authors: Ampere A. Tseng
articles_hidden.abstract: Focusing on the Dai people of Yunnan, China, this study explores their demographics and Theravada Buddhist practices, examining their influence on neighboring ethnicities. It investigates how Theravada Buddhist temples serve as cornerstones of cultural identity and community cohesion, offering novel insights into the trajectory of Theravada Buddhism within Dai communities. The study employs two innovative approaches to estimate the Theravada Buddhist population in Yunnan and China. Firstly, it leverages data from the Pew Foundation survey conducted in neighboring countries. Secondly, it analyzes temple density in Xishuangbanna and Dehong. Both approaches converge on a figure of roughly 1.1 million Theravada Buddhists residing in Yunnan in 2016. Furthermore, the study estimates the total Theravada Buddhist population in Mainland China to be approximately 1.14 million in 2015 and 1.16 million in 2020. Significantly, the research reveals that the dominance of the Dai people within Theravada Buddhist communities comprised 87.7% of Theravada Buddhists in Yunnan. These findings shed light on the interplay among religious affiliation, temple density, and demographic profile, providing the religious landscape in Dai- dominated regions.

articles_hidden.title: Cultural Cognitive Scaffolding
articles_hidden.authors: Helena Miton
articles_hidden.abstract: In many domains, human life has undergone dramatic changes—globalized exchanges, complex technological systems, large societies—that would both require and result from rapid cognitive change. In this work, I introduce the Cultural Cognitive Scaffolding Hypothesis, which posits that (1) human cognition is uniquely culturally evolvable because our cognitive processes rely on environmental resources that are largely culturally evolvable, and, as a consequence, (2) it is these specific cultural innovations, called cultural cognitive scaffolds (CCS), that are responsible for much of the rapid, recent changes in human cognition. Importantly, to achieve this effect, these cultural innovations must balance cognitive impact and cultural success. The historical expansion of exchange networks offers an ideal case to illustrate how diverse cultural innovations helped manage the high uncertainty associated with exchanges across larger physical and cultural distances, and a window into how cultural success can be achieved for different cultural innovations. Finally, this framework has important implications for our understanding of the uniquely open-ended character of human culture.

articles_hidden.title: Evidence and Overreach in the Rubin and Commission Reports
articles_hidden.authors: Geoffrey T Wodtke
articles_hidden.abstract: The report on “The Status of Scholarly Standards in Sociology,” authored by Dr. Ashley Rubin, claims that sociology has been “compromised” by “politicization.” In particular, it claims that “institutionalized political commitments now influence the field’s norms, priorities, and evaluation of scholarship” (pg. 5) to such an extent that “we can no longer call sociology, as a field, a data-driven social science of society” (pg. 107). I agree that some of the phenomena Rubin identifies warrant concern and deserve serious consideration and reflection. However, my assessment of the report concludes that its broad diagnosis far outruns the proffered evidence.

articles_hidden.title: Bridging the Four Exits: Using Free Tools to Empower Senior High School Students
articles_hidden.authors: Kian Anthony R. Dait
articles_hidden.abstract: Senior High School (SHS) in the Philippines was designed to prepare students for four possible exits: Higher Education, Employment, Entrepreneurship, and Middle-Level Skills Development. In practice, however, the college pathway remains more familiar to many students than the other options. This essay examines how existing free and publicly available learning resources can help make the four exits more practical and understandable for students. It considers resources such as the TESDA Online Program, open educational platforms, digital project portfolios, youth programs, entrepreneurship initiatives, and international learning opportunities. The discussion also draws attention to the limits of these resources. Free online learning does not automatically mean equal access, since students still need devices, internet connectivity, time, and guidance. The essay therefore proposes a connected approach in which students first identify a possible direction, determine the skills they need, choose relevant learning resources, apply what they learn, and document appropriate evidence of their work. Schools, teachers, guidance counselors, and local communities can support this process by helping students navigate existing opportunities rather than creating another separate system. The goal is not to encourage students to collect certificates, but to help them make informed choices and develop evidence that supports their next step after SHS.

articles_hidden.title: Explaining historical persistence in Germany's electoral geography across 130 years: a cleavage-perspective on continuity in spatial patterns of party support
articles_hidden.authors: Leon Gawenda
articles_hidden.abstract: This article studies the long-run persistence of electoral geographies. Drawing on cleavage theory, I argue that spatial patterns of party support persist where cleavages remain politically salient and the social groups they mobilise stay in place. I evidence this argument for Germany, combining electoral and census data from the German Empire (1890–1912) and reunified Germany (2002–2021) at the municipality, county and electoral-district level. The spatial analyses reveal substantial continuity in the electoral geographies of the mainstream left and right. The analysis traces both to one source, the persistent spatial distribution of Catholics. Christian democrats continued historical strongholds of the Center Party where Catholics stayed concentrated, while the SPD persists as its mirror image in the non-Catholic space. Persistence therefore rests on the stability of the religious geography and cleavage, not on the class cleavage and the economic geography, which has changed markedly. The findings position cleavage-based persistence as a complement to cultural-transmission accounts of historical legacies, locating continuity in the ongoing mobilisation of stable social groups rather than in transmitted attitudes alone.

articles_hidden.title: When the Children’s Rights Normative Culture (CRNC) is Full of Holes: The Child’s Right to Mental Health in Post-Conflict Sool and Sanaag
articles_hidden.authors: Guleid Ahmed Jama; Marieke Janne Hopman
articles_hidden.abstract: This paper aims to understand the situation of children’s mental health rights in Sool and Sanaag. We apply the Children’s Rights Normative Culture (CRNC) model (Hopman et al. 2026) to a dataset of 85 research conversation conducted between May and November 2025 (40 children, 45 adults) in the two cities. A key finding from the research is that children’s mental health is not recognised as a distinct rights issue within the socio-legal orders applicable in the research area. Moreover, there is no clearly articulated or enforceable socio-legal obligation (from any socio-legal order) concerning the protection of children’s mental health. Nor do the socio-legal norms seem to establish specific remedial measures for children experiencing mental health difficulties. The language of rights is largely absent from people’s understanding of children’s mental health. Across clan, community, religious, and state normative orders, children are mainly seen through the family framework. The paper suggest that 1) children’s mental health should be seen as a children’s rights, 2) families, particularly mothers, and the community, should be engaged as key entry point for societal change, 3) space should be created for children where they can safely share their experiences and views at all levels, including the family, schools, community and post-conflict peacebuilding initiatives.
